We compare two main families of rebalancing policy once their rules are public: a reactive policy (R) that sends idle drivers to cover requests just lost, and an anticipatory policy (A) that plans moves on a demand forecast. Each driver is an LLM agent maximizing its own net income, given no rules (N) or the rules at the directive's level of detail (L). We test two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, which understand the rules equally well, in a three-zone model and in Manhattan. With the rules disclosed, drivers follow the platform more closely: in Manhattan, the share of relocation offers they decline falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Yet the effects differ by policy. For the platform, disclosure costs R 3.7% of its profit in Manhattan, as R now pays for moves drivers used to make for free, while A's profit is unchanged; the two policies, which tie on profit under full compliance, end 6.1% apart. For drivers, disclosure raises income in the small model under both policies and LLMs; for users, it raises the service rate there by 10 to 18 percentage points. In

e27d16bf49c87763b47291ce.title_original: A Spectral Renormalization-Group View of Learning
e27d16bf49c87763b47291ce.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00422v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study how the layers in deep neural networks (NNs) converge, using Wilsonian Renormalization-Group (RG) ideas to organize the spectral picture. During training, these layers often develop heavy-tailed power-law (PL) spectra, and the strongest checkpoints often appear near the PL exponent $\alpha\approx 2$. This pattern raises a simple question: why should this value mark a well-trained layer? The answer is both statistical and physical. Our statistical hypothesis is that $\alpha=2$ marks the boundary between stable if not optimal learning and overfitting via non-self-averaging. The physical answer is that the same value makes the spectral energy gain scale evenly across logarithmic spectral scales, which is the proposed Wilsonian marginal condition. We then apply the ERG trace-log condition, the proposed SETOL theory, which we justify by taking volume-preserving, scale-invariant transformations to remove arbitrary layer scale along the proposed RG flow. The resulting spectral RG flow connects the HTSR and SETOL theories to optimizers such as Muon, and motivates a new optimizer extension, WW-PGD. Together, these results point toward a spectral Renormalization-Group view of learning, in which NNs may approach shared spectral structure in the settings studied here.

55f98568c4b8a1ef541a82fd.title_original: CuriousTogether: Implications of Curiosity and Cultural Grounding in Multi-Agent LLM Interactions
55f98568c4b8a1ef541a82fd.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01301v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, exhibiting emergent collective behaviors, yet the role of curiosity as a driver of such dynamics remains understudied. We introduce CuriousTogether, a framework evaluating curiosity-driven multi-agent LLM interactions across three complementary dimensions: novelty-seeking, epistemic and social curiosity. Across eight tasks spanning reasoning, creative generation, and social bias mitigation, curiosity-guided multi-agent settings yield improvements over non-curious ones on seven out of eight tasks, with gains of up to 20.6% in story generation (semantic diversity) and a 14.9 pp reduction in stereotype rates. Furthermore, country-conditioned cultural grounding show benefits for story generation and social tasks, but can hurt precision-oriented reasoning. Finally, we show that inference-time multi-agent curiosity-based approach offers favorable quality-token trade-offs, compared with single-agent baselines. Together, these findings support curiosity-guided interaction as a practical mechanism for improving multi-agent collaboration, with downstream benefits for reasoning, creative, and societal tasks.

0ff52bf89f1c30910faaca27.title_original: Iterative Gumbel Planning for Continuous Control
0ff52bf89f1c30910faaca27.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02236v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for r

2e6261a6be641a08c8b989dd.title_original: Maswao: An automatically collected, prepared, and benchmarked dataset for South African Sign Language
2e6261a6be641a08c8b989dd.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02903v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advancements in sign language processing can be attributed to developments in both large-scale dataset collection and algorithmic complexity in areas such as pose estimation techniques, signal processing through Transformer models, and model optimization. However, only a handful of sign languages, such as the American, British, and German, from over 200 globally recognized sign languages, reap the benefits of such advancements, while the rest lag behind. In this study, we aim to address this technological disparity by proposing a framework for the automatic collection and preparation of sign language datasets, with very minimal human-labour intervention, using the South African Sign Language (SASL) as a testbed. Specifically, we automatically collect SASL video content using public resources such as news broadcasts. Additionally, we convert their accompanying audio streams into text using available Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tools. Furthermore, we crop the sign language area in the videos and use gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion to determine end-of-sentence points within long videos to create our weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpora -- the Maswao (Signs) dataset. Finally, we benchmark the weakly aligned dataset on the task of Sign-to-text Translation using Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformer models to compare their individual intricacies. Our results show that Transformer models

a550cb200538a4b3c9c2b499.title_original: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
a550cb200538a4b3c9c2b499.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05278v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy$\unicode{x2014}$answers that are correct and in the target language$\unicode{x2014}$slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions

538c12057e60b2fe54d683f4.title_original: AutoPYara: Next-Gen YARA Rule Generator for Malware Family Clustering
538c12057e60b2fe54d683f4.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Millions of malware variants threaten users daily, such that clustering these samples is key for fast incident response. AutoYara is the current state-of-the-art for automatic YARA rule generation, but the task remains challenging on realistic datasets, where intra-family diversity and noisy clustering can degrade rule quality. We present AutoPYara, a solution armored with: (1) precise cluster centroid selection based on similarity hashing, and (2) an improved heuristic for estimating subclusters within a malware family using historical VirusTotal data. We implement AutoPYara as an open-source Python package (pip install autopyara) to support reproducibility and practical use. We show that AutoPYara, (1) increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points; (2) reduces variance by 7.1 percentage points, comparing the average variance AutoPYara exhibits to that of AutoYara; and (3) improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10%. AutoPYara produces robust and effective YARA rules than prior automatic approaches in practical settings.

0ac1a0adf6cef34add163270.title_original: I Don't Care How You Hide It, I Care What You Do: Runtime Detection of Malicious ML Models
0ac1a0adf6cef34add163270.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pre-trained machine learning (ML) models shared through public platforms can be weaponized to execute malicious payloads during loading or inference. Existing scanners prove inadequate for detecting malicious models as they rely on static analysis and function denylists, support limited serialization formats, and miss attacks that replace denylisted functions with equivalent alternatives, exploit unsupported loading paths, or abuse legitimate framework APIs. To address this problem, we present ModelShield, the first runtime behavioral detection system for malicious ML models that attributes observed system-level behavior to specific model operations. It combines application-level instrumentation of ML framework APIs with eBPF-based syscall tracing, tracking model behavior across spawned threads and processes to separate model-triggered activity from environment noise. Attributed syscall sequences are classified using 195 detection patterns mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. We implemented ModelShield to support 17 ML frameworks and 36 formats. On an independent dataset, it is the only evaluated tool to achieve zero false positives, with false negatives limited to payloads that produce no malicious runtime behavior. It detected all 29 published evasion variants spanning function substitution, loading-path obfuscation, and TensorFlow API abuse, where no existing scanner achieved complete coverage. Across 145,000 models scanned fro
0ac1a0adf6cef34add163270.title_ko: AI 모델의 악성 행위 탐지를 위한 런타임 행동 분석 시스템 'ModelShield'
0ac1a0adf6cef34add163270.summary_ko: 공개 플랫폼의 사전 학습된 AI 모델이 로딩 및 추론 과정에서 악성 코드를 실행하는 위협에 대응하기 위해 'ModelShield'가 개발되었다. 이 시스템은 ML 프레임워크 API와 시스템 호출을 추적하여 MITRE ATT&CK 기법 기반으로 모델의 악성 행동을 실시간 탐지한다. 기존 스캐너 대비 높은 탐지 성능과 낮은 오탐률을 입증했으며, Hugging Face 등에서 실제 악성 모델을 성공적으로 포착했다.

90ba24cb50e232df92585563.title_original: Gain-Dependent Entropy Characterization of a Zener Avalanche Noise TRNG via Dual NIST Standards: Toward Low-Cost Hardware Entropy for ICS Deployments
90ba24cb50e232df92585563.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: True random number generators based on Zener avalanche noise offer a low-cost entropy source for industrial control system and IoT edge devices, yet the relationship between amplifier gain, coupling capacitance, and entropy quality remains uncharacterized under current NIST standards. This paper presents a comprehensive entropy assessment of an op-amp-based Zener avalanche noise generator across five gain configurations and two coupling capacitor values, evaluated against the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite and the SP~800-90B entropy source assessment using 1.44 billion raw bits per configuration. We identify a three-phase autocorrelation structure, attributed to comparator saturation-recovery dynamics, consistent across all gain settings. A direct-current substitution experiment, replacing the Zener diode with a stable voltage source at the same bias point, reduces switching activity by approximately 97%, confirming that Zener avalanche noise, rather than amplifier self-excitation, is the necessary entropy source. The coupling capacitor is further shown to govern comparator overdrive and entropy quality independent of this source mechanism, with the smaller capacitance improving entropy, throughput, and bias. The combined results identify an optimal gain configuration achieving a perfect statistical test score, NIST-compliant min-entropy, and peak entropy throughput at a bill-of-materials cost under five dollars, offering

83877b142fef2dfdcb4c10b8.title_original: Jev as an LLM Safety Guardrail: An Empirical Study of Input Filtering, Selective Output Review, and Over-Refusal
83877b142fef2dfdcb4c10b8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: External safety filters can prevent unsafe requests from reaching a large language model (LLM), but may also reject legitimate queries. We present an end-to-end empirical evaluation of Jev, a probabilistic decision model, as a safety guardrail for a Qwen2.5-1.5B-based pipeline. Three configurations are compared on 970 benchmark prompts: an unfiltered LLM, Jev input filtering, and tiered Jev input filtering with selective output review. Across 720 prompts labeled harmful (520 AdvBench and 200 XSTest-unsafe), the fraction recorded as answered decreases from 527/720 (73.2%) without filtering to 17/720 (2.4%) with input filtering. On 250 XSTest-safe prompts, however, non-answer/refusal increases from 3/250 (1.2%) to 27/250 (10.8%). Tiered filtering yields 40/720 (5.6%) harmful-prompt answers and 10/250 (4.0%) benign-prompt refusals, with 79/970 (8.1%) of prompts requiring output review. Joint optimization of the tiered thresholds improves macro-F1 from 0.9351 to 0.9512, while reducing harmful-prompt answers and output-review frequency at the same benign-refusal rate. Matched-budget comparisons reveal modest additional gains over a retuned single gate on the evaluation data, although these gains are not consistently observed on a held-out split.

524b2a0cab13a70e56a0729a.title_original: NotaryMark: Multi-Bit Watermarking for Black-Box DatasetUsage Auditing in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
524b2a0cab13a70e56a0729a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) models increasingly require data, more publicly available yet licensed data is being harvested and used without authorization. Although several previous studies have proposed watermarking methods for dataset copyright auditing, their applicability to the text-to-image (T2I) setting remains notably limited. The core drawback is that watermarks embedded by existing techniques are often treated as noise and are gradually filtered out and attenuated during the latent noising-denoising process of diffusion model training. We propose NotaryMark, to our knowledge the first multi-bit watermarking method specifically designed for black-box auditing of T2I training dataset use. The core idea of NotaryMark is to align the watermark with the latent denoising of diffusion models, thereby overcoming the signal decay that plagues existing multi-bit methods during sampling. We evaluate NotaryMark across three datasets and three diffusion models spanning watermark capacities from 8 to 1024 bits. With a watermark capacity below 32 bits, it achieves a high average bit accuracy of 0.85-0.90. With a watermark capacity exceeding 32 bits, it maintains bit accuracy between 0.67 and 0.80, consistently outperforming existing multi-bit watermark methods whose bit accuracy is around 0.42-0.60. Furthermore, we design a voting-based aggregation scheme to boost the bit accuracy with a modest budget of 30 queries. Bui

4d5875dcc9b572c58732f269.title_original: Beyond a Single Commit: Anchor-Guided Reconstruction of Multi-Commit Patches
4d5875dcc9b572c58732f269.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability patch identification plays a critical role in software security by linking reported vulnerabilities and the corresponding fixes, enabling reliable vulnerability analysis, mitigation, and automated security tool development. As software systems evolve in complexity, vulnerability remediation has increasingly shifted from single-commit fixes to multi-commit fixing processes. Although many studies have been proposed to identify fixing commits associated with target vulnerabilities automatically, they often suffer from inaccurate semantic analysis or excessive workload for language models. These limitations reduce both the effectiveness and comprehensiveness of fixing commit identification. To improve patch identification, we propose an effective and comprehensive patch identification framework, HARPOON, which not only enhances the accuracy of identifying individual fixing commits, but also investigates dependencies among commits to achieve comprehensive commit recognition for target vulnerabilities. Experimental results show that HARPOON significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches. HARPOON successfully identified 895 vulnerability patches that were not previously maintained in public vulnerability databases. Among them, 663 are previously unrecorded fixes associated with 323 CRITICAL- or HIGH-severity vulnerabilities.

7d9550a2dc45d992bd6e436a.title_original: Authorization Drift in LLM Agents: Evaluating Boundary Compliance in Multi-Step Tool Use
7d9550a2dc45d992bd6e436a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns. Data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions, making the potential consequences of authorization drift more interpretable.

9ee35ae8aaea706f8aa44bc3.title_original: Federated Forensics: Jurisdictional constraints as a design driver for multi-agency federated learning
9ee35ae8aaea706f8aa44bc3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital forensic investigations increasingly cross borders, and law enforcement agencies need to build analytical models together without centralizing their data. Federated Learning (FL) keeps data local, yet neither FL nor its frameworks enforce the jurisdictional, governance, and accountability rules that multi-agency forensic work requires. This paper takes a design-first approach to that gap. First, we derive seven requirements that a federated learning system must meet in a forensic setting. Second, we propose Federated Forensics, a three-layer reference architecture whose middle layer, unlike in existing hierarchical FL designs, sits at a jurisdictional border and can use a model update locally while blocking it from crossing that border. Third, we build a prototype of the architecture and test it on a malware-family classification task. In a prototype evaluation, the policy gate blocked every restricted update at the border with zero violations, and restricted-class accuracy rose from 0% under today's compliant alternative to 93.0%, only 4.4 points below ignoring the restriction.

f377f2016da1bd9a60075795.title_original: Verification of Security Properties of Cryptographic Protocols
f377f2016da1bd9a60075795.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developing cryptographic protocols that are free from vulnerabilities is very challenging, as evidenced by numerous design flaws and implementation bugs in widely used protocols. Recent work has leveraged model checking to generate negative test cases, that is test cases that include the behavior of Dolev-Yao attacker. In this paper, we address the problem of analyzing execution traces produced by testing protocol implementations with such negative test cases. We propose a method for detecting violations of security properties by model-checking execution traces. Our approach employs a model checker based on DLTL, a Linear Temporal Logic with freeze operators, and supports automation of the testing process through pre- and post-processing steps. These steps, respectively, bridge the gap between different levels of abstraction and synthesize the results produced by the model checker.We present experimental results as a proof of concept for the feasibility of the proposed method.

645d2f5c5672d2c8997aafd7.title_original: Cutpurse: Decomposing Explanation-Guided Model Extraction on Tabular Data
645d2f5c5672d2c8997aafd7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explanation APIs are often treated as increasing model-extraction risk, but an end-to-end attack comparison cannot show whether an explanation reveals model-specific information or merely supplies a convenient next-query coordinate. We study this distinction for explanation-guided extraction of tabular classifiers. We separate an explanation into an attribution channel, which ranks influential features, and a coordinate channel, which supplies candidate feature values for perturbing those features. We then test whether the useful bin edges are privileged to the service or reproducible from the adversary's own data. Across six datasets and five target families, using attribution rankings to choose which features to perturb provides no systematic extraction advantage. Lime's discretization bin edges can improve fidelity by up to 41 percentage points on continuous features, but those edges are quantiles of the explainer's background data rather than properties of the target model. In controlled comparisons, an attacker-side grid reproduces the useful bin-edge gains without querying an explanation API. We use these findings to derive Cutpurse, which combines a self-computed grid with diverse query generation and boundary search. Against a service that withholds bin edges, Cutpurse improves fidelity by 16.3 percentage points on continuous-feature targets. It also exceeds the undefended published attack by 7.0 percentage points. Thus,

b2de380127a7f970cdc7512b.title_original: Robust & Scalable Website Fingerprinting via Minimal DRAM Traffic
b2de380127a7f970cdc7512b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Website fingerprinting attacks infer websites visited by users and threaten their privacy. These attacks are classified as on-path, which monitor network traffic, and co-located, which exploit shared system resources. Existing co-located attacks, such as sweep-counting and loop-counting, achieve over 90% accuracy but suffer significant performance degradation on many-core systems. Loop-counting accuracy drops from 93% on 8 cores to 50% on 24 cores, while sweep-counting accuracy decreases from 84% to 45% across multiple Core Complex Dies (CCDs). To address these limitations, we propose memory-chasing, a scalable website fingerprinting attack that exploits DRAM traffic interference through pointer-chasing traversals with minimal interference. By counting DRAM accesses over fixed intervals, the attack generates distinctive traces for website classification. Evaluated on the top 50 websites, memory-chasing achieves 96% accuracy on a 24-core system, 86% across multiple CCDs, 80% across multiple sockets, and 97% in an open-world setting. Extensive evaluation across hardware configurations, browsers, operating systems, isolation mechanisms, system noise, and countermeasures demonstrates its robustness and scalability.

1924486e8821a0edbf666849.title_original: Performance Bottlenecks in Computing ZK Proofs on a GPU
1924486e8821a0edbf666849.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Zero-knowledge proofs allow one party to prove the correctness of a statement or execution of a computation while revealing no more than the statement of correctness itself. Recent use cases, such as AI datasets, suggest the need for faster proof generation over increasingly large constraint sets. This paper explores efforts in optimizing zero-knowledge proof generation, specifically PlonK, using GPUs, for applications that are not amenable to solution via incrementally verifiable computing (IVC). Our intention with this work is to improve ZK performance by introducing fundamental changes in the low-level architectural structure of proof generation. These changes affect performance curves for most current proof generation algorithms. In particular, this paper explores the trade-offs between increased parallelization on GPUs and the resultant memory management problems that occur due to this parallelization. We implement a parallelized PlonK in order to analyze these trade-offs and make arguments concerning the nature of data flows within the proving protocol. Our results lead us to consider multi-GPU environments to maximize performance for large circuit sizes. Such environments introduce issues of communication, efficient hardware management, data partition, and data transfers. This paper further discusses the use cases that motivate multi-GPU implementations, their cost models, and the use of remote direct memory access (RDMA)

5c57c0375b95695e886be038.title_original: ReplayAudit: Auditing Outsourced LLM Fine-Tuning via Sealed Records and Selective Replay
5c57c0375b95695e886be038.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Auditing outsourced LLM fine-tuning requires checking an untrusted provider's training while controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, while checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps. We present ReplayAudit, a telemetry-guided auditing system that seals training records before challenges and independently replays sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling; replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. We relate sampling probabilities to replay work and evaluate the system on real LoRA training. A 7B BF16 prototype rejects a false update-norm report during a random audit; targeted checks also reject false loss reports and skipped updates. We calibrate sampling budgets offline to at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. For two learning-rate deviation settings, executing these budgets on the same honest 1.5B trajectory reduces median complete-audit wall time by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the corresponding audit instead costs 38% more. These results show how deviation capture and actual replay work jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing.

fd941a793b76e9b919e528e0.title_original: GuardrailAgent: An Agentic Framework for Jailbreak Defense
fd941a793b76e9b919e528e0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite undergoing safety training to align with human values, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that circumvent built-in safeguards and elicit malicious behaviors given by the adversary. Existing defenses are mostly static and fail to adapt to new or unknown attack strategies, providing limited resilience. To address these, we propose a multi-agent defense framework, GuardrailAgent, that offers adaptive, end-to-end protection. The system autonomously gathers and summarizes attack characteristics into a continuously updated knowledge base that supports both input- and output-side detection. A feedback module integrates misclassified cases for iterative improvement at minimal cost. Tested on over ten representative jailbreaks, the framework achieved a 93.1% input-side detection rate, 93.9% overall detection, and a 95.8% F1 score, while rapidly adapting to unseen attacks. These results demonstrate GuardrailAgent's outstanding capability to maintain LLM safety in the face of evolving jailbreak tactics.

db78b0c87244c8c54d44ad55.title_original: A Cross-Domain TARA-to-NAC Rule Mapping Methodology: From Automotive OEM Networks to Energy Storage Systems
db78b0c87244c8c54d44ad55.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Threat analysis and risk assessment under ISO/SAE 21434 ends with cybersecurity goals, but existing methods give little structured guidance for turning those goals into enforceable network access control rules. Compliance standards such as IEC 62443, ISO/SAE 21434, and ISO/IEC 27001 are usually applied as parallel efforts rather than as one enforcement architecture. This paper presents a six-step methodology that maps cybersecurity goals from a threat analysis and risk assessment to network access control rules, each placed at a named enforcement point and traceable to the threat records behind it. It also presents a unified compliance framework that treats IEC 62443 and ISO/IEC 27001 as a fixed substrate and domain-specific regulation as an interchangeable overlay. The methodology is applied to an automotive original equipment manufacturer plant network, addressing multi-tier supplier authorization and legacy operational technology devices, and then to utility-scale battery energy storage, where North American Electric Reliability Corporation Critical Infrastructure Protection standards and ISO/IEC 27019 replace the automotive-specific standard while the substrate stays constant. In the automotive example, 37 threat entries and 24 cybersecurity goals yield 23 rules covering 11 of the 13 in-scope goals; the energy example yields six rules. Three derived rules have no equivalent in the cited standards. Both examples are desk-base

e34b3464fe4da568b59da489.title_original: PhotoFinish: Portable Timerless Probing of Microarchitectural Latencies
e34b3464fe4da568b59da489.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Timing measurements are a fundamental building block of microarchitectural attacks, enabling software to convert otherwise invisible latency differences into architectural observations. Thus, restricting high-resolution timers is a common defense, especially in constrained environments such as web browsers. Timerless probing primitives provide an alternative approach. Instead of reading or constructing a timer, they observe architectural events that correlate with the microarchitectural state. However, such primitives typically rely on platform-specific behavior, and none generalizes across the wider computing landscape. In this paper, we present PhotoFinish, a portable timerless probing primitive that converts latency differences directly into an architectural value. PhotoFinish races an operation under test against a fixed reference in two parallel threads that then write unique values to the same shared location, resulting in a latency-dependent architectural value. PhotoFinish only requires parallel execution and shared memory, without constructing or reading a clock. We evaluate PhotoFinish on 38 CPUs spanning four ISAs and demonstrate reliable cache state classification across widely different microarchitectures, with comparable fidelity when compiled to WebAssembly and executed inside a browser. We further use PhotoFinish in AES T-table and Evict+Reload attacks, show that it applies beyond caches to TLB and execution-engi

cdfea5579bae3c06ced00e07.title_original: SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training
cdfea5579bae3c06ced00e07.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning training is difficult to verify within a scientific workflow: its architecture, hyperparameters, and procedure are rarely fixed until training has been attempted, and two honest runs never produce the same weights, so recomputation cannot serve as a check. We present SciCheck, a framework in which the scientist explores training configurations freely and posts a blueprint to a provenance ledger for each candidate they want verified, and a verifying scientist judges the resulting run in two layers: a statistical judge model that compares per-step gradient statistics against the verifier's own reference run, and a spot-check that re-executes randomly chosen training segments whose checkpoints are committed to the ledger one epoch at a time. On an MLP, a CNN, and an autoencoder at 100k-500k parameters, under gradient sign flipping, label poisoning, and fabricated runs, SciCheck reaches F1 of 0.966, 0.906, and 0.976 while rejecting 0-4.4% of honest runs. For the attacks we test, the spot-check accounts for most of this accuracy, and we characterize what each layer can detect. The effective-signal statistic falls as $(1-2s)^2$ under a sign flip of severity $s$, so gradient statistics alone catch strong enough sign flips, while fabricated runs that replay genuine statistics look no more anomalous than honest runs to any statistical detector we test. The spot-check catches fully fabricated segments with probability at lea

b66a253305a05cfed1a45c3b.title_original: Aegis OS: A Transactional Multi-Tenant Operating System Runtime for Eliminating Authorization Fatigue in Autonomous Coding Agents
b66a253305a05cfed1a45c3b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous coding agents such as Google Antigravity (agy), Anthropic Claude Code (claude), and OpenAI Codex CLI (codex) execute multi-step software engineering workflows on workstations and cloud hosts. Existing agent environments face a Security-Autonomy Dilemma: operators must choose between per-action confirmation prompts, which interrupt workflows on 45%-57% of tool calls and induce authorization fatigue, or unconfined execution (--yolo / --dangerously-skip-permissions), which exposes host files, SSH/cloud credentials, and API tokens to prompt injection and hallucination risks. Furthermore, concurrent agents editing a shared working tree clobber one another's changes, while passing large artifacts inline through LLM context windows incurs high token overhead. We present Aegis OS (aegis-os), a transactional, multi-tenant Agent Operating System Runtime in Rust exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. Aegis OS shifts the authorization boundary from individual tool calls to transactional workspace boundaries. Each agent runs inside a kernel-enforced OS sandbox (macOS Seatbelt and Linux Bubblewrap with default-deny --tmpfs $HOME isolation and a Unix-socket egress bridge) backed by a Copy-on-Write (CoW) shadow workspace (APFS clonefile; single-open Linux FICLONE reflinks), an identity-pinned HTTP Egress Proxy with L7 method/path-scoped secret injection and outbound DLP, and an A2A IPC b
b66a253305a05cfed1a45c3b.title_ko: 자율 코딩 에이전트 보안을 위한 다중 테넌트 운영체제 런타임 'Aegis OS'
b66a253305a05cfed1a45c3b.summary_ko: 자율 코딩 에이전트 사용 시 발생하는 인증 피로와 보안 취약점을 해결하기 위해 트랜잭션 기반 에이전트 운영체제 'Aegis OS'가 제안되었다. 이 시스템은 커널 수준의 샌드박스와 트랜잭션 작업 공간을 통해 개별 호출마다의 승인 절차를 최소화하면서도 프롬프트 인젝션 및 무단 파일 접근을 효과적으로 차단한다. 실험 결과 인증 요구 사항을 90% 이상 줄이고 공격 성공률을 0%로 낮추는 성과를 거두었다.

00c8d813faad70e97353b2b2.title_original: RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
00c8d813faad70e97353b2b2.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08711v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit vulnerabilities to adversarial perturbations that can induce unintended responses. These vulnerabilities can be identified via intentional attacks and subsequently used to improve model safety. In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model. To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at https://github.com/taikunudel/RL-ATTACK.

7a6dac0196d757ee656da0a1.title_original: On Differentially Private Mechanisms for Linear Regression
7a6dac0196d757ee656da0a1.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08737v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the classic least-squares linear regression problem under differential privacy (DP) in the batch and the continual observation setting. In the latter setting, the mechanism receives a stream of $n$ data points $(x_i,y_i)$ ($x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$) and must output an estimate of the optimal parameters at each time step $i$. Although differentially private linear regression has been extensively studied in the batch setting, the problem remains underexplored for the continual setting, with prior work being restricted to constrained linear regression and update time polynomial in $n$. In this work, we introduce ContinualAdaSSP, the first mechanism for unconstrained linear regression under continual differential privacy. Our mechanism's suboptimality gap is proportional to $\sqrt{d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. It requires $O(d^2\log{n})$ space and $O(d^2\log{n}+d^{\omega})$ update time, where $d$ is the dimension of the input space. We also study fundamental limits of differentially private linear regression by showing the first lower bounds for the box-constrained least-squares linear regression problem. Our lower bounds are proportional to $\min(n,\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\log^{1.5}d})$ for $(1,O(\frac{1}{n}))$-DP, and $\min(n,\frac{d}{\epsilon})$ for $\epsilon$-DP, and are derived using a reduction from a fingerprinting code problem from [Peter et al., 2024], providing new insights into the inherent hardness o

817b8ce14dd20f8afb3d7d74.title_original: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever
817b8ce14dd20f8afb3d7d74.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09214v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Authors increasingly deposit replication datasets---the data and code behind publications---in archives, and journals increasingly require them to, under progressively onerous rules. But a deposit alone proves little, so authors keep paying: months for the journal's reanalyses, years answering readers' questions, and rancor as failed replications become accusations because no record establishes what actually ran. We introduce a replication certificate: a cryptographically signed record of the deposited files and logged output. It replaces the journal's reanalyses with evidence anyone can check in seconds, which no one, including the archive, can backdate, and no one can fake without risking detection. Certification asks little of anyone and benefits everyone: The author deposits, then reruns the analysis once under a random seed the archive computes from the deposit's hash and a blockchain block; the archive signs, timestamps (in that blockchain), and stores the record---confidential data included---without rerunning anything; the journal merely checks a website for the certificate; and anyone can check or replay any step decades later.

c41e4c1942aa40c07b30e23b.title_original: Consensus-Constrained Dual-Federated Optimization with Client-Side Dynamic Weighting for Distributed Android Device Threat Defense
c41e4c1942aa40c07b30e23b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09470v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Smartphones, smart-home hubs, and wearables are increasingly exposed to sophisticated Android malware, while centralized threat-detection pipelines raise privacy and scalability concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without collecting raw client data, but partial participation and variation in local model quality can destabilize global optimization. In this article, we propose DW-FedADMM, a federated optimization framework that combines primal-dual coordination with performance-dependent client-side weighting. The dynamic coefficient modulates each participating client's local state before the augmented-Lagrangian update, while the dual variables regulate disagreement between local and global model states. We evaluate DW-FedADMM on three Android malware benchmarks, namely Drebin, Malgenome, and TUANDROMD, with 5, 10, and 15 clients holding IID data shards, partial client participation, and communication budgets of 5 and 10 rounds. Each configuration is repeated with ten random seeds. DW-FedADMM obtains the highest seed-averaged accuracy on Drebin (97.64% +/- 0.20%) and the best mean accuracy in 9 of the 18 dataset-client-round configurations, including 7 of the 9 configurations with a 10-round budget. Pooled over all configurations, it reaches 95.42% accuracy, 94.62% F1-score, 96.06% precision, and 99.45% AUC, compared with 95.32%, 94.51%, 95.56%, and 99.41% for FedADMM, while also giving the l

f4e4bf435afcae314f721926.title_original: On the Order of Privacy and Smoothing in Functional Mean Estimation
f4e4bf435afcae314f721926.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09799v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is a leading framework for privacy protection, yet privacy mechanisms tailored to functional data analysis (FDA) remain relatively underexplored. For functional mean estimation, we investigate a fundamental question regarding the ordering of privatization and estimation by comparing two canonical pipelines: Fit-Then-Protect (FTP), which smooths trajectories before privatization, and Protect-Then-Fit (PTF), which privatizes observations at discrete time points before smoothing. When data are observed without error, we prove that FTP achieves strictly smaller mean squared error than PTF asymptotically (as the sample size increases) under the same $\mu$-Gaussian differential privacy ($\mu$-GDP) budget in both finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and infinite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). Simulation studies support our theory and explore settings with observation error and fitting constraints, demonstrating that FTP outperforms PTF under small observation noise, whereas PTF can become preferable in high-noise settings. In addition to this comparison, we establish a novel GDP guarantee for Gaussian perturbations taking values in a Banach space, extending existing results beyond the RKHS setting.

f70f207738bcc156c9869da2.title_original: A Blockchain-Based Audit Mechanism for Trust and Integrity in IoT-Fog Environments
f70f207738bcc156c9869da2.excerpt: arXiv:2405.00844v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The full realization of smart city technology is dependent on the secure and honest collaboration between IoT applications and edge-computing. In particular, resource constrained IoT devices may rely on fog-computing to alleviate the computing load of IoT tasks. Mutual authentication is needed between IoT and fog to preserve IoT data security, and monetization of fog services is needed to promote the fog service ecosystem. However, there is no guarantee that fog nodes will always respond to IoT requests correctly, either intentionally or accidentally. In the public decentralized IoT-fog environment, it is crucial to enforce integrity among fog nodes. In this paper, we propose a blockchain-based system that 1) streamlines the mutual authentication service monetization between IoT and fog, 2) verifies the integrity of fog nodes via service audits, and 3) discourages malicious activity and promotes honesty among fog nodes through incentives and penalties.

f57318815574243860817e9a.title_original: Privacy Filters are Captured by Residues: A Characterization of Free Natural Filters and the Cost of Adaptivity
f57318815574243860817e9a.excerpt: arXiv:2602.15815v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study privacy filters, which enable privacy accounting for differentially private (DP) mechanisms with adaptively chosen privacy characteristics. We show that the worst-case privacy loss of interacting with any privacy filter is characterized by a Bellman equation. We apply this theory to develop residue filters, which unify existing privacy filters. We develop the Gaussian DP (GDP) residue filter, which strictly improves upon the na\"ive GDP filter. We show that, in the average case, this new filter asymptotically permits as many pure DP queries as in the non-adaptive case and a factor $\pi/2$ more pure DP queries than the na\"ive GDP filter. We also show that residue filters capture the natural filter, which promises greater utility by leveraging exact privacy accounting techniques. Earlier privacy filters consider only simple privacy parameters such as R\'enyi-DP or GDP parameters. Natural filters account for the entire privacy profile of every query, promising more efficient use of a given privacy budget. We show that, contrary to other forms of DP, natural privacy filters are not free in general. We present a characterization of when a family of private queries admits free natural filters for a given budget. In particular, only families of privacy mechanisms that are totally-ordered when composed admit free natural privacy filters with respect to an arbitrary privacy budget. Finally, we show that, while the natural a

1bc960fe882c44e043b01049.title_original: A Practical Post-Quantum Distributed Ledger Protocol for Financial Institutions
1bc960fe882c44e043b01049.excerpt: arXiv:2603.05005v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Traditional financial institutions face inefficiencies that can be addressed by distributed ledger technology. However, a primary barrier to adoption is the privacy concerns surrounding publicly available transaction data. Existing private protocols for distributed ledger that focus on the Ring-CT model are not suitable for adoption for financial institutions. We propose a post-quantum, lattice-based transaction scheme for encrypted ledgers which better aligns with institutions' requirements for confidentiality and audit-ability. The construction leverages various zero-knowledge proof techniques, and introduces a new method for equating two commitment messages, without the capability to open one of the commitment during the re-commitment. Subsequently, we build a publicly verifiable transaction scheme that is efficient for single or multi-assets, by introducing a new compact range-proof. We then provide a security analysis of it. The techniques used and the proofs constructed could be of independent interest.

cdd65c1f144fcb104c599088.title_original: Backdoor Channels Hidden in Latent Space: Extending Cryptographic Undetectability to Modern Neural Networks
cdd65c1f144fcb104c599088.excerpt: arXiv:2605.13214v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent cryptographic results establish that neural networks can be backdoored such that no efficient algorithm can distinguish them from a clean model. These guarantees, however, have been confined to stylised architectures of limited practical relevance, leaving open whether comparable undetectability extends to modern, end-to-end trained networks. We construct such an attack mechanism for deep neural network architectures, closely aligned to the cryptographic notion of undetectability, by identifying backdoor channels as learned latent directions, and show that the question of undetectability reduces to a hypothesis test between two unknown distributions over model parameters, which we conjecture to be intractable in practice. The consequence of this reframing is significant: if exploitable channels within a network's latent space are statistically indistinguishable from naturally learned directions, an attacker need not introduce foreign structure but can instead exploit the geometry the network already possesses. Demonstrating the approach on ResNet and Vision Transformer architectures trained on standard image classification datasets, the attack achieves both consistently high success rates with negligible clean accuracy degradation, and resists a comprehensive suite of post-training defences, none of which neutralise the backdoor without rendering the model unusable. Our results establish that cryptographic backdoors n

ec4adf6fcf90cb838bd22a44.title_original: Resilient Liquid Democracy: Mitigating Voting Power Imbalances via Secure Delegation Networks
ec4adf6fcf90cb838bd22a44.excerpt: arXiv:2607.01730v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Liquid democracy lets voters either vote directly or delegate their voting power to another trusted participant. It is often deployed in political parties, municipal participation platforms, and the governance of decentralized autonomous organizations. Existing approaches make delegations publicly visible as they form, which results in herding driven by popularity, makes coercion verifiable, and leaves the election fragile when popular delegates abstain. We propose a novel liquid democracy mechanism that removes these vulnerabilities, while keeping the tally fully auditable. Delegation choices are sealed with decentralized timed-release encryption, while they are formed and before revealed in full for tallying. Each voter determines ranked backup delegates together with a personal fallback ballot so that delegation failures do not result in abstaining. Experiments grounded in real-world voting data show that the mechanism keeps voting power dispersed, whereas transparent formation concentrates it into few hands. Strikingly, vote loss under targeted delegate failures falls from 26% to 3%.

7d09c66270a3e727b976ce2c.title_original: AuditLock: Pre-Specified Verification Audits for Synthetic Tabular Data Releases
7d09c66270a3e727b976ce2c.excerpt: arXiv:2608.14753v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A statistical office with a synthetic version of a protected file must decide whether it may be released for a stated purpose. We study the locked audit, a pre-specified and simultaneous form of the verification servers used in official statistics. Before a protected audit sample is opened, the custodian fixes the use, the candidates, the analyses, a tolerance for each and the schedule. The audit then reports simultaneous finite-sample bounds on paired loss gaps, and a declared negative control must fail. We correct an anytime-valid sequence that an earlier release had implemented with a variance penalty four times too small. Two confirmatory rounds were pre-specified in a hash-locked local ledger and publicly timestamped only after the audits. The control and ideal-generator outcomes were near-certain by design. A Gaussian copula certified in every cell, but only inside the rounding step of the tolerance rule. A second transparent candidate certified once, against a written prediction. Learned models, at library defaults and 4,000 training rows, certified in one of 18 fits in round 1 and in none of 12 tables in round 2. The paper is a protocol and an evidence record, not a claim that any generator is private or deployable.

addfdaf0ba51527c78d0b3e2.title_original: Optimizing Credential Blast Radius Through Trust Boundaries and Delegation Under Post-Quantum Authentication Costs
addfdaf0ba51527c78d0b3e2.excerpt: arXiv:2609.04566v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Partitioning interacting services into independently rooted trust domains limits issuer-compromise reach while increasing calls across trust boundaries. Post-quantum replacements for public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms can increase crossing latency on constrained or lossy paths. We formulate the joint selection of trust domains and credential-derivation structures under policy and latency constraints, linking separate service-interaction and credential-derivation graphs through domain assignment. Credential blast radius measures weighted service impact after compromise. A linear upper bound supports optimization, while a joint event model gives exact expected impact. We identify when risk from issuers trusted across domains can be incorporated into this linear score, avoiding separate issuer-propagation calculations for each candidate. Although the general problem is NP-hard, we identify restricted cases that can be solved efficiently and exactly. Joint optimization yields lower blast radius than choosing boundaries first in 195 of 230 exhaustive synthetic comparisons, especially under chained delegation. A trace-derived replay used measured post-quantum costs, synthetic risk inputs, a fixed derivation family, and one to six trust domains. Under independent compromise events, mean expected impact was up to 36% lower than with one domain within the latency budget. The framework turns risk assumptions an

7d7b5dc639e9f30391f6010a.title_original: When Agents See Differently: Exposing UI Desynchronization Threats in Mobile Agents
7d7b5dc639e9f30391f6010a.excerpt: arXiv:2609.16732v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mobile agents may act on interface content that users cannot see or easily notice, making their actions harder to oversee. We characterize this gap as human-agent UI desynchronization and investigate how attackers can exploit it through perturbations embedded in applications before deployment. Beyond accessibility metadata, we identify two mechanisms that expose misleading cues to screenshot-based agents: content rendered in display-occluded regions under compatible device configurations, and low-contrast text that remains encoded in screenshots but is difficult for users to notice. We develop an automated framework that searches application-specific perturbation strategies, optimizes their content using representative tasks, and realizes the perturbations in deployable applications. The perturbation content remains fixed at runtime and requires neither access to future user instructions nor detection of agent use. Using a benchmark of 546 tasks across 13 applications, we evaluate five mobile-agent frameworks and three backbone models. The attacks achieve average misleading rates of 77.4% in static observation-space evaluation and 67.2% in dynamic application-level evaluation, where success denotes selection of an attacker-designated decoy control. We invited 195 participants to assess the perceptibility of our visual perturbations and found that none spontaneously noticed the low-contrast text. These findings expose a secur

5df14ccd5acfe0b4117f81c6.title_original: Erase the Mark, Preserve the Motion: Temporally Consistent Removal of Video Watermarks
5df14ccd5acfe0b4117f81c6.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22457v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in video generation have increased the demand for reliable watermarking for copyright protection, yet the robustness of video watermarks against removal attacks remains underexplored. Most watermark-removal methods originate from the image domain: signal optimization injects imperceptible pixel-domain perturbations, whereas generative resynthesis produces a visually similar instance through diffusion synthesis. When extended to videos, the former introduces temporally varying noise that causes visible flickering, while the latter regenerates fine-grained structures inconsistently across frames, leading to structural motion inconsistency. To evaluate video watermark robustness, we propose PoseRegen, a pose-consistent reconstruction framework that removes watermarks while preserving the original content and motion. PoseRegen first applies a temporally shared viewpoint transformation to disrupt watermark-bearing spatial patterns and then jointly reconstructs the transformed sequence with a pose-conditioned video model. A frozen video DiT processes the complete sequence with its reference-video latent, and full-sequence Flow Matching supervision keeps identity and background consistent across frames. To further preserve motion structure, we introduce a lightweight Pose-Conditioned Motion Consistency Adapter that adapts the frozen backbone to temporally ordered pose guidance and constrains body-part trajectories t

bfa43cd52f2ba23ca99eee8e.title_original: Differential privacy with adjustable preservation of multivariate relationships
bfa43cd52f2ba23ca99eee8e.excerpt: arXiv:2610.26460v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper derives an exact attenuation formula for multivariate cross-moments under differential privacy achieved through randomized response. From a proposed alternative formulation of randomization matrices compliant with differential privacy guarantees we show that, under attribute-level randomization and where the randomization of the whole distribution is characterized by Kronecker products, any cross-moment of the anonymized dataset involving distinct attributes is equal to the original cross-moment multiplied by attenuation parameters, themselves determined by the part of the overall privacy budget allocated to each attribute. This characterization enables explicit and transparent controls of multivariate relationships preservations in differential privacy through privacy budget allocation. A simple numerical illustration demonstrates that identical total budgets can yield substantially different covariance-preservation profiles. The results also make the multiplicative loss of higher-order interactions explicit and thus can support mechanism design guided by analytical priorities.

cf7aaf4e0dcf13b9c3cc2910.title_original: What Concepts Lie Within? Detecting and Suppressing Risky Content in Diffusion Transformers
cf7aaf4e0dcf13b9c3cc2910.excerpt: arXiv:2605.10180v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rise of text-to-image~(T2I) models has increasingly raised concerns regarding the generation of risky content, such as sexual, violent, and copyright-protected images, highlighting the need for effective safeguards within the models themselves.Although existing methods have been proposed to eliminate risky concepts from T2I models, they mainly focus on the erasure of risk-associated textual or latent representations, limiting their ability to defend against adversarial prompts without explicit risk words, especially in recent Diffusion-Transformer-based T2I models. To bridge this gap, we investigate how semantic concepts activate the generation process within Diffusion Transformers~(DiTs) and discover that attention heads exhibit concept-specific sensitivity. This property enables both the detection and suppression of risky content. Building on this discovery, we propose a training-free inference-time safeguard for image generation in DiTs. Specifically, our method quantifies each textual token's sensitivity across all attention heads as an Attention Head Vector~(AHV), which serves as a discriminative signature for detecting risky generation tendencies. In the inference stage, we propose a momentum-based strategy to dynamically track token-wise AHVs across denoising steps, and a sensitivity-guided adaptive suppression strategy that suppresses the attention logits of identified risky tokens based on head-specific ri

5dc42cb1e025ffef531fa94c.excerpt: arXiv:2607.21551v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give an unconditional construction of information-theoretically secure one-time private-key unclonable encryption for one-bit messages, with efficient encryption and decryption and exponentially small unclonable-indistinguishability advantage. Previous work by Bhattacharyya and Culf (Nature Physics, 2026) and Bhattacharyya, Broadbent, and Culf (arXiv:2603.08916) either only showed inverse-polynomial security loss or required inefficient encryption/decryption operations; we avoid both of these caveats. Our scheme's key is a uniformly random non-identity phase-free Pauli on $n$ qubits, and bit $a$ is encrypted as a random $(-1)^a$ eigenstate of that Pauli. We prove that the probability that both receivers recover the bit is at most $1/2 + O\left(2^{-n/2}\right).$ By a lower bound due to Broadbent, Culf, and Rochette (IACR Communications in Cryptology, 2026), this is the best probability bound achievable with $n$-qubit ciphertexts while ensuring perfect correctness (up to the constant hidden in the $O(\cdot)$).

CVE-2026-115204.description: The AZEXO Store Locator WordPress plugin through 1.4 does not perform capability or nonce checks on its AJAX actions and does not sanitise a request header used to build a file path, allowing any authenticated user such as a subscriber to write a file with an arbitrary name, location, and content, leading to remote code execution.

CVE-2026-115212.description: The mView 豆瓣电影 WordPress plugin through 1.0.3 does not validate the type, name, or source of a remotely fetched file, nor perform any capability or authorization check, before saving it to a web-accessible directory, allowing any authenticated user such as a subscriber to upload arbitrary PHP files and achieve remote code execution.

CVE-2026-115213.description: The EASY-JS-WPAPI Client HANDLE for the WordPress REST-API WordPress plugin through 2.0 does not prevent the administrator credentials it stores from being disclosed to unauthenticated users and does not correctly verify authentication, allowing unauthenticated attackers to obtain administrator credentials and gain full administrator access to the site.

CVE-2026-115237.description: The Grand Job WordPress plugin through 1.2.1 does not correctly verify the password reset code before updating a user's password, allowing unauthenticated attackers to set the password of arbitrary accounts, including administrators, and fully take over the site.

CVE-2026-115256.description: The Mail Debug for WooCommerce WordPress plugin through 1.3.0 does not perform any capability, authentication, or nonce check on one of its email-logging actions, which is exposed to unauthenticated users and is not restricted to its own data, allowing anyone to read the full body of every email the site has sent, including password-reset emails whose reset key lets an attacker take over an administrator account.

CVE-2026-118201.description: The Limit Login Attempts Security WordPress plugin before 3.4.1 does not enforce its two-factor authentication on every password-authentication route, so an attacker who already knows a protected user's password can authenticate through an alternative login interface and obtain that user's access without completing the second factor.

CVE-2026-118202.description: The Limit Login Attempts Security WordPress plugin before 3.4.1 does not confirm that its two-factor authentication step succeeded before completing a login and treats a failure to build that step as success, so an attacker who holds a protected user's password can bypass the second factor by sending a request header that breaks the step.

CVE-2026-120409.description: The All-in-One Video Gallery WordPress plugin before 5.1.1 does not check whether a video is password protected before serving it through its standalone player page and its download link, allowing unauthenticated visitors to obtain the media source of password-protected videos, such as unlisted YouTube or Vimeo links and external file URLs.

CVE-2026-121759.description: The Fusion Page Builder WordPress plugin before 1.7.1 does not check that the user owns the content it moves to the trash, which could allow users with a role as low as Contributor to trash arbitrary posts and pages, or delete them permanently where the trash is disabled.

CVE-2026-121874.description: The Post Duplicator WordPress plugin before 3.0.18 does not restrict settings saves to its own options, allowing a site administrator on a multisite network who is not a Super Admin to overwrite arbitrary options of their site, including the role definitions, and so grant themselves network-management capabilities.

CVE-2026-121875.description: The Post Duplicator WordPress plugin before 3.0.18 does not validate the capabilities assigned to roles through its permissions settings, allowing a site administrator on a multisite network who is not a Super Admin to grant any role arbitrary capabilities, including the network-management capabilities reserved to the Super Admin.

CVE-2026-123064.description: The WP BASE Booking of Appointments, Services and Events WordPress plugin before 6.5.1 does not properly restrict access to one of its user-creation actions, allowing authenticated users with Subscriber-level access and above to create a new administrator account and thereby escalate their privileges.

CVE-2026-123088.description: The UniPAY Payment Gateway For WooCommerce WordPress plugin before 2.4 does not perform any authorization check before returning an order's order-received URL for an attacker-supplied order id, exposing the order's secret key in the redirect and allowing unauthenticated attackers to enumerate orders and disclose customers' personal data (name, email address, phone number and address).

CVE-2026-123091.description: The Vigilant WordPress plugin before 2.11.0 does not enforce its two-factor authentication on login forms other than the default WordPress one, allowing an attacker who knows a user's password to skip the second factor and log in as that user.

CVE-2026-123128.description: The GemBooking WordPress plugin before 1.7.1 does not serialise concurrent booking requests per team member, allowing unauthenticated users to create overlapping confirmed bookings for the same team member across different bookable items by sending simultaneous requests.

CVE-2026-123129.description: The Event Tickets Manager for WooCommerce WordPress plugin before 1.6.0 does not validate the ticket-type price sent to one of its unauthenticated AJAX actions when the referenced product has no ticket types configured, and stores the submitted price site-wide, where it is applied to the next event ticket added to any cart, allowing unauthenticated visitors to buy event tickets at an arbitrary price, including for free. This is due to an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-34898.

CVE-2026-123131.description: The GemBooking WordPress plugin before 1.7.1 does not properly verify that a REST request is addressed to its own routes before temporarily granting staff users administrative capabilities, allowing users with the GemBooking WordPress plugin before 1.7.1's Staff role to delete arbitrary posts and update the site's settings.

CVE-2026-123145.description: The WooCommerce Stripe Payment Gateway WordPress plugin before 11.1.0 does not exclude the account password from the checkout fields it saves to order metadata during express checkout, causing the password a customer chooses when creating an account at checkout to be stored in plaintext in the database, readable by anyone with access to order data or the database. Version 10.9.0 stored the passwords. Version 10.9.1 stopped new ones from being stored but left existing ones in place, and version 11.1.0 removes them on update. Passwords stored this way should be considered exposed.

CVE-2026-101031.description: The `example_dag_decorator` example Dag shipped with Apache Airflow validated an IP address fetched over HTTP with Python's `ipaddress` module and then placed it into a shell command. `ipaddress` accepts IPv6 zone identifiers containing arbitrary characters, so when example Dags are loaded (`load_examples` enabled), a user who can trigger that Dag with a custom `url` parameter could point it at a server whose response injects shell commands run on the worker. This is an incomplete fix for CVE-2025-54941; users who upgraded for CVE-2025-54941 should upgrade again. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later, or to disable example Dags (`load_examples = False`), which is recommended for production.

CVE-2026-107474.description: The Apache Airflow connections API did not mask the apprise provider's `config` connection extra, which can embed notification-service credentials. A user with permission to read connections could retrieve it in cleartext, although Airflow 3 treats connection credentials as write-only. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later. Airflow 2.x is also affected; Airflow 2 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix, so Airflow 2 users should upgrade to Apache Airflow 3.4.0 or later.

CVE-2026-111395.description: Apache Airflow did not reject reserved serialization keys inside a Dag run's `conf`. A user allowed to trigger a Dag that uses a deadline alert with an asynchronous callback could pass a `conf` that, once the deadline was missed, either crashed the scheduler repeatedly or was rebuilt into objects inside the Triggerer. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later.

CVE-2026-111403.description: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') vulnerability in WP Inventory WP Inventory Manager wp-inventory-manager allows Reflected XSS.This issue affects WP Inventory Manager: from n/a through 2.5.9.

CVE-2026-111421.description: Apache Airflow's Task Execution API stored XCom values written by a task without the reserved-key check applied elsewhere, so a Dag author's task could write an XCom that, when a user later viewed it through the API with deserialization enabled, made the API server instantiate classes from the `airflow.*` namespace with arguments the Dag author chose. This is an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-59242: users who applied that fix in apache-airflow 3.3.1 remain affected through this route and should upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later.

CVE-2026-111452.description: Apache Airflow's secrets masker matched sensitive key names only in their snake_case form, so values stored under camelCase keys such as `privateKey`, `connectionString`, `webhookUrl` or `accessKey` — for example in a Connection's extra or a Variable — were not redacted in task logs, rendered template fields or API responses. A user who can read task logs or rendered templates, but is not meant to see those credentials, could read them in cleartext. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later. Airflow 2.x is also affected; Airflow 2 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix, so Airflow 2 users should upgrade to Apache Airflow 3.4.0 or later.

CVE-2026-111453.description: Apache Airflow's API endpoint for deleting an asset's queued events checked Dag edit permission against the `dag_id` query parameter, but deleted the queued events of every Dag the caller could read. An authenticated user with edit permission on one Dag and read access to others could suppress asset-triggered runs of Dags they cannot edit. This is an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-75157: users who upgraded to apache-airflow 3.3.2 for that fix are still affected and should upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later.

CVE-2026-111454.description: Apache Airflow's asset API endpoints returned the IDs of Dags that are scheduled on, produce, or consume an asset without checking whether the caller may read those Dags. An authenticated user with asset read access could learn the IDs of Dags they are not authorized to see. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later. Airflow 2.x is also affected; Airflow 2 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix, so Airflow 2 users should upgrade to Apache Airflow 3.4.0 or later.

CVE-2026-111455.description: Apache Airflow's asynchronous connection test checked permissions when the test was queued — only create permission when the connection ID did not exist yet — but, when the test completed with `commit_on_success`, wrote the tested connection under that ID. A user allowed to create but not edit connections could overwrite a connection someone else had created in the meantime. Only deployments that enable the non-default `[core] test_connection` setting are affected. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later.

CVE-2026-113504.description: Apache Airflow's secrets masker stopped descending into nested structures after five levels, so a secret registered with the masker — for example a Connection password or a Variable value — that appeared more than five containers deep under non-sensitive keys was shown in cleartext in task logs and rendered template fields. A user who can read task logs or rendered templates, but is not meant to see those secrets, could read them. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later. Airflow 2.x is also affected; Airflow 2 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix, so Airflow 2 users should upgrade to Apache Airflow 3.4.0 or later.

CVE-2026-113508.description: Apache Airflow's logout endpoint attempted to revoke the presented token on the server, but any failure during revocation was silently ignored and logout still reported success. When the auth manager redirects logout to an external logout URL (for example the FAB or Keycloak auth managers), server-side revocation is the only thing that invalidates the Airflow token; it failed on database errors and, reliably, for tokens from an external issuer accepted via `[api_auth] trusted_jwks_url` whose token identifier is longer than 32 characters. Anyone holding a copy of a user's token from before logout could keep using it against the Airflow API until it expired. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.4.0 or later.
