We study four encodings that place skeletal motion in different geometric spaces: Gaussian joint heatmaps on the pixel lattice, which we show to be a morphological dilation of the joint point set by a quadratic structuring function; root-relative joint positions in Euclidean space; local joint rotations on $\SO$ through a continuous 6D embedding; and a redundant full kinematic encoding. For each, we train VQ-VAE tokenizers whose codebooks lie on the unit hypersphere, varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension. Beyond reconstruction, we measure codebook utilization and the effective vocabulary size, i.e., the number of equiprobable spherical Voronoi cells with the same entropy as the observed token distribution. Rotation and position encodings keep converting additional codewords into effective vocabulary, whereas the full kinematic encoding saturates at a few hundred effective cells and heatmaps at fewer than sixty. The smallest code dimension gives the highest utilization for three of the four encodings, and the effect

82a757fb6a62d6ce5da3f47a.title_original: Jointly Optimizing Memory, Computing and Offloading for Energy-Efficient DNN Inference
82a757fb6a62d6ce5da3f47a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In edge intelligence systems, computation offloading and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) are widely used to improve energy efficiency. However, as applications like deep neural network (DNN) inference evolve in complexity, their demands for memory resources have progressively increased, establishing memory as a critical bottleneck that impacts both latency and energy consumption. In this paper, we propose a joint optimization scheme integrating memory, computing and offloading for energy-efficient DNN inference. We formulate the energy minimization problem under deadline constraints as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, where the main challenge arises from the coupling between offloading and resource optimization. To address this issue, we decompose the original problem into two subproblems under a fixed offloading policy. The local subproblem is transformed into an equivalent geometric programming (GP) problem to derive the optimal memory frequency and computing frequency, while the edge subproblem is solved via convex optimization. An efficient coordinate descent (CD) algorithm is further developed to jointly optimize all variables. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with the gap from the optimal policy being at most 9.3%, and reduces the energy consumption of devices by up to 16.1% compared with benchmarks without memory frequency opt

c091b89abac7306d8dcaeec7.title_original: Statopia: A Prover--Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics
c091b89abac7306d8dcaeec7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11110v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing long proof developments. We present Statopia, an ecosystem that jointly develops Statopia Prover, an independent agent specialized for formalizing and proving results in statistics and machine learning, and Statlib, a Lean~4 library built with the prover and organized for automated use. The prover controls its own execution without relying on external coding agents. It is built for formal proof discovery and checking existing proofs. A natural-language proof, when available, guides its search but is not required: from a statement alone, the prover develops the argument itself and constructs a Lean proof. Its workflow integrates source preparation, statement review, library supported planning and proof construction. Dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups support parallel, resumable proof development. Statlib's shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and it

d7ca9eb9c5ee3b0cc1a6d734.title_original: CrossLiDAR: Controllable Multi-Sensor LiDAR Sequence Generation
d7ca9eb9c5ee3b0cc1a6d734.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11131v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-fidelity LiDAR simulation remains a bottleneck for scalable development and validation of autonomous systems. Existing generators can synthesize realistic scans, but they are typically constrained to a single sensor configuration, offer limited control over structure and geometry, and drift in long-horizon 4D generation. We present CrossLiDAR, a unified transformer-based framework capable of generating controllable and spatio-temporally consistent multi-sensor LiDAR sequences. Our approach leverages a rectified flow objective with a Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT) backbone, within a compact latent space of range images. To support multiple LiDAR sensors, an Inter-sensor Module enables interaction across sensors, while a ControlNet-style branch provides structural conditioning (e.g., BEV priors or 3D bounding boxes). For modeling the temporal consistency, CrossLiDAR generates short $N$-frame sequences and extends them autoregressively to improve long-horizon coherence. Our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average improvement of 29.56\% in JSD and 15.36\% in MMD evaluated on nuScenes and the Waymo Dataset. CrossLiDAR bridges the gap to modern autonomous-driving simulation by enabling calibration-consistent multi-sensor LiDAR rollouts over long horizons for controllable, scenario-based testing.

d00a9e162ac54f0f8981d487.title_original: DISCOVER: Online Variance-Guided Data Discovery for Budgeted Multimodal GRPO
d00a9e162ac54f0f8981d487.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11145v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning have made verifiable rewards a central post-training paradigm for improving multimodal reasoning. However, methods such as GRPO remain data- and compute-inefficient, spending rollout and annotation budget on prompts that provide little learning signal. We propose DISCOVER, an online data-discovery framework for budgeted multimodal GRPO that enables vision-language models to dynamically identify prompts that are most useful for the current policy. DISCOVER first organizes the multimodal sample pool into semantic clusters and queries a small set of density-diverse representative samples to obtain initial reward observations. During training, it estimates the utility of unannotated samples by transferring sparse reward feedback from queried samples. Since sample utility changes as the policy evolves, DISCOVER dynamically updates these estimates with recency-weighted rollout observations. It then selects only high-utility prompts for annotation using a policy-conditioned score that accounts for reward variance and difficulty. Once the discovery budget is exhausted, DISCOVER continues with utility-based replay. Experiments on ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B show that DISCOVER substantially improves multimodal mathematical reasoning under a strict 10% unique-sample budget, outperforming budget-matched random selection, hard-example sampling, full-pool GRPO under the same training-

d0d5ce84e22374a74727f984.title_original: Do Benign-Trained Hidden-State Probes Detect Tool Errors Under Adversarial Conditions?
d0d5ce84e22374a74727f984.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11172v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Although hidden-state probes efficiently monitor model operation, it remains unclear whether probes trained on benign tool use remain useful for detecting incorrect actions under adversarial conditions. In this research, we assess this problem from the perspective of operational tool-action correct- ness. we use four AgentDojo suites, four conditions, and three models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and GLM- 4.6V-Flash (9B). We perform a five-fold, task-grouped out-of-fold (OOF) evaluation for each model. We train step-specific logistic- regression probes only on benign and non-defended trajectories and evaluate them on held-out trajectories for benign, prompt- injection, system-override, and tool-poisoning conditions. We compare our hidden-state probe to mean tool-call-token entropy, negative mean tool-call-token log-probability, and self-consistency uncertainty. The paired tests highlight six significant differences after Holm correction. All of the tests involve Qwen2.5-14B- Instruct under the system-override condition, with all three scalar uncertainty metrics obtaining higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and average precision (AP) than the hidden-state probe. These results suggest that benign-trained hidden-state probes should not be assumed to reliably detect operational tool-action errors under adversarial conditions.

a7f94da326e908b43bcb6079.title_original: Guidance at Pure Noise Erodes Speaker Similarity in Few-Step Token-Conditioned Flow-Matching TTS
a7f94da326e908b43bcb6079.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11179v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Text-to-speech systems built from a language model and a flow-matching mel decoder now run the decoder with two to four Euler steps instead of the official ten or more. At two steps the word error rate (WER) is unchanged, but speaker similarity (SIM) drops by one to six points. This paper shows that most of this loss comes from classifier-free guidance on the first step. At pure noise the network can only return the conditional mean, so guidance shifts every trajectory by nearly the same vector. Later steps do not remove this shift, and its size grows with the length of the first step, so it is negligible with ten or more steps and accounts for most of the loss with two. Two training-free samplers are derived from this analysis. First-step unguided sampling (FSU) leaves the first step unguided and recovers $84$--$91\%$ of the two-step SIM loss on CosyVoice~2/3 with no significant WER increase. FSU-Mid replaces the two Euler steps by one midpoint step with an unguided first evaluation, recovers $77$--$85\%$ on IndexTTS-2 and matches the ten-step teacher on CosyVoice~2 and GLM-TTS. Both use three network function evaluations, one fewer than the official two-step sampler, and FSU-Mid gives the highest mean recovery among eight published guidance rules re-run at two steps on four decoders.

474e56433c02171d2544f0c7.title_original: Not Yet in the Profile: Uncertainty-Aware Dynamic User Profiling by Learning from Future Interactions
474e56433c02171d2544f0c7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11204v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: On the Web, user profiling builds compact user representations from interaction histories for efficient personalization, and dynamic user profiling updates them as users' behavior and preferences change. However, new user behavior can be ambiguous, and its interpretation differs across users. To address this, we introduce Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Profile Manager (UAPM), which separates the claims in a user profile from interpretations of new behavior that are not yet confirmed, through a Profile, a Buffer, and a Rulebook. UAPM records user-specific interpretation and update rules in the Rulebook, keeps ambiguous evidence in the Buffer outside the Profile as evidence for later decisions, and writes supported general and situational characteristics to the Profile. We train UAPM with Privileged On-Policy Distillation with Dual Specialization (POPD-DS), which learns from recorded future interactions during training without access to them at deployment. Its first stage, Dual Specialization, distills a stronger model into a current-only Student and a future-informed model that becomes the Teacher. In the second stage, privileged on-policy distillation (POPD), only the fixed Teacher receives future interactions and guides the Student's own management decisions alongside task rewards. Experiments on three Web personalization tasks show that UAPM outperforms multiple baselines under the same downstream input budget, improving on the

00be8d5520d353d28b375260.title_original: Viscot-steer: Disentangling and Transferring Visual Chain-of-Thought via Activation Steering
00be8d5520d353d28b375260.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11209v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual chain-of-thought (visual-CoT), also known as "thinking with images", equips LVLMs with the ability to locate and use key visual evidence for reasoning. However, acquiring such visual-CoT capabilities requires costly post-training and tightly couples them to a specific backbone, making transfer to other LVLMs difficult. Existing cross-model transfer methods typically treat visual-CoT as a monolithic capability, using a unified representation that ignores the functional distinction between grounding and reasoning and introduces stage-irrelevant interventions. To address this problem, we propose Viscot-steer, a training-free activation steering framework for transferring visual-CoT capabilities across heterogeneous LVLMs. Specifically, Viscot-steer first disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning vectors and extracts them from the source-model layers associated with the corresponding capabilities. It then aligns the vectors with the activation space of the target model and steers the grounding and reasoning layers during bounding-box prediction and reasoning-trace generation, respectively. Across benchmarks covering high-resolution visual understanding, general visual perception and reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning, Viscot-steer transfers capabilities from different visual-CoT models to architecturally diverse LVLMs and outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 perce

5f5436c42422a07e7f7201ab.title_original: Deterministic Narrative Gravity: Bridging Theory of Mind and Historical Simulation through ABM-LLM Architectures
5f5436c42422a07e7f7201ab.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11212v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Historical social simulation faces a fundamental reproducibility challenge: the stochastic nature of large language models (LLMs) introduces a digital butterfly effect that prevents exact replication across multi-turn runs. Furthermore, the inability to control low-level server parameters in commercial LLM hosting environments severely limits reproducibility. To overcome this opacity, we present a deterministic multi-agent framework coupling LLMs to an Agent-Based Modelling (ABM) pipeline grounded in Theory of Mind (ToM) and Cognitive Archaeology, and validate exact artifact identity within local, pinned execution environments using SHA-256 hashing. Run locally at temperature zero with clean per-call model reloads, the system injects differentiated cognitive states per turn through dissonance-driven behavioural modes and gated internal voices. Evaluating seven model configurations spanning 4B to 31B parameters against an ablated baseline reveals clear operational boundaries. Small models ($\leq$8B) suffer from context capacity overload, producing repetitive, specular dialogue loops. However, at $\geq$12B parameters, the ABM scaffolding breaks the monotonous response patterns seen in ablation. Crucially, these scaffolded models exhibit spontaneous diegetic expansion: they coherently expand scenario lore through tactically motivated, anachronism-free details rather than escalating into aggression. By resisting the structural pul

e72834c058bbe139758317c6.title_original: Disentangling Where and When:Factored Spatio-Temporal Explanations for Video Action Recognition
e72834c058bbe139758317c6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11214v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for video action recognition typically conflate spatial appearance and temporal dynamics into a single saliency or importance map. We propose a perturbation-based framework that disentangles these contributions into a spatial appearance mask ($M_a$) and a temporal motion mask ($M_m$). The two masks are jointly optimized against a frozen action recognition model through factored perturbation architecture, with nearest frame replacement to identify important temporal dynamics. A separation penalty discourages the appearance mask from spending budget on frames that the motion mask has already discarded. A ReLU-based area constraint penalizes explanations larger than an assigned budget. To evaluate these explanations, we introduce a separation protocol that sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames independently, backed by proofs characterizing the proposed method. Across EPIC-Kitchens-55, EGTEA Gaze+, and Something-Something V2, our method attains the lowest deletion AUC against leading baselines while producing masks roughly five times sparser.

9b05ac0fdf4ab65c115f3a3b.title_original: Replay Fidelity in LLM Agent Evaluation: Randomness, Hidden State, and Test Oracles in AppWorld
9b05ac0fdf4ab65c115f3a3b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11216v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reproducibility in large language model (LLM) agent evaluation depends on replay fidelity: which parts of an execution trace are reconstructed, controlled, and compared. This matters for agent debugging, failure analysis, and counterfactual evaluation of stateful tool use. We audit all 71 unsuccessful executions in a fixed historical AppWorld corpus using 284 isolated fixed-code replay attempts. Reconstructed declared settings admit 42 cases under printed-output, pre-oracle database-delta, and native-verdict/test-count checks; resetting the random-number generator before each interaction admits 68. The 26-case gap contracts to four under database/oracle checks, with one endpoint unknown. Mechanism studies identify four materialized-state discrepancies despite matching outputs and verdicts. In one admitted endpoint pair, an identical API call yields matching responses but different row effects; common future Python RNG removes that deterministic difference in two paired repetitions. A separate JWT credential-equality program and alignment controls expose authentication/write differences, with missing repetitions retained. For all 10 affected post-oracle export cases, native export from retained output trackers restores the reference comparison without changing original cached contents. A purposeful 12-case BFCL pilot shows no discrepancy under its tested public-state, return, and verdict checks. We preserve resource censoring a

e3203d9acfdbec117d26a388.title_original: scBIG++: Learning Across Genes and Cells to Predict Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
e3203d9acfdbec117d26a388.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11217v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting single-cell transcriptional responses to genetic and chemical interventions supports gene-function discovery and regulatory analysis. Existing studies often focus only on highly variable genes, restricting the expression changes available for downstream analysis. Cells exposed to the same intervention can also show heterogeneous expression responses, with coordinated gene programs active to different degrees. We propose scBIG++, a full-gene perturbation prediction framework that models this heterogeneity by connecting expression-adaptive gene modules with population-conditioned generation. To preserve shared gene structure while accommodating cellular variation, Gene-Relation Clustering organizes genes into common windows, within which Dynamic SoftSub learns expression-dependent submodule memberships. This shared organization enables Set-GCAE to exchange information about corresponding gene groups across control cells, placing individual representations in their source-population context. The cell representations initialize a latent flow, while their pooled summary and the perturbation representation condition response generation. Generated states are decoded into expression profiles covering all assayed protein-coding genes retained after preprocessing, supporting comprehensive analysis of perturbation-induced expression changes. Experiments across six genetic and chemical settings spanning 6,539--19,451 genes demo

ce0962b6d81e7e57be6630c7.title_original: SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs
ce0962b6d81e7e57be6630c7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11223v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width. Under this unified weight-traffic me

6508eb6a117f2684ef34a12a.title_original: Do Feature Interactions Break Explainability? Provable Explanations for Any-Order Neural Additive Models
6508eb6a117f2684ef34a12a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11224v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for neural networks are often heuristic and lack provable guarantees. A common alternative to such methods that was studied in recent years is to compute a cardinally-minimal subset of input features that is provably sufficient to determine the model's prediction. For general neural networks, however, finding such explanations is computationally intractable. In contrast, recent work showed that this problem becomes more tractable for a particular family of neural networks, namely neural additive models (NAMs), though standard NAMs are highly restrictive because they exclude feature interactions altogether. In this work, we study the computation of provably minimal and sufficient explanations for neural networks with restricted feature interactions, bridging the gap between fully general neural networks and purely additive models. We first prove that even with constant-order interactions, the problem is $\Sigma_2^P$-hard, implying that worst-case exponential complexity is unavoidable. We then identify two provably tractable settings: one based on sparsity in the interaction structure and another based on a stronger interaction-aware notion of sufficiency. Under either of these settings, we develop algorithms that compute provable explanations for neural networks with any-order interactions while retaining much of the computational efficiency of additive models. Empirically, we show that these explan

982115508c601119d6c87027.title_original: MCSA: Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation in SO(3) Equivariant GNNs for Interatomic Potentials
982115508c601119d6c87027.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11226v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) based on Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs) have achieved remarkable progress in atomistic modeling. However, accurately representing atomic interactions across different spatial scales remains challenging. In this work, we investigate the radial spectral properties of SO(3)-equivariant message passing and establish that the cutoff radius controls the characteristic spatial-frequency scale of radial interactions. Based on this analysis, we propose Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation (MCSA), a plug-and-play module that aggregates radial kernels with different cutoff radii to enrich multi-scale geometric representations. To achieve efficient implementation, we exploit the compact support of radial kernels to fuse cutoff-dependent radial weights before angular tensor-product operations, avoiding redundant angular computations while preserving rotational equivariance. Extensive experiments across representative EGNN backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in energy, force, and stress prediction, as well as enhanced accuracy in higher-order properties, including phonon dispersion and lattice thermal conductivity. Further evaluations on layered materials with distinct interaction scales demonstrate the effectiveness of physically motivated cutoff selection. Code is available at: https://github.com/JF-Tan/MCSA.

58a44e1e4bd52a9814b3a085.title_original: TLRS-DPO: Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization
58a44e1e4bd52a9814b3a085.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11232v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a simple and widely used alternative to RLHF for aligning large language models (LLMs), but its sequence-level objective cannot precisely locate or suppress the local patterns that make an otherwise acceptable response unsafe or undesirable. We propose TLRS-DPO (Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization), which augments DPO with fine-grained token-level control while remaining fully offline and reference-based. TLRS-DPO introduces a token-level robust compensation term that converts the policy-reference log-ratio on rejected responses into localized risk scores, a curriculum-style schedule that gradually increases the strength of this compensation during training, and a risk-adaptive screening mechanism that selectively penalizes only high-risk tokens instead of entire sequences. This design bridges sequence-level preference fitting and token-level behavior control, and can be implemented as a drop-in modification to standard DPO trainers. Empirically, TLRS-DPO improves alignment quality and safety-relevant behavior with minimal impact on helpfulness compared to strong DPO baselines.

d4d6f7d36b852e17d8a2d06d.title_original: FRESCO: A Novel Consistency Control for Asynchronous Pipeline Parallel Training
d4d6f7d36b852e17d8a2d06d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11238v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism can accelerate distributed model training, but suffers from instability caused by inconsistent gradient computations. We identify a fundamental source of this inconsistency: error signals are coupled to forward-time features, not just parameter states. This means that parameters may evolve as long as they preserve forward-equivalence. Leveraging this insight, we introduce FRESCO, which frames asynchronous updates as a constrained optimization problem: it finds the minimal update modification that acts trivially on the activation subspace. We demonstrate that FRESCO consistently outperforms representative asynchronous baselines in LLM pre-training, with the gains most pronounced under deep pipelines and high inconsistency levels: at pipeline depth 32, it reaches the same loss as the strongest baseline with 43% fewer iterations and 30% less wall-clock time, while requiring 8~921$\times$ less memory overhead. Moving beyond the current limitations, FRESCO establishes a new foundation for high-utilization pipeline parallel training, providing a scalable path for large-model development on diverse, resource-constrained systems.

2e9999dfe65bf8f26866d2b8.title_original: A Layer-wise Study of How Style Rewriting Breaks the Calibration of Zero-Shot LLM Fake-News Detectors
2e9999dfe65bf8f26866d2b8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11239v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked to judge whether a news article is true, and their stated confidence is often taken at face value. We test what happens to that confidence when an article's writing style, but not its facts, is manipulated, as in recent \emph{style attacks} on fake-news detectors. Tracing how the prediction and its confidence form layer by layer inside the network, we study three model families (LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B) on three fake-news benchmarks, and find the same three patterns in every model--dataset pairing. First, on the original articles the models are competent and largely honest judges: they settle on an answer, briefly become overconfident, and then correct their confidence in the final layers. Second, style-rewritten articles break this self-correction: the models become far less accurate, under the strongest attack, worse than random guessing, yet remain just as confident, so they are \emph{confidently wrong} precisely when a warning is most needed. Third, nearly all of the damage comes from rewriting into sensational or emotionally charged styles, while sober, neutral rewrites leave the models' honesty largely intact. The practical implication is that an LLM's confidence about veracity cannot be trusted as a safety signal when an article's style may have been manipulated.

4657efd102d24669b8941d3e.title_original: Auto-GlaKG: Automated Biomarker Reasoning for Explainable Glaucoma Detection
4657efd102d24669b8941d3e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Interpretable glaucoma detection requires a transparent connection between fundus images, clinically meaningful biomarkers, and diagnostic predictions. Knowledge graph (KG) reasoning provides this structure, but performance measured using annotated biomarkers does not establish performance when only images are available. We present Auto-GlaKG, an automated framework that combines image-based biomarker prediction with fixed clinical-prior rules. A ResNet50 network predicts the cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) and six morphological signs using biomarker supervision, and a KG reasoner aggregates their signed rule contributions into a glaucoma score. On 689 fundus images evaluated using stratified, group-aware five-fold cross-validation, Auto-GlaKG achieves a pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.951 (95\% confidence interval: 0.931--0.969), with sensitivity of 0.970 and specificity of 0.779. The matched image classifier also achieves an AUC of 0.951, while the rule stage adds 0.2~ms per image. Replacing predicted CDR with its annotation increases fold-mean AUC from 0.953 to 0.995. The framework provides an explicit rule-level account of image-based predictions and identifies CDR estimation as a priority for validation using independently measured biomarkers.

aea69d6286fb6b32fe63d92c.title_original: Primitives and Paths: Predicting What Post-Training Can Do from What the Base Model Already Has
aea69d6286fb6b32fe63d92c.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11260v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Does reinforcement learning teach language models new capabilities, or merely amplify ones acquired during pre-training? The literature offers evidence for both: pass@$k$ studies suggest RL reweights latent behaviours while some controlled composition studies demonstrate gains beyond simple amplification. We argue that this question has no answer independent of the capability state of the base model, and propose a two-dimensional state space for post-trainability. The first axis, \emph{effective full-solution support}, measures whether successful trajectories can be sampled under a feasible exploration budget. The second axis, \emph{atomic primitive coverage}, measures whether the constituent skills of a solution can be executed when the burden of composition is removed. Together, these dimensions motivate three regimes -- amplification, composition-limited, and acquisition-limited -- each predicting a distinct empirical signature and calling for a distinct intervention. We propose a prospective measurement protocol and investigate the framework using synthetic composition tasks across three small language models. We find that primitive mastery alone does not guarantee that RL can learn a composition. Checkpoints that execute every primitive reliably can fail to improve when complete solutions are never sampled during training, whereas modest composition supervision that establishes nonzero support enables substantial RL gains

6c849c25e417e988ae3a30a0.title_original: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models
6c849c25e417e988ae3a30a0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11261v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-

687eb3be449bb0ad89223780.title_original: Beyond Node Attributes: A Controlled Evaluation and Ablation of Local Interaction Statistics for Ethereum Phishing Detection
687eb3be449bb0ad89223780.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11263v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Methods for detecting phishing accounts on Ethereum are usually evaluated as complete pipelines that differ in features, architecture, and training protocol, which makes the contribution of interaction information hard to isolate. This paper evaluates the Unlabeled Feature Extension (UFE), a block of 12 local interaction statistics computed from each account's incoming and outgoing call and transfer edges without reading class labels. UFE is appended to the 14 source features of HEIG-Phish and tested with six model families: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, Graph Attention Network, GraphSAGE, and Meta-IFD. Within each pair of Baseline and Plus variants, the data partition, model configuration, random seed, decision threshold, and sampled neighborhoods are identical; only the input feature block changes. Across 20 predetermined stratified partitions of the same 2,763 labeled externally owned accounts, UFE increased test Macro-F1 by 1.0 to 9.1 percentage points across the six models. Every pair improved on all 20 partitions, all Nadeau-Bengio corrected 95% confidence intervals lie above zero, and the false-positive rate decreased for all six models. An exact-edge Random Forest ablation over 10 predetermined partitions associates most of the gain with the incoming transfer-edge sum attribute; once this feature is present, an incremental contribution of the remaining 11 UFE columns was not established. The results sup

7d9cdd4d6637555e37cab6d6.title_original: ErosionBench: Probing Alignment Decay in Enterprise Multi-Agent Systems
7d9cdd4d6637555e37cab6d6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11266v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As enterprises delegate consequential work to multi-agent LLM systems, benign-looking requests can escalate into unsafe actions as they propagate across sessions through poisoned shared state, long-context documents, and trusted peer messages: no single message is malicious, yet the assembled tool action is. Prior benchmarks isolate a single agent under prompt injection or score multi-agent attacks by their final output, leaving cross-session erosion of shared state out of scope. We introduce ErosionBench, an environment-grounded benchmark that executes such attacks and verifies alignment decay at the process level, scoring the realized tool call against authorized intent and provenance with deterministic contracts, not output text. Each scenario is authored as a deterministic state graph before any prose is rendered, so every state change traces to a known cause. It spans four enterprise domains and four decay mechanisms across 1,728 scenarios with matched benign controls, labeled against the OWASP Top-10 for LLM Applications, plus 198 image-based attacks, each paired with a text equivalent, so a defense must survive the same attack in either channel. Perimeter defenses suppress attacks only by over-refusing 54-92% of legitimate work, so a low attack-success rate can conceal severe over-refusal. As a reference defense, we propose a calibrated Meta-Auditor pairing synchronous state checks with asynchronous trajectory monitorin

c0307207539bb714fac6f6fd.title_original: A Unified Framework for License Plate Identification and Character-Recognition
c0307207539bb714fac6f6fd.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11289v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents a unified framework for license plate detection and character recognition on low-power edge hardware. The proposed network uses a shared CSP-Darknet and PANet feature encoder with an anchor-free localization head and a RoIAlign-based sequence-recognition branch. Character decoding is performed directly on aligned feature maps, avoiding image-space plate cropping and a second recognition backbone. The model is trained on an AI-assisted dataset of approximately 37,000 manually verified images covering license plate layouts from all 50 United States. The dataset includes variations in illumination, viewpoint, weather, blur, occlusion, and plate design. The framework is converted to an INT8 TensorRT engine and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 8 GB memory. The INT8 model shows an mAP50 of 97.8% and a full-sequence accuracy of 90.7%. It records 147 FPS at 6.8 ms end-to-end latency, with 315 MB inference memory and 9.4 W average power consumption. Relative to the YOLOv8s+CRNN baseline, the proposed deployment provides a 7.1x throughput increase and a 77.8% reduction in allocated inference memory

b377a14066ff37fd7a149652.title_original: EASE-KV: Diagnosing the Gap Between Memory Availability and Effective Use
b377a14066ff37fd7a149652.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11299v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reusable key-value (KV) memory avoids repeatedly prefilling retrieved text, but stored and injected memories do not necessarily become usable evidence. We present EASE-KV, a controlled framework for understanding this gap under fixed candidates and a frozen language model. EASE-KV separates three interfaces: whether required relations are preserved during encoding, whether preserved memories receive appropriate influence during allocation, and whether outcome supervision can identify useful allocations. Matched experiments show that causal encoding improves compositional accuracy by 25.0 percentage points over block-diagonal encoding, while the tested inference-time bridging methods fail to recover the lost contextual information. With unchanged stored states, diagnostic evidence-guided allocation improves LongMemEval accuracy from 31.2% to 38.4%, demonstrating that memory influence can be controlled without re-encoding. However, controllability does not guarantee learnability: binary correctness provides informative reward contrast for 53.0% of sampled query groups, compared with 73.6% under the evaluated shaped-reward setting. These findings show that effective KV memory requires more than retrieval and injection: the required relations must be encoded, preserved memories must receive appropriate influence, and supervision must distinguish better allocations from worse ones.

d602e16be18ba99cdb32b2e7.title_original: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
d602e16be18ba99cdb32b2e7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11305v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents that call tools are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in tool outputs can steer an agent into calls the user never asked for. We present a runtime audit that derives an executable intent graph from the user's objective and the deployment's tool catalog with one LLM call per task, and checks every tool call against it with a deterministic loop that makes no LLM call (median 5.7 microseconds per call). Two further mechanisms recover utility. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, because the harm of an attack lies in its write or outward step. The calls that remain flagged are escalated to a reasoning guardian, in the spirit of tool-integrated reasoning models such as START: a reasoning model that sees only the objective, the plan, the call history without tool outputs, and the flagged call, and can verify facts with a restricted Python-expression tool. A current agent showed no baseline attack success, so end-to-end validation remains open.

981df034251d8d3580f0a2a6.title_original: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
981df034251d8d3580f0a2a6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11306v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and robots.txt directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and robots.txt, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

47afee0b827db5491fc91fec.title_original: PROLA: Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation for Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling
47afee0b827db5491fc91fec.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11318v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.

afc6de93ad5811241a70fdb0.title_original: MoT3DVG: A Benchmark for Outdoor 3D Visual Grounding with Motion-Aware Descriptions and Temporal Cues
afc6de93ad5811241a70fdb0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11334v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.

df123821319eff677f34830c.title_original: Where Should a Gate Look? Input vs. State Gating in Diagonal State Space Models
df123821319eff677f34830c.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11336v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern state-space models owe much of their computational efficiency to their linear, often diagonal, dynamics. Classical recurrent neural networks instead allow nonlinear state-to-state interactions, which can be beneficial when memory updates need to depend on the past context. In this paper, we ask whether state feedback through a simple gate regulating memory updates can enhance the expressivity of diagonal state-space models. To investigate this question, we compare gates that depend on the current input, the recurrent state, or both. We establish a strict expressivity separation: for scalar models, state gating solves induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary size and sequence length, whereas input gating fails on a finite instance under standard stability assumptions on the state transition matrix. Experiments show that state gating retains its advantage on induction-head tasks in higher-dimensional models, whereas input gating performs better on selective copying tasks. Together, our results show that even a simple, diagonal form of state-feedback gating can unlock capabilities unavailable to input-controlled models, while input and state gating offer complementary strengths and achieve the strongest overall performance when combined.

35be2b72c972374e05f72b84.title_original: Agentic Attribution of Cloud Resource Ownership
35be2b72c972374e05f72b84.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11340v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Security tools raise findings across cloud environments, and AI agents now investigate and prioritize them. A finding is still resolved by people: it has to reach the people responsible for fixing it and accountable for the resource it concerns. Ownership is the organizational context that decides who that is. Where recorded, it is declared by hand in configuration management databases or owner tags and goes stale unless kept current; accounts are shared, and automation creates much of the infrastructure. The knowledge sits in work records, code history, audit logs and identity directories, encoded in each organization's own conventions. Recovering it poses four challenges: the signal is scattered across sources, none of them authoritative; the conventions that carry it differ between organizations; reaching an owner takes multi-hop links; and those related to a resource differ in the strength of their relation. We define ownership as a set of entities, people or teams, each related to the resource by one of five patterns ordered by strength. We present a reference architecture for agentic ownership attribution that derives ownership from these records instead of declaring it: it profiles an organization offline into tested signal procedures and an ownership playbook, then attributes each resource with a coordinator agent and parallel investigators, with confidence computed by rules. On 100 resources of 50 Amazon Web Services

68a937f3cd4cf7d84783a160.title_original: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
68a937f3cd4cf7d84783a160.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11342v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

cc5fcf463cc0affbd7a008c3.title_original: D3Tree: Learning to Prune Block-Diffusion Draft Trees for Efficient Verification
cc5fcf463cc0affbd7a008c3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11371v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Block-diffusion drafters propose a whole block of tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees built from their position-wise marginals increase the expected accepted length of speculative decoding. Every tree node occupies a query row in target verification, so under concurrent serving low-yield branches compete with other requests for verification capacity. Existing tree methods select verified nodes by draft probability under a fixed or cost-selected per-request budget, and thus always retain a prefix of the drafter's ranking. We present D3Tree, which learns which nodes of a block-diffusion draft tree are worth verifying. A tree-size head with 2H+2 parameters predicts each candidate's conditional survival from the draft state, the candidate embedding, and its draft log-probability. Thresholding the product of these scores along parent chains yields an ancestor-closed subtree whose size adapts to each request and decoding round. The head is trained on a frozen drafter with conditional labels on the full candidate tree; an optional joint mode also steers the drafter toward the retained reference path. At serving time, D3Tree verifies whole trees under light load and, under heavy load, allocates one batch-wide node budget by predicted survival, sized to the target's matrix-multiplication tiles. Retained trees share one ancestor-masked target pass, while construction, pruning, and scheduling run on the GPU and overlap with the h

f26fbd5fbdb1c8e65eb137a3.title_original: LLM-based Multi-Criteria Deep Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Efficient 5G UPF Selection
f26fbd5fbdb1c8e65eb137a3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11372v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: User plane function (UPF) selection in 5G networks is an active area of research, with various limited approaches proposed to enhance network efficiency and manage resources effectively. In this paper, we address this gap in the related literature by proposing a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) UPF selection method that utilizes a dynamic, multi-objective reward function and validating it on a real-world 5G emulation platform. The proposed method is based on the large language models' (LLMs) translation of network operator intents and the network data analytics function (NWDAF) abnormality alerts. The experimental results validated in the real-world experimental setup demonstrate that our dynamic DRL solution achieves an effective balance between latency, power consumption, and traffic distribution, outperforming the heuristic baselines and fixed DRL by 16.89%. These findings highlight the real-world applicability of our approach for dynamic, intent-driven UPF selection.

66b7b8e60fee543c1cb586eb.title_original: Does Predictive Performance Translate to Causal Performance? Evaluating tabular foundation models as nuisance learners for causal effect estimation
66b7b8e60fee543c1cb586eb.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11381v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) achieve strong predictive performance, but their value for causal inference is unclear. We evaluated whether PFNs, which predict through in-context learning, could match or outperform conventional nuisance learners in supporting accurate causal estimation and reliable uncertainty quantification (inference). Learners modeled propensity scores and outcome regressions within doubly robust estimators of average causal effects, with and without cross-fitting, across synthetic and semi-synthetic settings with varying confounding complexity and effect heterogeneity. Under simple parametric data-generating processes, the PFNs were competitive with correctly specified parametric regressions and ensembles containing them. In more complex settings, they outperformed all conventional learners evaluated, including richly specified Super Learner ensembles, for both accuracy and uncertainty quantification. As sample size increased, only the two PFN models (TabPFN and Mitra) consistently approached nominal confidence interval coverage, whereas under-coverage persisted for conventional learners. In some settings, PFNs achieved near-nominal coverage and well-calibrated standard errors even without cross-fitting. At the smallest sample size (n=200) and in the higher-dimensional semi-synthetic settings, PFNs and other flexible learners exhibited poor coverage without cross-fitti

938266dd7f42e7a7ffbb04d7.title_original: The comparison of density estimation for transfer learning in Banach, Hilbert, Euclidean spaces
938266dd7f42e7a7ffbb04d7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11382v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Domain adaptation or DA methods are indispensable when target labels or computational resources are scarce, yet the domain kernel density and subspace alignment approaches completely assume a Hilbertian geometry. They measure distributional discrepancy with symmetric L2 divergences over Euclidean feature spaces or reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). This preprint summarizes the manuscript Non-Hilbertian Domain Adaptation. Total Variation Alignment via L1 Density Regularization on Feature Manifolds, which proposes Banach Manifold Transfer Learning or BMTL. BMTL makes two coupled design decisions. The first one is that features are embedded on a geodesic manifold rather than treated as points of a flat Euclidean space, and the second one is that the density matching regularizer is formulated in an L1 Banach norm, whose minimization is equivalent, by Scheffe's theorem, to contracting the Total Variation or TV distance between domain densities, a bounded metric that weights all regions of the sample space uniformly. The L2 formulation, by contrast, squares deviations and therefore amplifies errors in the tails, over emphasizing density outliers that do not reflect meaningful distributional shift. Experiments on MNIST-USPS, COIL20, and Office+Caltech10 show consistent gains; the L1 variant beats an otherwise identical L2 ablation on every task, for example 92.44% vs. 89.80% on USPS->MNIST and surpasses the strongest baseline

91636dbce7d1edfbfc688d10.title_original: Vietnamese Legal Ontology: Every legal answer, traced to the article that grounds it
91636dbce7d1edfbfc688d10.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11426v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A legal answer is only as good as the article it rests on. Vietnam's largest open legal corpus pairs 109,543 published questions and answers with 573,851 legal documents, yet its citations are free text: "Khoan 3 Dieu 101 cua Bo luat nay" ("Clause 3, Article 101 of this Code") names neither the code nor its version. Following the five stages of NVIDIA Auto Ontology, Discover, Ground, Validate, Expose and Learn, we turn four open datasets into a knowledge graph of 11.5 M nodes and 16.0 M edges in which every node and edge carries its source record and method, with no duplicate keys, dangling edges or schema violations. Of 67,868 cited provisions, 61,487 resolve to a dated law version, 51,694 to a parsed article, clause or point, and 19,012 are confirmed word for word. The ontology then shows what flat records hide. 36% of the 78,361 answers whose citations resolve now cite a law that is no longer in force; 2,525 verified citations point to an article number that says something else in the current law; 2,520 citations were re-versioned because their words match a different version than their date suggests; and 5,575 document numbers are shared by several local authorities, one of them by 72. Every number in this paper is computed from the graph.

e38574dbfd1c873121fa4682.title_original: How to "train" a surgeon? Benchmarking generalist agents in surgical scene understanding
e38574dbfd1c873121fa4682.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11437v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluating general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for surgical scene understanding remains limited due to scarce surgical data and fragmented evaluation protocols. We address these challenges through a two-stage evaluation framework for surgical scene understanding. In Stage I, we introduce SurgKnowBench, a diagnostic benchmark that harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks and evaluates proprietary and open-source MLLMs to map the boundary of pretrained surgical competence. SurgKnowBench reveals that current models retain partial visual priors but remain weak on relational and procedural understanding and workflow assessment. Building on this failure frontier and motivated by the scaffolded nature of surgical training, we introduce SurgAgentGym, an agentic environment where general-purpose MLLM agents can use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general-purpose visual grounding for surgical tasks. SurgAgentGym evaluates whether generalist agents can improve surgical understanding at inference time through tool-mediated evidence use, without additional surgical training. Our results show that agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks. This opens a path toward future studies of agentic surgical understanding.

d3636f4b37ecda9bed0fc51a.title_original: Learning to Rank Propagators in Constraint Programming
d3636f4b37ecda9bed0fc51a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11447v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The order in which propagators are executed can substantially affect the performance of constraint programming solvers, yet propagator priorities are typically determined by fixed, manually designed heuristics. In this work, we explore learning instance-dependent propagator priorities from static problem features. We formulate the task as a learning-to-rank problem, addressing the challenge that the quality of a priority assignment can be measured through solver runtime, while the desired priorities of individual propagators are not directly observable. A self-attention-based model jointly scores the propagators present in an instance and is trained using pairwise preferences derived from solver runtimes measured under randomized propagator priority assignments, with a Plackett-Luce-based ranking objective. Predicted rankings are mapped to the discrete priority levels of the Choco solver before search begins, without modifying its propagation or search procedures. We evaluate the approach on XCSP3 instances and demonstrate that propagator ordering can have a substantial impact on solving time. On a test set of 698 instances, picked out as most difficult by problem class, the learned priorities increase the number of solved instances from 634 to 654, reduce median solver runtime by 27.93%, and reduce aggregate penalized runtime (PAR1) by 12.65% compared with Choco's default priorities. We further observe that improvements vary

94a889b978d54ee1a480f365.title_original: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?
94a889b978d54ee1a480f365.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11450v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget

f5ba79a6c2da90cfd10086f9.title_original: MOMENT-DP: Momentum Aware Evaluation of Correlated Noise for Differentially Private Training
f5ba79a6c2da90cfd10086f9.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11457v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Temporally correlated noise can substantially improve the utility of differentially private optimization, yet candidate mechanisms are commonly designed or evaluated using only partial information about the optimization process, such as workload structure, learning-rate schedules, or local curvature. We study whether persistent optimizer state provides additional information that can change the relative utility of privacy-valid correlated-noise mechanisms. We introduce MOMENT-DP, an optimizer-state-aware framework that models how temporally correlated privacy noise propagates through momentum-based optimization. For locally quadratic objectives, MOMENT-DP expresses privacy-induced final loss through an optimizer transfer operator that jointly captures curvature, learning-rate scheduling, momentum, and temporal noise covariance. NoiseCurve's curvature-aware quadratic criterion is recovered exactly as the zero-momentum, constant-learning-rate special case. Changing only momentum while holding curvature, schedule, privacy calibration, and candidate mechanisms fixed induces genuine mechanism-ranking reversals. The effect persists outside exact quadratic dynamics in per-example-clipped private logistic regression, while remaining unresolved in the neural regime we study. These results establish optimizer state as an under-modeled, decision-relevant axis in evaluating temporally correlated privacy noise.

990b3a921c749471bd48592b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Aligning two models without paired data requires a distance that both share, yet existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry. This is either an arbitrary choice or imposed by their loss function. We show that, under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of one data-generating process. This holds whether the models are encoders, decoders or both, and whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment map preserves this distance and the distribution of representations, and is identifiable if and only if the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold. We show that this symmetry breaking holds generically. Identifiability makes the alignment coupling the unique optimum of Gromov--Wasserstein and of its weighted combinations with a linear program. The linear program alone has the same optimum if almost every data point has a distinct distribution of distances. The coupling, and with it the alignment map, is recovered exactly from permuted samples, even without identifiability, and consistently from independent ones. Our method, Neural Gromov--Monge Alignment (NGMA), uses no pairs or labels and outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It relies on pullback distances to align image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, where Euclidean distances fail.

e99235269bea2e2cf3bca9fe.title_original: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
e99235269bea2e2cf3bca9fe.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without

1dc3c682bc251866eb684f44.title_original: TID System for Speech-COSER Challenge 2026: ASR Track
1dc3c682bc251866eb684f44.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11497v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We describe the system submitted by Telef\'onica Innovaci\'on Digital to the Speech-COSER Challenge 2026, which features spontaneous speech from elderly speakers recorded in rural Spain. For ASR, we perform CTC-based pseudo-forced alignment scores audio-text match quality to guide a two-stage LoRA curriculum, followed by post-hoc magnitude pruning of the LoRA matrices to enhance generalization. An ensemble of seven systems combined via ROVER achieves 36.25\% unnormalized and 22.17\% normalized WER.

81605fa299fe1b67addc4b7d.title_original: JoMoHa: Joint Model--Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning
81605fa299fe1b67addc4b7d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11499v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The performance of language agents depends jointly on model weights and the harness. Optimizing either alone can be constrained by the other component, limiting overall performance gains. Our analysis of naive alternating training reveals progressive incompatibility between the model and harness, which increasingly interferes with task execution and may also undermine model training, leading to performance degradation. To coordinate the evolution of models and harnesses, we introduce JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly train an executable harness generation policy and a task execution policy through reinforcement learning. JoMoHa outperforms the evaluated weight-only and harness-only baselines and achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld. By learning both task execution and runtime improvement from its own generated trajectories, JoMoHa performs recursive self-improvement (RSI).

29e07c95130b31cdfeeb4e25.title_original: Data-informed Adaptation of Foundation Models for Causal Effect Estimation
29e07c95130b31cdfeeb4e25.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Due to the fundamental problem of causal inference -- the impossibility of observing counterfactual outcomes -- there is always a gap between the training goal (outcome, propensity) and the inference target (CATE, ATE). Traditional causal effect estimation revolves around setting assumptions, selecting identification strategies, and choosing causal estimators, while more recently, Causal Foundation Models (CFMs), built on Prior-Data-Fitted Networks (PFNs), ease this process by pretraining on massive synthetic prior datasets. Despite their success, such amortization makes causal inference less transparent, obscuring which assumptions the model implicitly relies on for a given dataset. The high diversity of real-world data-generating processes (DGPs) and Structural Causal Models (SCMs) makes it hard to know, a priori, which causal inference strategy is compatible with a given dataset. In this work, we focus on this compatibility between an observational dataset and method-specific assumptions, and find that geometric characteristics of data embeddings -- specifically, the variogram -- provide a useful signal of whether a given causal estimation strategy is appropriate. We develop MoE-Learner, a mixture-of-causal-experts framework that embeds a dataset under multiple assumption-specific views and uses the variogram as a counterfactual-free router to assess each expert's validity. Rather than eliminating causal assumptions, this s

f015e25519c90c3a740da1f1.title_original: On the Relative Security of Prompt Injection: Mechanised Definitions, Defences and Verdicts for LLM Agents
f015e25519c90c3a740da1f1.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11506v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An LLM agent that reads untrusted content, such as an email or a web page, may follow instructions hidden in it. Noninterference is too strong for such agents, since a useful agent lets untrusted content influence what it does and may disclose the user's data by design, and declassification needs a release policy written for each task. We instead state security relative to a reference agent, which runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content. An agent is relatively secure if every leak it has is a leak the reference already has. Our framework, PlanTERS, instantiates relative security, a notion from speculative execution, with a small agent language in which the attacker chooses how the model follows instructions, a composition with runtime monitors, and attacker models that differ in what they observe. A fence theorem shows that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read, and never granting them back, makes every plan relatively secure at the event level on finite runs, for every model behaviour in which each injection is a single call and the model obeys on a schedule fixed in advance; with a fairness condition, this extends to possibly infinite runs. We prove or refute relative security for agents with fences, budgets, approvals, loops and dual LLMs, in Isabelle/HOL.

f389d01bc282c86fbddebea0.title_original: Review the Episodes, Refine the Lessons: Simple Memory Evolution for Embodied Agents
f389d01bc282c86fbddebea0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11509v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent studies of embodied agents based on frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) develop harness engineering around the MLLM, such as harnesses with post-trained policies and recursive self-improvement loops. Yet whether these additions exceed the native capability of the MLLM remains unexplored. We introduce SimplEvo to explore how far an MLLM can improve under direct control when it retains its execution experience in self-written text memories. It requires no weight updates, post-trained policies, or privileged information. The MLLM writes a coordinate-free task memory once from a single demonstration. Under a strict train-test protocol, it then creates a bounded working memory on training episodes only and refines it after each episode with lessons on procedure, completion, and recovery. Both memories stay fixed at test time. On EBench, SimplEvo lifts the success rate (SR) of GPT-6-Astra under direct control from 46.7% to 81.7%, and tops the RoboDojo leaderboard with 69.63% SR and a score of 75.32. Compared with memories that also store past visual frames, SimplEvo reaches a similar SR with text memory alone while using fewer tokens. With its memories fixed, SimplEvo also generalizes to unseen layouts and randomized scene configurations. Moreover, the working memory transfers across models: written by GPT-6-Astra, it can be reused as is by weaker MLLMs and improve their performance without any adaptation of the

02c760e935078415b67045f9.title_original: Detecting Common Golfing Faults Using AI and Video-Derived Biomechanical Features
02c760e935078415b67045f9.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11515v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding how an athlete moves can improve both technique and safety, yet outside the laboratory technique is still assessed by eye. We present a pipeline that detects named golf swing faults from ordinary video, without markers or calibration. Instead of learning end to end, it tracks body pose and the clubhead in a body-centered frame, and classifies the biomechanical quantities a coach would measure, such as the height of the clubhead above the swing plane, with shallow boosted trees. We demonstrate the approach on two common faults, coming over-the-top (OTT) and early-extension (EE). On 160 swings and 143 swings from public sources it detects OTT and EE with a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.975 and 0.911 respectively. Because every feature is a biomechanical quantity a coach already uses, measured at a known phase of the downswing, each decision can be traced to the signals and the moments of the swing that drove it. The signals the model relies on most are the same ones a coach checks when diagnosing these faults. The pipeline processes phone video on a consumer laptop in seconds, so it could feasibly be developed into an app for golfers of all abilities and extended to other sports in which technique is judged against a biomechanical reference.

bf7e8c40bcea3613de2dc3ff.title_original: Hydra: Towards Transferable Multi-Task Learning on Temporal Graphs
bf7e8c40bcea3613de2dc3ff.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11520v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-world evolving networks are naturally modeled as temporal graphs (TGs), where capturing temporal dynamics is essential for predicting future graph properties that support downstream decision-making. Existing temporal graph methods have been developed primarily for single-task prediction, and little is known about their generalization across tasks or transfer to unseen networks. This leaves the challenge of multi-task graph property prediction in TGs largely open. We address this challenge by introducing Hydra, a novel architecture that integrates local connectivity features from temporal GNNs with a spectral learning module that captures global connectivity patterns. This design enables joint learning of local and global information under a multi-task objective. In multi-task classification, Hydra achieves an 8.9% relative gain in AUC over the strongest competitor. In multi-task regression, Hydra achieves competitive results in all three tasks, while obtaining the best results in two tasks with a 8.2% relative gain in MAE compared to the strongest baseline. Moreover, Hydra delivers these gains with a 22% reduction in training time compared to temporal transfer models. These results provide the first systematic evidence that multi-task transferable learning on temporal graphs is effective. By delivering consistent top-ranked performance, Hydra highlights multi-task training on temporal graphs as a promising direction towar

3eed9024098442cc5e4e975e.title_original: K-PWM: Control-Oriented Structured Bilinear World Models under Partial Observation
3eed9024098442cc5e4e975e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11521v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World models learn internal simulators of environment dynamics for prediction, planning, and control, yet learning them from limited, noisy, and partial observations remains challenging. While much progress has focused on pixel-based observations, many physical systems instead provide vector-valued measurements that reveal only part of the underlying state. We introduce K-PWM, a probabilistic world model for prediction and control under partial observation. K-PWM couples Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics with a nonlinear observation decoder and performs probabilistic latent-state inference through the learned model via extended Kalman filtering and smoothing, without a separately trained inference network. Its bilinear structure enables exact propagation of the maintained Gaussian belief through the latent transition and efficient rollouts for uncertainty-aware model predictive path integral (MPPI) control. For training K-PWM, we present a generalized expectation conditional maximization (GECM) procedure with closed-form updates for the generators, noise covariances, and latent prior, complemented by gradient-based decoder learning. A Koopman-consistent initialization selects the latent dimension from data and initializes the action-dependent dynamics. With limited training data, K-PWM achieves lower long-horizon prediction error than the evaluated baselines on partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems, while substantially re
