With updated guideline evidence explicitly provided, revision recognition exceeded full incorporation across 14 models, with a 20.1-percentage-point gap in the strongest model. For Qwen3-4B, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions, 80.2% were clinically correct, and 58.5% fully incorporated them, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point gap. Two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses yielded a 40.3-percentage-point gap in this enriched validation sample; 61 of 144 responses with incomplete incorporation were clinically incorrect. Prompting Qwen3-4B to prioritize revised evidence reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness without significantly improving full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of revised guidance as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability.

e9b0741578d5c36848e0faff.title_original: The Value of Memory in Language Agents
e9b0741578d5c36848e0faff.excerpt: arXiv:2610.31303v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language agents carry information from past experience into future tasks whose demands may be unknown or change over time. Valuing this memory requires following the decision capability available in history, retained in storage and realized through use, together with the costs of recovery and revision. We develop a decision-theoretic account that connects these stages. Drawing on comparison of statistical experiments, information acquisition and the value of computation, we express original, retained and realized value in units of avoided task loss. Recovery and revision extend this account to attainable risk-cost profiles and preservation across uses. Unknown demand produces a family of value comparisons, while interactive feedback makes future work depend on the agent's actions. A cost-aware simulation condition and five minimal counterexamples establish how information timing, access, computation and demand shape these comparisons; a pointer with zero mutual information about an answer can reduce the cost of exact recovery. Complete-split studies on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S and PersonaMem cover 3,075 questions and two readers. They show complementary value from saved state and recovered evidence, task-dependent performance orderings, and the role of reuse in amortizing construction costs. Multi-project workflows connect correction to preservation and validation costs. Together, the theory and studies support decisions about

f865744989f7e49ce9031014.title_original: DriveMind: Mind-Evolving Belief Tracking for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving
f865744989f7e49ce9031014.excerpt: arXiv:2610.32069v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.

7cec2e289c6c6c7aaed17851.title_original: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
7cec2e289c6c6c7aaed17851.excerpt: arXiv:2610.33465v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discovering equations from data provides governing laws, constitutive relations and closure models for scientific understanding and prediction. Yet a method that succeeds on one system may fail on another or on noisy data, so discovery depends on expert trial and error. Unsuccessful searches can still reveal useful parts of an equation, but these clues must be recognized and combined. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for agent-guided equation discovery built on composable discovery and cumulative experience. Seven complementary equation discovery methods and shared computational modules form reusable building blocks, connected through a common equation representation. Researchers can launch discovery with one command and guide it with partially known equations. LegoSR Agent selects methods, revises searches using feedback and combines partial findings into new hypotheses. Its Experience Library consolidates graded outcomes into lessons that guide later tasks across equation families. Evaluation covers 134 algebraic regression problems, 40 ordinary differential equation targets and 17 partial differential equation problems at several noise levels, together with three case studies. On noisy differential equation benchmarks, LegoSR Agent nearly matches the recovery coverage of seven expert-tuned methods combined and exceeds a generic agent with the same model, tools and budget by up to 29.4 percentage points, with 51-61%

c7357e428870cdc6effdb4b7.title_original: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
c7357e428870cdc6effdb4b7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36116v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of ne

5182b9c709d0ce4dcbdab581.title_original: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training
5182b9c709d0ce4dcbdab581.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37161v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling supervised fine-tuning for working agents requires not only broad coverage of professional tasks, but also expert demonstrations that faithfully carry out professional workflows to completion. However, missing or inconsistent task information can disrupt expert demonstrations, weakening the resulting supervision. We introduce WorkFactory, a scalable task-construction framework that turns professional intents into executable task environments through hybrid intent sourcing, semantic workflow planning, and execution-based repair. Starting from these intents, WorkFactory constructs a Semantic Workflow Graph that explicitly represents information requirements, dependencies, and locations within the task environment. The graph guides the instantiation of task environments, while an adversarial execution-refinement loop exposes missing or inconsistent information and steers targeted repairs that preserve the original intent. Using WorkFactory, we construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and train the WorkPilot family at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales on the resulting teacher trajectories. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B rising from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling experiments with up to 110k tasks further show that larger models benefit more from additional task data but exhibit diminishing returns at smaller data sca

2c4491fa9ee2ab7772a0bd3f.title_original: LiveSearch: Questions as Executable Verifier Code for a Live Benchmark of Professional-Source Financial Search Agents
2c4491fa9ee2ab7772a0bd3f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37166v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In finance, the answer that matters is usually the current one: prices, rates, and disclosures hold only as of a given day, so retrieving up-to-date facts is a core capability of a financial agent. Yet most financial benchmarks overlook timeliness. They fix each answer at annotation time, so the gold goes stale as markets move and, once leaked into training data, rewards recall rather than search and analysis. We introduce LiveSearch, a live benchmark that stores each question as executable verifier code: a typed program of calls to a professional financial data service, followed by a declarative extractor. The question is frozen, while its gold answer is determined by executing the program against professional financial data at evaluation time, and a daily job re-executes it with no human or language model in the loop. A memorized answer is thus likely outdated, and a model must reach the current one through tools and analysis. Construction is equally automatic: a language model only verbalizes programs enumerated from real tool responses and never chooses an answer. Under general web search, six contemporary tool-calling models reach 70.9% to 76.7% answer accuracy. Over three consecutive days, 70% of served questions change their gold value, and even under tolerance-aware matching, a literally reused earlier snapshot fails on a majority of questions within a single day. Per-question tracking uncovers dynamic shifts in corr

4004574cf933486a98e0409e.title_original: When the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers (and the Same Answer Isn't Always Right): A Taxonomy of Failure Mechanisms, Testing, and Mitigation Strategies for LLM-Assisted Evidence Synthesis Read-and-Evaluate Tasks
4004574cf933486a98e0409e.excerpt: arXiv:2610.39070v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment sett

d6cb7c746671750a567e9da9.title_original: P-ContextBench: From Personal Fact Recall to Personalized Agent Behavior
d6cb7c746671750a567e9da9.excerpt: arXiv:2610.40959v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for personal tasks, yet evaluating their safe use of personal context remains difficult because such contexts are private, fragmented, dynamic, and socially situated. We introduce P-ContextBench, a realistic, verifiable, and scalable benchmark for evaluating personal-context understanding. P-ContextBench constructs population-structured, life-story-grounded digital humans from demographic seeds reflecting the U.S. population. Rather than using explicit, static profiles, P-ContextBench embeds traits, routines, goals, and constraints as implicit evidence across fragmented, evolving synthetic mobile-app records. It evaluates five capabilities: single-source fact recovery, multi-source fact recovery, temporal state tracking, inference of higher-level personal patterns from routine behavior, and safe handling of requests conflicting with persona-specific constraints through compliance, warning, clarification, or refusal. A multi-stage validation pipeline checks persona plausibility, context recoverability, information leakage, evidence preservation, test-case grounding, and human-judge agreement. We instantiate P-ContextBench with 100 personas, 10,088 hidden facts, 18,261 app-trace fragments, and 4,810 verified test cases. The pipeline supports configurable generation across scales and demographic groups. Cost-effective state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs relevant to personal agents ach

06969e4d1e860fc382f4e0c2.title_original: Lifelong Learning of Scheduling Rules with Surrogate-assisted Genetic Programming for Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
06969e4d1e860fc382f4e0c2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.41158v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used to learn scheduling rules for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS). However, trained rules tend to only generalise to tasks of similar scales and distributions, and when task characteristics change, learned rules often suffer significant performance degradation. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained rules on new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where prior knowledge is lost. This motivates the need for GP methods that can adapt to new tasks while preserving past knowledge, leading to a lifelong learning paradigm. However, lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely under-explored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a surrogate-assisted GP method for lifelong learning to handle sequential heterogeneous DFJSS tasks with job or batch arrivals. The framework includes three key components: an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism to regulate knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints to enhance estimation accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods and demonstrating the potential of lifelong GP in dynamic scheduling environments.

0cb2776b2f18dc7b969e329a.title_original: Scaling Science: Toward a Chain Reaction of Discovery
0cb2776b2f18dc7b969e329a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00580v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific discovery advances when evidence from different investigations is brought into contact. Yet paper-centric communication leaves experimental results fragmented, delayed, or unreported, creating a "scientific memory wall" between growing computational capabilities and the evidence accessible to AI systems. Breaking this wall requires a paradigm shift in AI for Science: moving from passively mining questions out of existing datasets to actively generating and recombining experimental data around unresolved scientific questions. In a network of intelligent laboratories, a failed or overlooked experiment in one domain could trigger a hypothesis in another, whose testing generates fresh evidence that stimulates further investigations. To enable these evidence-driven chain reactions, we propose Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI), an architectural blueprint that connects shared scientific memory with distributed experimental loops. ESI preserves experimental records -- including negative and anomalous results -- in computable representations, allowing models to recombine evidence across domains into testable hypotheses. Rather than following fixed screening pipelines, the system jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods according to scientific value, reliability, and cost, directing distributed laboratories to produce the exact evidence needed next. Their physical feedback revises both hypotheses and evaluator

288903628d2936601de8203e.title_original: Autonomous Analysis of Thermoelectric Materials Big Data by Multi-Agentic AI and Construction of a Knowledge Base and Specialized AI
288903628d2936601de8203e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00627v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large databases of paper-derived experimental materials data hide essential information on materials. Their analysis is demanding, large-scale and complex, making manual knowledge extraction very difficult. To address this challenge, we developed Multi-Agentic AI (MAA) for automated, autonomous analysis of materials experimental big data and a specialized AI built on the obtained knowledge. MAA's nine role-specific AI agents, under predefined instructions and quality checks, autonomously perform data extraction, compositional feature generation, machine-learning modeling, feature-importance analysis and knowledge-base recording, iterating while inheriting previous knowledge. Delegating numerical processing to code makes large-scale data tractable; recording every choice and result enables later tracing to sources. In four thermoelectric-data experiments varying theme and cycle counts, the knowledge graph grew: knowledge clustered by theme and vocabulary was shared across themes. The specialized AI, searching and reading these records, answered materials questions citing sources. Retrospective verification also revealed errors, traced through the records to their sources.

fbb1b66faaaf14c4a774b847.title_original: CHATDIFY: Automating End-to-End Dify Workflow Synthesis from Natural Language via Multi-Agent Collaboration
fbb1b66faaaf14c4a774b847.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01563v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The proliferation of Large Language Models has catalyzed powerful application development platforms like Dify, which enable users to build sophisticated LLM-powered workflows through modular node orchestration. However, manually configuring these workflows requires deep platform expertise and remains time-consuming and error-prone, creating a significant barrier for non-expert users. To address this challenge, we propose \textsc{ChatDify}, a novel multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end Dify workflow synthesis from natural language descriptions. \textsc{ChatDify} employs an Actor-Critic architecture comprising three specialized agents: the \textit{Planner Agent} that decomposes user requests into structured execution plans, the \textit{Executor Agent} that performs context-aware parameter synthesis and schema-augmented DSL compilation, and the \textit{Reviewer Agent} that ensures reliability through hybrid verification with closed-loop refinement. We evaluate \textsc{ChatDify} on a curated benchmark of 100 production-inspired tasks across three state-of-the-art LLM backends, achieving 0.96, 0.91, and 0.75 success rates with Qwen-3.7, GLM-5.1, and DeepSeek-v4, respectively. These results demonstrate its robustness and practical applicability for lowering the technical barrier to creating sophisticated LLM applications.

456e9a752490fed6e857387d.title_original: DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects
456e9a752490fed6e857387d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03412v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM agents are judged by what they deliver, and in professional work what gets delivered is a project, not a task. A project pays off only if the whole package holds together, and one weak part can limit the value of the rest. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test agents on one task at a time, leaving a gap between the capability we measure and the outcome that makes agents useful. To address this gap, we introduce DeliverBench, which tests whether agents can carry a project from brief to final delivery. Reconstructed from real materials with 13 domain experts, its 11 projects span settings such as financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting. They comprise 150 subtasks, with 2-15 subsequent releases of new materials and client feedback per project. Later subtasks build on the agent's own earlier deliverables, so unresolved errors can carry into downstream work. Expert rubrics assess each subtask submission and the final delivery package. Across seven model-harness systems, the best scores 65.0/100 on final delivery and passes 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. Together, these results suggest that task-level capability does not simply compose into delivery; delivery also depends on keeping the work coherent as it evolves.

c9f9619b13498094483b3ee3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03601v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance an

0f8a21294737058bf77cae2f.title_original: Training LLM Agents to Automate LLM Post-Training with RSI-Dojo
0f8a21294737058bf77cae2f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03698v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aims to enable AI systems to autonomously build and improve AI systems themselves, including models, harnesses, and underlying infrastructure. Within this broader agenda, a central capability is enabling agents to train and improve base models. However, existing studies on automated model training primarily focused on workflow- or harness-level optimizations, rather than internalizing the ability to conduct post-training into the model itself. Developing this capability requires executable model training environments that can produce high-quality trajectories demonstrating how to select data, train models, diagnose failures, and iteratively improve results. In this paper, we introduce RSI-Dojo, a collection of executable model training environments designed to teach LLM agents to conduct post-training. To construct RSI-Dojo, we develop RSI-Craft, an automatic pipeline that converts human research artifacts into executable model training environments. RSI-Craft automatically collects research papers from top venues, instantiates datasets and metrics into a unified interface, and reproduces evaluation dependencies. It then filters tasks by data size, execution reliability, and discriminability, yielding RSI-Dojo with 281 seed model training tasks. Building on RSI-Dojo, we employ a trajectory collection method with an improved harness to collect high-quality model-training trajectories from fron

e0bfb8b32a068f812f1e34e0.title_original: Counterexample-driven autonomous research with application to excess radiated energy in a Z-pinch
e0bfb8b32a068f812f1e34e0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03721v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in artificial-intelligence-assisted mathematics show that open-ended machine search can outperform human mathematicians, yet transferring this paradigm to physics requires refactoring the research workflow. We introduce Simjecture, an open-source framework in which language-model agents pursue human-defined physical conjectures. The framework tackles two central challenges in this transfer: first, because physics is empirical and no model is final, it structures inquiry around counterexample-driven falsification and prospective hypothesis repair; second, because physical theories must interact with the real world, it uses computational physics as an executable testbed while separating the qualification of numerical instruments from scientific claim review so solvers and diagnostics can be adapted within a recorded investigation. We apply the framework in a 136.3 h investigation to tackle the long-standing problem of radiated energy exceeding the imploding-shell kinetic energy in a Z-pinch. The investigation reveals competing effects of energy conversion, retention, and release timing. Stronger coherent helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation and increasing retained energy. In a matched fine-grid test, broadening the trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation maximum by 1.80 ns and recovers an early 153 J bolometric deficit to within 0.08% by 44 ns, with a spect

0087387e6388f19732e4491f.title_original: Embodied AI for Scientific Discovery: From Physical Action to Scientific Evidence
0087387e6388f19732e4491f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.04371v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific experiments are increasingly selected, executed and interpreted by learned systems that act through physical interfaces. Robot learning builds physical competence, whereas AI for science chooses which experiment to run, each reporting different endpoints. This review treats their interface as one problem, embodied AI for science, where the experiment itself is partially observed: specimen state, apparatus state and measurement processes are latent, actions are costly and irreversible, and missingness depends on execution and outcome. We organize the literature by three closures operating at distinct levels: operational closure (the experiment realized is the one intended), epistemic closure (the result updates beliefs or selects subsequent experiments) and evidential closure (the record supports a claim). We analyze workflows through a record-linked evidence cycle - Record, Diagnose, Calibrate, Confirm - as analytic functions with feedback. A taxonomy crosses these closures with six delegated decisions and five embodiment classes. Our formulation separates commanded, realized and observed conditions and models diagnosis with explicit resource, risk and sample-change costs. We compare experiment-selection methods by terminal decision, review perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policies, world models, recovery and transfer by evidence emission requirements, and compare chemistry, materials, biology, microsc

f18b0f4c6918e3d9e3ef90b3.title_original: CogniLife: Continuous Cognitive Distillation for Deployed Multi-Expert Agent Marketplaces
f18b0f4c6918e3d9e3ef90b3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.04483v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.

b73fde8521bca25f0c4f985e.title_original: EnzymeRSI: A dual-loop recursive self-improvement system for enzyme design
b73fde8521bca25f0c4f985e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06321v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Enzyme engineering usually optimises which candidates to assay within a fixed model and workflow; when the bottleneck is a mismatched method or a failing workflow, that route is hard to escape. We present EnzymeRSI, a dual-loop system for recursive self-improvement (RSI). The outer loop evolves harness assets without changing model weights; the inner loop develops prediction and selection algorithms under controlled conditions; a cloud laboratory system is specified for closing the physical loop with quality-controlled feedback. The outer loop raised the mean development-set Spearman correlation on ProteinGym by 0.044 across five assays, reaching 0.335 on CD19 and 0.683 on OPSD (rhodopsin); of the two first places, only CD19 was produced by the outer loop itself. In ThermoMPNN self-improvement the inner loop reached a PCC of 0.849, and on TadA-Bench a Spearman correlation of 0.307 in 1.13 h. We examined the system's experimental decision-making in three enzyme systems. For the luciferase RLuc, 10 of the 32 nominated substitutions not pre-specified reached at least twice wild-type activity in a single round. For the cytidine deaminase A3A, a variant selected by a rule that caps loss of unmodified C raised 5mC conversion in the weaker CT context from 11.4% to 46.5% and reversed the substrate preference in both contexts. For the DNA polymerase KOD-E, 189 single-substitution variants defined a landscape on which different object

be4934f6928d45362871dee6.title_original: Informed Posterior Sampling: More Efficient Online Learning with Few Offline Demonstrations in Average-Reward MDPs
be4934f6928d45362871dee6.excerpt: arXiv:2310.11531v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study efficient online reinforcement learning in the infinite horizon setting when there is an offline dataset to start with. We assume that the offline dataset is generated by an expert but with an unknown level of competence, i.e., it is not perfect and not necessarily using the optimal policy. We show that if the learning agent models the behavioral policy (parameterized by a competence parameter) used by the expert, it can do substantially better in terms of minimizing cumulative regret than if it does not do that. We establish an upper bound on regret of the exact informed PSRL (iPSRL) algorithm that scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$. This requires a novel prior-dependent regret analysis of Bayesian online learning algorithms for the infinite horizon setting. We then propose the informed RLSVI (iRLSVI) algorithm to efficiently approximate the iPSRL algorithm. Empirical results show that small offline expert datasets are sufficient for iRLSVI to outperform online-only algorithms on hard exploration domains.

4dc5e0ce5b3fcc1cc903cc2d.excerpt: arXiv:2311.11091v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Deep Tensor Network is a family of sequence operators built from contractions of queries, keys, and values. Tensor Attention mixes tokens through the Gram operators $Q(K^\top K)Q^\top$ and $K(Q^\top Q)K^\top$; Tensor Interaction mixes channels through operators derived from $C=Q^\top K$. Associativity lets us evaluate these products exactly without forming $n\times n$ token matrices. For query/key width $d$ and value width $d_v$, the Gram constructions use $O(d^2+dd_v)$ work and summary state per causal token, or $O(d^2)$ when $d_v=O(d)$. We derive prefix recurrences and distinguish trace, diagonal, and row normalization, including the conditions under which the weights are nonnegative and row-stochastic. The unmasked token operators are positive semidefinite with rank at most $d$, but their entries can be negative. We also give exact evaluations and costs for Hadamard and matrix-exponential variants.

3b991f6bcd5f89b5b76c1b85.title_original: Generalized Influence Functions for Better Model Change Estimates
3b991f6bcd5f89b5b76c1b85.excerpt: arXiv:2312.05586v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Influence functions (IFs) approximate the effect of removing or reweighting training data on a trained model, but their linear approximation often lacks the accuracy required for reliable post hoc model editing. We identify two culprits and propose generalized influence functions (GIFs) and pseudo-LiSSA (p-LiSSA) to address each in turn. First, classical IFs update all parameters indiscriminately, leading to unnecessary updates to data-irrelevant parameters. GIFs instead restrict edits to a data-relevant subspace and leave the remaining parameters fixed. We theoretically show that GIFs achieve a tighter error bound than classical IFs when the parameter subset is properly selected, and that effective subspace selection requires avoiding low-curvature directions while retaining a sufficiently large component of the target gradient. Second, LiSSA iterations are destabilized by negative Hessian eigenvalues, which existing methods handle via $\ell_2$ damping, at the cost of a biased inverse-Hessian-vector product (iHVP) estimate. p-LiSSA eliminates this bias by solving the restricted inverse-Hessian problem without such damping. We further show that the presence of low-curvature directions slows p-LiSSA convergence, and that the data-relevant subspace selected by GIFs mitigates this. Across five image and text unlearning benchmarks, GIFs update only 10% of the parameters yet preserve accuracy up to 2.12 percentage points be

5ee8213b484fc683502b4b33.title_original: Learning temporal formulas from examples is hard
5ee8213b484fc683502b4b33.excerpt: arXiv:2312.16336v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the problem of learning linear temporal logic (LTL) formulas from examples, as a first step towards expressing a property separating positive and negative instances in a way that is comprehensible for humans. Given positive and negative words, the goal is to find a smallest formula satisfied by the positive words and not by the negative ones. We study the computational complexity of this problem for all fragments of negation-free LTL built from the operators F (eventually), G (globally), X (next), $\wedge$ (conjunction), and $\vee$ (disjunction), without the until operator. We show that the problem is in NP for all fragments, that it is in polynomial time for the fragments containing none of the pairs $\{X,\wedge\}$, $\{X,\vee\}$, $\{F,\wedge\}$ and $\{G,\vee\}$, and that it is NP-complete for all other fragments, already for alphabets with two or three letters. We also show that the fragment with only X and $\wedge$ has a polynomial time 3-approximation algorithm, but no polynomial time approximation scheme unless P = NP. These results motivate the search for efficient heuristics.

1327b9487a81e839f518f4bb.title_original: CombAlign: Enhancing Model Expressiveness in Unsupervised Graph Alignment
1327b9487a81e839f518f4bb.excerpt: arXiv:2406.13216v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unsupervised graph alignment finds the node correspondence between a pair of attributed graphs by only exploiting graph structure and node features. One category of recent studies first computes the node representation and then matches nodes with the largest embedding-based similarity, while the other category reduces the problem to optimal transport (OT) via Gromov-Wasserstein learning. However, it remains largely unexplored in the model expressiveness, as well as how theoretical expressivity impacts prediction accuracy. We investigate the model expressiveness from two aspects. First, we characterize the model's discriminative power in distinguishing matched and unmatched node pairs across two graphs. Second, we study the model's capability of guaranteeing node matching properties such as one-to-one matching and mutual alignment. Motivated by our theoretical analysis, we put forward a hybrid approach named CombAlign with stronger expressive power. Specifically, we enable cross-dimensional feature interaction for OT-based learning and propose an embedding-based method inspired by the Weisfeiler-Lehman test. We also apply non-uniform marginals obtained from the embedding-based modules to OT as priors for more expressiveness. Based on that, we propose a traditional algorithm-based refinement, which combines our OT and embedding-based predictions using the ensemble learning strategy and reduces the problem to maximum weig

935e427e53326e5133ae8cb7.title_original: A systematic framework for generating novel experimental hypotheses from language models
935e427e53326e5133ae8cb7.excerpt: arXiv:2408.05086v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural language models (LMs) have been shown to capture complex linguistic patterns, yet their utility in understanding human language and more broadly, human cognition, remains debated. While existing work in this area often evaluates human-machine alignment, few studies attempt to translate findings from this enterprise into novel insights about humans. To this end, we propose a systematic framework for hypothesis generation that uses LMs to simulate outcomes of experiments that do not yet exist in the literature. We instantiate this framework in the context of a specific research question in child language development: dative verb acquisition and cross-structural generalization. Through this instantiation, we derive two novel, untested hypotheses: (1) the alignment between argument ordering and discourse prominence features of exposure contexts modulates how children generalize new verbs to unobserved structures; and (2) that this alignment in the first postverbal argument of the exposure context has a more noteworthy effect. Additionally, we also design a set of experiments that can test these hypotheses in the lab with children. This work contributes both a domain-general framework for systematic hypothesis generation via simulated learners and domain-specific, lab-testable hypotheses for child language acquisition research.

cddb5b76bd8d4814a372d61b.title_original: Graph Fourier Neural Kernels: Learning Full PDE Trajectories Across Geometries and Anisotropic Parameter Fields
cddb5b76bd8d4814a372d61b.excerpt: arXiv:2410.04655v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-fidelity simulations of time-dependent nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) are expensive to repeat across families of domains and parameter fields, a cost that recurs in design optimization, uncertainty quantification, and computational medicine. Most neural-operator surrogates require each domain to be mapped onto a common grid or reference shape, and few predict the full time course. We introduce Graph Fourier Neural Kernels (G-FuNK), a neural operator for second-order semilinear PDEs with a diffusive principal part that transfers across geometries and anisotropic diffusion tensors without coordinate maps or diffeomorphisms. A weighted graph and its Laplacian supply a spectral basis that encodes geometry and anisotropy. Shared layers act in this basis, at a cost linear in mesh size after one partial eigendecomposition per geometry, and a neural ODE integrator propagates the learned generator to full spatiotemporal trajectories on unseen domains. Across anisotropic heat flow, stiff reaction-diffusion, FitzHugh-Nagumo, and patient-specific left-atrial electrophysiology on CT-derived surfaces, G-FuNK reproduces held-out trajectories with relative $L^2$ error between 0.046 and 0.160. Its accuracy is comparable to that of a geometry-aware Fourier neural operator on regular domains, and its predictions are unchanged when a rectangular domain is rotated. On left atria, whose venous and valvular openings pre

95995e5e813b1209bd2a52f8.title_original: Embedded Decomposed Transformer for explainable multivariate time series forecasting
95995e5e813b1209bd2a52f8.excerpt: arXiv:2412.12227v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time series forecasting is an important problem with diverse real-world applications. This paper introduces the Embedded Decomposed Transformer (EDformer) for multivariate time series forecasting. EDformer decomposes the input signal into seasonal and trend components using two complementary strategies: time-domain Average Pooling (AP) based on moving-average smoothing and Frequency-Aware (FA) decomposition based on low-pass filtering in the Fourier domain. The reconstructed multivariate seasonal component is embedded across inverted dimensions, after which attention captures cross-variate correlations and a feed-forward network learns nonlinear representations for each variable. The trend component is forecast through projection and combined with the seasonal prediction to produce the final forecast. We evaluate both decomposition variants on several real-world datasets, showing that EDformer achieves competitive performance, while their relative effectiveness varies across datasets, experimental settings, and temporal characteristics. We further conduct an ablation study isolating the contribution of decomposition, inverted embedding, and the frequency cutoff ratio; a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis over learning rate and batch size; and a statistical significance analysis using Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to substantiate the reported performance differences. Finally, model explainability techniques a

30b819f0cb153fd904cc6f86.title_original: ViDE: Tuning-Free Video Coherence via Temporal Attention Reweighting and Prompt Blending
30b819f0cb153fd904cc6f86.excerpt: arXiv:2412.17254v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite the substantial progress in long video generation, multi-prompt synthesis often encounters inconsistencies resulting from the training-inference gap caused by length extension techniques and coarse prompt interpolation. To overcome these issues, we propose the Video Diffusion with hidden states Editing (ViDE) framework, which consists of two key components. The first is the Time-frequency based Temporal Attention Reweighting (TiTAR) algorithm, which leverages the relationship between inconsistencies and diagonal elements of temporal attention. By reweighting the attention scores via the Discrete Short-Time Fourier Transform (DSTFT), TiTAR effectively reduces frame inconsistencies, a capability further corroborated by a Fourier-based analysis. The second component, PromptBlend, reduces inconsistencies in multi-prompt settings through fine-grained prompt alignment and adaptive interpolation, enabling smooth semantic transitions. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ViDE, demonstrating consistent and significant improvements over multiple baselines.

2c22b55de82e47ba54c72074.title_original: EcoSearch: A Constant-Delay Best-First Search Algorithm for Program Synthesis
2c22b55de82e47ba54c72074.excerpt: arXiv:2412.17330v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many approaches to program synthesis perform a combinatorial search within a large space of programs to find one that satisfies a given specification. To tame the search space blowup, previous works introduced probabilistic and neural approaches to guide this combinatorial search by inducing heuristic cost functions. Best-first search algorithms ensure to search in the exact order induced by the cost function, significantly reducing the portion of the program space to be explored. A key limitation of existing best-first search algorithms is that they slow down over time: the delay between outputting successive programs grows with the number of programs already generated. We ask whether best-first search algorithms with constant delay exist. We design Eco Search, a new best-first bottom-up search algorithm. It combines the cost tuple representation of Bee Search with the per non-terminal data structures of Heap Search, thanks to a new frugal expansion strategy, and it uses bucket queues instead of priority queues, which is possible because the costs stored in each queue always lie in a window of constant width. We prove that Eco Search is the first constant-delay best-first search algorithm for pre-generation cost functions. Experimentally, we evaluate Eco Search on two classic program-synthesis benchmarks (DeepCoder and FlashFill) and observe that Eco Search solves 12% to 70% more tasks than its predecessors, and reach

9d3e0a48389c37c9b78199e2.title_original: Why Transformers Struggle with Distribution-Independent In-Context Learning
9d3e0a48389c37c9b78199e2.excerpt: arXiv:2502.03503v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With in-context learning (ICL), transformer models adapt to new tasks from illustrative examples at inference time without updating their parameters. A common interpretation is that transformers implement implicit learning algorithms in their forward pass. We test this interpretation and ICL capability under distribution shift in noiseless polynomial regression, where the context uniquely determines the target function. Models that are near-perfect in distribution exhibit sharp performance degradation under shifts in the input or target-function distribution. This behavior persists across polynomial degrees and multiple training interventions, and in higher-dimensional nonlinear regression. We identify two architectural mechanisms that explain this breakdown: output saturation at finite boundary values linked to final normalization, and attention concentration on a small subset of the context, which can limit context-dependent adaptation required for ICL. Controlled experiments, architectural ablations, targeted interventions, and theoretical analysis provide strong evidence for both mechanisms and their consequence: strong in-distribution ICL does not imply distribution-independent ICL, which calls for caution when using ICL instead of explicit retraining or adaptation under distribution shift.

f12acb94175c985924f8e732.title_original: Language in the Flow of Time: Time-Series-Paired Texts Weaved into a Unified Temporal Narrative
f12acb94175c985924f8e732.excerpt: arXiv:2502.08942v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While many advances in time series models focus exclusively on numerical data, research on multimodal time series, particularly those involving contextual textual information, remains in its infancy. With recent progress in large language models and time series learning, we revisit the integration of paired texts with time series through the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, which posits that representations of different modalities converge to shared spaces. In this context, we identify that time-series-paired texts may naturally exhibit periodic properties that closely mirror those of the original time series. Building on this insight, we propose a novel framework, Texts as Time Series (TaTS), which considers the time-series-paired texts to be auxiliary variables of the time series. TaTS can be plugged into any existing numerical-only time series models and effectively enable them to handle time series data with paired texts. Through extensive experiments on both multimodal time series forecasting and imputation tasks across benchmark datasets with various existing time series models, we demonstrate that TaTS can enhance multimodal predictive performance without modifying model architectures. Our Code is available at https://github.com/iDEA-iSAIL-Lab-UIUC/TaTS.

85078e18a2944a672679fdf3.title_original: Exploring specialization and sensitivity of convolutional neural networks under simultaneous image augmentations
85078e18a2944a672679fdf3.excerpt: arXiv:2503.03283v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Drawing parallels with the way biological networks are studied, the authors adapt the treatment--control paradigm to explainable artificial intelligence research and enrich it through multi-parametric input alterations. A framework for investigating internal inference impacted by input data augmentations is proposed to address the real-world scenario with multiple simultaneously applied treatments instead of observing a single effect. The internal changes in network operation are reflected in activation changes measured by variance, which can be decomposed into components related to each augmentation by employing Sobol indices and Shapley values. To facilitate distinguishing model-related specifics from the self-interactions of augmentations, an auxiliary variable responsible for their permutations has been incorporated into the analysis. The resulting quantities enable one to visualize sensitivity to different variables and use them as features for further analysis and processing, including guided masking of activations. In addition, a method for single-class sensitivity analysis is introduced through a pipeline that involves class selection according to their match with the prediction bias generated by targeted damaging of the activations. Three convolutional networks, namely AlexNet, VGG11, and ResNet18, have been evaluated via the designed framework, with two vision transformers, ViT-b-16 and Swin-t, partially comp

716a1a2ecd2208334ad35406.title_original: Certified Lipschitz Bounds for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Decision Models
716a1a2ecd2208334ad35406.excerpt: arXiv:2503.07992v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study certified upper bounds on Lipschitz constants for hybrid quantum-classical decision models, which combine classical neural-network layers with parameterized quantum circuits. We pair an SDP-based certificate for classical layers with an exact spectral characterization for probability-output quantum models. For hybrid architectures, these componentwise estimates are connected through the encoding maps to obtain a certified composition bound for the complete model. The resulting bounds support sensitivity analyses relevant to robustness, stability, generalization, and fairness.

df0b447b85fd8d55aabcf8d6.title_original: Graph and Simplicial Complex Prediction Gaussian Process via the Hodgelet Representations
df0b447b85fd8d55aabcf8d6.excerpt: arXiv:2505.10877v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting labels for graph-structured data is crucial in many scientific applications. Recently, Gaussian processes with graph-level inputs have been proposed as flexible non-parametric models for classification tasks. In this work, we extend this framework to regression tasks and to simplicial complexes, enabling the modelling of attributes defined on edges and higher-order simplices. Drawing on Hodge theory, we construct representations based on the Hodge decomposition, allowing the model to distinguish between exact, co-exact, and harmonic signal components. We introduce Hodgelet representations as rich, learnable topological descriptors of simplicial complexes and show that our framework improves predictive performance across a range of applications. Our work broadens the applicability of Gaussian processes to prediction tasks at the graph and simplicial-complex levels.

ba53ee8b5afb3f444eccbe23.title_original: Malware families discovery via Open-Set Recognition on Android manifest permissions
ba53ee8b5afb3f444eccbe23.excerpt: arXiv:2505.12750v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Malware are malicious programs that are grouped into families based on their penetration technique, source code, and other characteristics. Classifying malware programs into their respective families is essential for building effective defenses against cyber threats. Machine learning models have a huge potential in malware detection on mobile devices, as malware families can be recognized by classifying permission data extracted from Android manifest files. Still, the malware classification task is challenging due to the high-dimensional nature of permission data and the limited availability of training samples. In particular, the steady emergence of new malware families makes it impossible to acquire a comprehensive training set covering all the malware classes. In this work, we present a malware classification system that, on top of classifying known malware, detects new ones. In particular, we combine an open-set recognition technique developed within the computer vision community, namely MaxLogit, with a tree-based Gradient Boosting classifier, which is particularly effective in classifying high-dimensional data. Our solution turns out to be very practical, as it can be seamlessly employed in a standard classification workflow, and efficient, as it adds minimal computational overhead. Experiments on public and proprietary datasets demonstrate the potential of our solution, which has been deployed in a business envi

9cd0477cf664be3365641b18.title_original: Speculative Decoding Reimagined for Multimodal Large Language Models
9cd0477cf664be3365641b18.excerpt: arXiv:2505.14260v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) deliver strong performance across vision-language tasks but suffer from high autoregressive decoding latency. Although speculative decoding can accelerate Large Language Models (LLMs) without changing their output distribution, directly applying existing approaches to MLLMs yields limited speedups because text and visual tokens exhibit distinct characteristics. We present Multimodal Speculative Decoding (MSD), a framework specifically designed for efficient MLLM inference. MSD is motivated by two key observations: text and visual tokens should be handled separately during drafting, and an effective draft model requires both strong language modeling and visual perception capabilities. Accordingly, MSD decouples text and visual token processing in the draft model and applies token-specific strategies to improve drafting efficiency. We further introduce a two-stage training strategy. The draft model is first trained on text-only instruction-tuning data to strengthen its language modeling ability and is then progressively exposed to multimodal data to develop visual perception while preserving its language competence. Extensive experiments across multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that MSD achieves up to $2.29\times$ inference speedup for LLaVA-1.5-7B and $2.46\times$ for LLaVA-1.5-13B without sacrificing generation quality. These results establish MSD as an effective and general app

4c65682ad7d0e8f96c2afb53.title_original: APE: Selective Fine-tuning with Acceptance Criteria for Language Model Adaptation
4c65682ad7d0e8f96c2afb53.excerpt: arXiv:2505.19912v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present Adjacent Possible Exploration (APE), a selective fine-tuning method for adapting large language models that systematically explores parameter modifications while maintaining model stability. Inspired by evolutionary optimization principles, APE evaluates multiple candidate parameter updates through fine-tuning on small data subsets and accepts only those exceeding a performance threshold. Unlike standard fine-tuning that follows single gradient directions, APE implements a filtered selection process that prevents destabilizing parameter changes while enabling systematic improvement. Our method achieves 33.9\% BLEU improvement and 36.2\% perplexity reduction on news summarization tasks while using minimal computational resources. The approach provides a practical framework for controlled model adaptation that balances performance gains with representational stability.

b0d5e704037b9008bbbffffd.title_original: Practical Adversarial Attacks on Stochastic Bandits via Fake Data Injection
b0d5e704037b9008bbbffffd.excerpt: arXiv:2505.21938v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Adversarial attacks on stochastic bandits have traditionally relied on some unrealistic assumptions, such as per-round reward manipulation and unbounded perturbations, limiting their relevance to real-world systems. We propose a more practical threat model, Fake Data Injection, which reflects realistic adversarial constraints: the attacker can inject only a limited number of bounded fake feedback samples into the learner's history, simulating legitimate interactions. We design effective attack strategies under this model, explicitly addressing both magnitude constraints (on reward values) and temporal constraints (on when and how often data can be injected). Our theoretical analysis shows that these attacks can mislead a class of bandit algorithms into selecting a target arm in nearly all rounds while incurring only sublinear attack cost. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our strategies, revealing vulnerabilities in stochastic bandit algorithms under practical adversarial scenarios.

8be352b3a37901918d0e29bd.title_original: Sentinel: Decoding Context Utilization via Attention Probing for Efficient LLM Context Compression
8be352b3a37901918d0e29bd.excerpt: arXiv:2505.23277v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieved contexts are often long, noisy, and redundant, motivating query-aware compression before answer generation. Native attention provides signals for context selection, but heterogeneous head behaviors complicate their direct aggregation into sentence-utility scores. We introduce Sentinel, a sentence-level compressor that learns to combine these signals through a signed linear readout across layers and heads. Only the readout is trained using existing QA evidence annotations, while the backbone remains frozen and sentence scoring requires no autoregressive generation. Across twelve LongBench tasks, Sentinel with a 0.5B backbone outperforms Full Context on multiple tasks under a 2,000-token budget with each of three readers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Despite English-only QA supervision, the same readout transfers to Chinese tasks without task-specific retraining. Length-stratified profiling further shows lower compression latency and GPU memory usage than LLMLingua-2 and CPC.

d105dff88b6f0ae17d3eb127.title_original: Tactile MNIST: Benchmarking Active Tactile Perception
d105dff88b6f0ae17d3eb127.excerpt: arXiv:2506.06361v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tactile perception has the potential to significantly enhance dexterous robotic manipulation by providing rich local information that can complement or substitute for other sensory modalities such as vision. However, tactile sensing is an inherently local sensor modality, providing information only at the points of contact. This strict locality necessitates the use of active perception techniques to acquire useful, task-relevant information from manipulated objects or the environment in general. Hence, the agent must actively guide sensors toward regions with more informative or significant features and integrate this information over time to understand a scene or complete a task. While active perception and tactile sensing methods have received significant attention recently, both fields lack standardized benchmarks. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Tactile MNIST Benchmark Suite, an open-source, Gymnasium-compatible benchmark specifically designed for active tactile perception tasks, including classification, localization, pose estimation, and volume estimation. Our benchmark suite offers diverse simulation scenarios, from simple toy environments to complex tactile perception tasks using vision-based tactile sensors. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive dataset comprising 13,580 synthetic 3D MNIST digit models and 153,600 real-world tactile samples collected from 600 3D-printed digits. Using this dataset, we trai

e26140c57368be22ad6ee2b7.title_original: Transferring Visual Explainability from Self-Explaining to Prediction-Only Vision Transformers via Task Arithmetic
e26140c57368be22ad6ee2b7.excerpt: arXiv:2507.04380v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In image classification scenarios where both prediction and explanation efficiency are required, self-explaining models that perform both tasks in a single inference are effective. However, for users who already have prediction-only models, training a new self-explaining model from scratch is costly in both labeling and computation. This study proposes a method to transfer the visual explanation capability of self-explaining Vision Transformer (ViT) models learned in a source domain to prediction-only, zero-shot-capable ViT models based on vision-language models (VLMs) in a target domain via task arithmetic, without target-side explanation supervision. The proposed method endows target models with explanation capability by adding an explainability vector induced by explanation supervision in the source domain based on the task arithmetic framework. Experiments on 10 diverse target datasets show that a single explainability vector learned on ImageNet-1k augmented with patch-level explanation supervision transfers consistently, improving explanation quality while largely preserving classification accuracy. Within-model faithfulness evaluation and comparisons with control vectors (e.g., random vectors of the same norm) show that the transferred explanations are faithful to the model's own predictions and that the effect is specific to the explainability vector. Beyond the transfer itself, we further investigate whether tr

90a6c2a20ef657f3a5d8db3e.title_original: Contrastive Nonmyopic Objective Cost-Tradeoff Acquisition for Longitudinal Data
90a6c2a20ef657f3a5d8db3e.excerpt: arXiv:2507.12412v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In many critical domains, features are not freely available at inference time: each measurement may come with a cost of time, money, and risk. Longitudinal prediction further complicates this setting because both features and labels evolve over time, and measurements missed at earlier timepoints may become permanently unavailable. We propose CAPE (Contrastive Acquisition-Plan Embeddings), a partitioning acquisition policy for longitudinal active feature acquisition. CAPE first defines NOCT, an oracle-based objective that scores a set of future feature-time acquisitions by its expected predictive loss together with its acquisition cost. Based on NOCT, CAPE learns a contrastive acquisition-utility manifold of masked partial observations, where proximity reflects the expected utility of future acquisitions. Offline, training states are embedded and partitioned at each rollout timepoint; candidate future plans are scored within each partition using plug-in NOCT, and the best partition-level acquisition plans are cached. During inference, CAPE retrieves the cached plan via nearest-centroid lookup, enabling low-latency adaptive acquisitions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world healthcare datasets demonstrate that CAPE outperforms nonparametric, greedy, and RL-based alternatives, achieving higher accuracy at lower acquisition costs. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/dzungdinhh/CAPE.

56ac56854c47fd5423e263ae.title_original: Understanding Developer Information Needs for Software with Embedded Natural Language Prompts
56ac56854c47fd5423e263ae.excerpt: arXiv:2507.17264v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Developers use foundation models (FMs) to create novel forms of intelligent software by writing natural language prompts embedded within a software's implementation---referred to as embedded prompts---that are also passed as a string within an FM's API. Developing software with embedded prompts requires developers to engage in iterative embedded prompt changes to obtain the desired behavior. While the information needs of traditional software have been investigated, the information needs of modern developers for embedded prompt changes are underexplored, despite these needs shaping how developers plan and justify embedded prompt changes. In this work, we perform a mixed-method exploratory study on the information needs of developers making changes to embedded prompts. We create, refine, validate, and apply a list of 50 information needs that developers have while making a change to an embedded prompt by interviewing 16 developers, observing 8 developers make prompt changes, surveying 50 developers, and evaluating 72 research and commercial tools. We find that embedded prompts are not well-supported by existing tools: 16 of the 50 information needs, including four of the most important ones, are unaddressed. We conclude with important design opportunities that should be addressed by future developer tools for embedded prompts.

a40f3b05a4854bccf6614485.excerpt: arXiv:2508.13288v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) is a powerful framework for quantifying uncertainty in machine learning models, offering reliable predictions with finite-sample coverage guarantees. When applied to classification, CP produces a prediction set of possible labels that is guaranteed to contain the true label with high probability, regardless of the underlying classifier. However, standard CP treats classes as flat and unstructured, ignoring domain knowledge such as semantic relationships or hierarchical structure among class labels. This paper presents hierarchical conformal classification (HCC), an extension of CP that incorporates class hierarchies into both the structure and semantics of prediction sets. We formulate HCC as a constrained optimization problem whose solutions yield prediction sets composed of nodes at different levels of the hierarchy, while maintaining coverage guarantees. To address the combinatorial nature of the problem, we formally show that a much smaller, well-structured subset of candidate solutions suffices to ensure coverage while upholding optimality. An empirical evaluation on three new benchmarks consisting of audio, image, and text data highlights the advantages of our approach, and a user study shows that annotators significantly prefer hierarchical over flat prediction sets.

e0e6c3d1359d5d5d532aa79e.title_original: Mechanistic Interpretability with Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators
e0e6c3d1359d5d5d532aa79e.excerpt: arXiv:2509.03738v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce sparse autoencoder neural operators (SAE-NOs), a new class of sparse autoencoders that operate in function spaces rather than fixed-dimensional Euclidean representations. We formalize the functional representation hypothesis, where data are explained through sparse compositions of structured functions. Unlike standard SAEs that represent concepts with scalar activations, SAE-NOs parameterize concepts as functions, enabling representations that capture not only a concept's presence, but also how and where it is expressed across the input domain. We achieve this through joint sparsity: concept sparsity selects active concepts, while domain sparsity governs where they are expressed. We instantiate this framework using Fourier neural operators (SAE-FNOs), parameterizing concepts as integral operators in the Fourier domain. This functional and spectral parameterization is particularly advantageous when data exhibit spatial structure across scales or when concepts are frequency-structured. We characterize SAE-FNO on vision data and demonstrate that it learns localized patterns, uses concepts more efficiently, and exhibits stable concept characteristics across sparsity levels. We further show that SAE-FNO adapts to changes in domain size and generalizes across discretizations, operating at resolutions beyond those seen during training, where standard SAEs fail. We also introduce lifting into SAEs and show theoret

0ab8635925ac3e3a05f51100.title_original: ChartHal: A Fine-grained Framework Evaluating Hallucination of Large Vision Language Models in Chart Understanding
0ab8635925ac3e3a05f51100.excerpt: arXiv:2509.17481v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable progress, yet hallucination remains a critical barrier, particularly in chart understanding, which requires sophisticated perceptual and cognitive abilities as well as rigorous factual accuracy. While prior work has investigated hallucinations and chart comprehension independently, their intersection remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ChartHal, a benchmark that features a fine-grained taxonomy of hallucination scenarios in chart understanding, along with a human-validated dataset of 1,062 samples. Our evaluation shows that state-of-the-art LVLMs suffer from severe hallucinations on ChartHal, including proprietary models such as GPT-5 and o4-mini, which achieve only 34.46% and 22.79% accuracy, respectively. Further analysis reveals that questions involving information absent from or contradictory to charts are especially likely to trigger hallucinations, underscoring the urgent need for more robust mitigation strategies. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ymcui/ChartHal

d7561df7d4379f1c587a129a.title_original: Entropy Guided Dynamic Patch Segmentation for Time Series Transformers
d7561df7d4379f1c587a129a.excerpt: arXiv:2509.26157v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Patch-based transformers have emerged as efficient and improved long-horizon modeling architectures for time series modeling. Yet, existing approaches rely on temporally-agnostic patch construction, where arbitrary starting positions and fixed lengths fracture temporal coherence by splitting natural transitions across boundaries. This naive segmentation often disrupts short-term dependencies and weakens representation learning. We propose a novel Entropy-Guided Dynamic Patch Encoder (EntroPE), as a temporally informed framework that dynamically detects transition points via conditional entropy and dynamically places patch boundaries. This preserves temporal structure while retaining the computational benefits of patching. EntroPE consists of two key modules, namely an Entropy-based Dynamic Patcher (EDP) that applies information-theoretic criteria to locate natural temporal shifts and determine patch boundaries, and an Adaptive Patch Encoder (APE) that employs pooling and cross-attention to capture intra-patch dependencies and produce fixed-size latent representations. Extensive experiments on long-term forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection demonstrate that the proposed method improves both accuracy and efficiency, establishing entropy-guided dynamic patching as a promising new paradigm for time series modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/EntroPE.

608e6c7dd1144ef3dc22aaea.title_original: Towards Continual Expansion of Data Coverage: Automatic Text-guided Edge-case Synthesis
608e6c7dd1144ef3dc22aaea.excerpt: arXiv:2509.26158v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The performance of deep neural networks is strongly influenced by the quality of their training data. However, mitigating dataset bias by manually curating challenging edge cases remains a major bottleneck. To address this, we propose an automated pipeline for text-guided edge-case synthesis. Our approach employs a Large Language Model, fine-tuned via preference learning, to rephrase image captions into diverse textual prompts that steer a Text-to-Image model toward generating difficult visual scenarios. Evaluated on the FishEye8K object detection benchmark, our method achieves superior robustness, surpassing both naive augmentation and manually engineered prompts. This work establishes a scalable framework that shifts data curation from manual effort to automated, targeted synthesis, offering a promising direction for developing more reliable and continuously improving AI systems. Code is available at https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/ATES.

7bea8e01b9f5cbb95d1e5ee1.title_original: Feedback Forensics: A Toolkit to Measure AI Personality
7bea8e01b9f5cbb95d1e5ee1.excerpt: arXiv:2509.26305v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Some traits making a "good" AI model are hard to describe upfront. For example, should responses be more polite or more casual? Such traits are sometimes summarized as model character or personality. Without a clear objective, conventional benchmarks based on automatic checks struggle to measure such traits. Evaluation methods using human feedback such as Chatbot Arena have emerged as a popular alternative. These methods infer "better" personality and other desirable traits implicitly by ranking multiple model responses relative to each other. Recent issues with model releases highlight limitations of these existing opaque evaluation approaches: goblin-obsessed, sycophantic and generally over-the-top personalities have resulted in model rollbacks and extensive media coverage. Despite these known issues, limited public tooling exists to explicitly evaluate model personality. We introduce Feedback Forensics: an open-source toolkit to track AI personality and related behavioural traits, both those encouraged by human (or AI) feedback, and those exhibited across AI models trained and evaluated on such feedback. Feedback Forensics is adaptive and can automatically find new traits appearing in models. We demonstrate the toolkit's usefulness in two steps: (A) first we analyse the personality traits encouraged in popular human feedback datasets including MultiPref, PRISM and data from Chatbot Arena; and (B) then use our toolki

8c999dcd93303044723fa58d.title_original: BioBlobs: Unsupervised Discovery of Functional Substructures
8c999dcd93303044723fa58d.excerpt: arXiv:2510.01632v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Protein function is often localized to cohesive substructures, such as catalytic triads, binding pockets, and structural motifs, that occupy only a small fraction of a protein's residues. Yet existing predictive pipelines typically aggregate residue-level embeddings and do not explicitly model or infer these functional substructures, leaving the central biological question unanswered: which substructure of a protein is responsible for its function? We introduce BioBlobs, an encoder-agnostic, end-to-end differentiable framework that compresses a protein into a small set of cohesive substructures (blobs) and predicts function from these blobs alone, so that each blob corresponds to a candidate functional region. Across diverse protein function prediction tasks and both sequence-only and structure-aware protein language models, BioBlobs is competitive with strong baselines while operating on only a small fraction of residues. Trained only on protein function labels, BioBlobs recovers expert-curated functional sites in InterPro and experimentally annotated catalytic sites in the Mechanism and Catalytic Site Atlas, demonstrating unsupervised functional substructure discovery and opening a path to large-scale functional site discovery in unannotated proteins. The discovered blobs adapt their spatial scale to the task, ranging from local catalytic sites to entire structural domains. Code is available at https://github.com/Oli

6e0c371acc1b14253dc67889.title_original: EvolveCaptions: Empowering DHH Users Through Real-Time Collaborative Captioning
6e0c371acc1b14253dc67889.excerpt: arXiv:2510.02181v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems often struggle to accurately transcribe speech from Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHH) speakers. Existing personalization approaches typically require substantial pre-recorded datasets and burden DHH users. We present EvolveCaptions, a collaborative, error-driven personalization system that connects caption correction with speaker-specific ASR adaptation. When transcribing a DHH speaker's speech, hearing partners repair transcription errors, and the system generates short, targeted clauses for the DHH speaker to record. These samples are used to incrementally fine-tune the model. In a study with 12 DHH and six hearing participants, EvolveCaptions reduced Word Error Rate (WER) across five scripted reading rounds, requiring an average of five minutes of additional speech recording. Participants found the interfaces usable but considered recording and correction effortful; acceptability depended on context and anticipated long-term benefit. These findings show the potential of collaborative, cumulative adaptation while exposing the labor and conditions needed to sustain it.

07212a7234dd059ddb92a43b.title_original: Equilibrium Matching: Generative Modeling with Implicit Energy-Based Models
07212a7234dd059ddb92a43b.excerpt: arXiv:2510.02300v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce Equilibrium Matching (EqM), a generative modeling framework built from an equilibrium dynamics perspective. EqM discards the non-equilibrium, time-conditional dynamics in traditional diffusion and flow-based generative models and instead learns the equilibrium gradient of an implicit energy landscape. Through this approach, we can adopt an optimization-based sampling process at inference time, where samples are obtained by gradient descent on the learned landscape with adjustable step sizes, adaptive optimizers, and adaptive compute. Empirically, EqM achieves the best FID among the tested methods, reaching 1.90 on ImageNet 256$\times$256, while remaining competitive on other metrics. Theoretically, we show under standard assumptions that real images are attracting critical points of the learned field and the energy interpretation applies when the field is conservative. Beyond generation, EqM is a flexible framework that naturally handles tasks including partially noised image denoising, OOD detection, and image composition. By replacing time-conditional velocities with a unified equilibrium landscape, EqM offers a tighter bridge between flow and energy-based models and a simple route to optimization-driven inference.

f2026bfa213d2aea75028fa8.title_original: Ergodic Risk Measures: Towards a Risk-Aware Foundation for Continual Reinforcement Learning
