First, Condition-Side Trajectory Guidance fuses LR-derived pixel evidence with the latent LR condition to guide the latent restoration trajectory. Second, Decoder-Side Pixel Grounding injects multi-scale pixel features into the frozen VAE decoder to ground the final rendering with LR-observed cues. To efficiently adapt large pretrained DiT models, we keep the latent autoencoder and main flow-matching backbone frozen, and train only lightweight restoration modules. We further study an efficient local-window attention variant for improved high-resolution efficiency and scalabilit

01e976e5a957405367887efd.title_original: Beyond Uniform Restoration: Empowering All-in-One Restoration with Pixel-Level Multimodal Guidance
01e976e5a957405367887efd.excerpt: arXiv:2608.09482v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: All-in-one image restoration is a unified low-level vision task that aims to effectively recover high-quality images from inputs degraded by various types and levels of corruption using a single model. Recent works have achieved remarkable progress by learning degradation-adaptive prompts or network architectures. However, these methods typically apply a uniform restoration strategy across the entire image, neglecting the fact that different regions may suffer from distinct degradation types and varying degrees of severity. In contrast, we propose to perform restoration at the pixel level, thereby enabling more fine-grained and precise control over the restoration process. Specifically, we present MGN-AIR, a novel pixel-level restoration framework for all-in-one image restoration. Our approach first learns to estimate a pixel-level visual prompt. Then, it leverages both textual and visual prompts to provide global and local degradation cues, guiding the model on where to look and how to restore at each pixel. We conduct extensive experiments on multiple all-in-one image restoration benchmarks, covering a wide range of tasks including denoising, deraining, deblurring, dehazing, desnowing, and low-light enhancement. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method consistently and significantly outperforms existing approaches.

6c88555a48b504ef0217222f.title_original: DDBench: A Benchmark for Agentic Debugging on Distributed Systems
6c88555a48b504ef0217222f.excerpt: arXiv:2608.14863v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-based coding agents have advanced rapidly on single-process SWE tasks, with frontier models now clustering in the high-70s on SWE-bench Verified. Distributed-system debugging, however, remains an under-explored regime: bugs span processes, nodes, and protocol interactions, with root causes rarely recoverable from source alone and brute-force exploration intractable across non-deterministic interleavings. This leaves two gaps in LLM and agent evaluation: no code-repair benchmark targets distributed-system bugs, and no controlled study isolates how much externally provided debugging context changes agent success on them. We introduce DDBench, a code-repair benchmark of 60 historical bugs mined from 13 open-source distributed systems, partitioned into three reasoning-scope tiers. DDBench evaluates every case under two matched conditions: a symptom-only condition where the agent receives only the bug symptom and repository, and a context-augmented condition where it additionally receives bounded debugging context (logs, traces, runtime state, and targeted code-investigation notes), isolating the effect of debugging context from model capability. The evaluation of 10 LLMs on DDBench reveals several findings. First, distributed debugging exercises a reasoning dimension that single-process benchmarks do not surface: models' pass rates span 45 pp, and pairwise bootstrap separates 6 of 15 top-tier model pairs at p < 0.05 on

eaf63bb0e37226f8cb1d4954.title_original: Co-RL: Unsupervised Reasoning Emerges from Diverse Cohort in Multi-agent RL
eaf63bb0e37226f8cb1d4954.excerpt: arXiv:2608.17253v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful approach for improving reasoning in language and vision-language models, yet its strongest successes still depend heavily on ground-truth supervision (e.g., verifiable reward). Such annotations are costly to obtain and become increasingly scarce as reasoning capabilities advance beyond what humans can reliably evaluate. Self-rewarding RL reduces this dependence by enabling models to derive reward signals from their own completions. However, training solely on self-generated feedback can reinforce existing biases, reduce response diversity, and ultimately lead to homogenized responses and training collapse. In this work, we show that unsupervised reasoning can emerge through cooperative multi-agent training. We introduce Co-RL, a framework in which multiple decoupled models, sharing no parameters, are simultaneously optimized through RL using rewards derived from the other agent. We further show that increasing cohort diversity, through heterogeneous model families, sizes, and rephrased training samples, reduces the correlated errors that drive self-reinforcing feedback loops. This diversity consistently improves reasoning performance and mitigates training collapse. Without any ground-truth labels, Co-RL improves the base models by 3.0-7.9% on average across seven benchmarks and by 1.6-4.4% across four multimodal benchmarks. It also outperforms the prior state-of-th

9b5bc0d6590d4568131a3929.title_original: Physics-Unrolled Neural Operator for Accelerating High-Fidelity Wireless Ray Tracing
9b5bc0d6590d4568131a3929.excerpt: arXiv:2608.18495v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Site-specific wireless design relies on ray tracing to predict how signal strength varies across a floorplan, but a converged indoor radio map takes tens of seconds to simulate and planning a single building requires thousands of them. A learned surrogate can remove most of that cost, yet training one runs into a second problem: high-fidelity labels are exactly what is too expensive to produce at scale, so the affordable labels come from finite-ray simulations that carry residual Monte Carlo noise. We address this with RayNO, a physics-unrolled neural operator that reconstructs the converged output of a ray tracer from one cheap low-fidelity run and scene priors. Rather than treating a radio map as a generic image, RayNO refines the field through three stages matched to reflection, diffraction, and scattering, each supervised by a label of matching physical complexity. We prove that when the label error is conditionally unbiased the learned operator can end up closer to the high-fidelity reference than the labels it was trained on, and we verify that condition directly in the simulator using repeated independent ray seeds. Across diverse floorplans, RayNO outperforms image-to-image baselines, wireless learning models, monolithic neural operators, and classical multi-fidelity regression on both image-quality and wireless deployment metrics, while reducing the cost of a high-fidelity map from roughly 28 s to 0.11 s.

be0f97793a5fdbaefd3c3a14.title_original: LAION-BVD: A 13-Million-Hour Open Video Dataset for Multimodal Pre-training
be0f97793a5fdbaefd3c3a14.excerpt: arXiv:2608.24845v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present LAION-BVD (LAION - Big Video Dataset), a large-scale open video dataset for multimodal learning, which contains 1.3B platform-specific video URLs collected from CommonCrawl. From these, we download 80M videos with a total duration of 13.5 million hours. The dataset is designed for multimodal pre-training across the video, audio, and image modalities. Using content-aware scene detection, we extract clips for which we synthetically generate video and audio captions. Models trained on these data achieve competitive performance on standard video-text and audio-text benchmarks, with consistent improvements as training or model scale increases. Additionally, we explore video frames as an alternative source of image-text data by extracting scene-changing frames. These frames exhibit a visual distribution distinct from standard web image corpora, and models trained on this dataset achieve strong image-text retrieval performance. We release LAION-BVD to the research community. It significantly expands open access to multimodal videos at an unprecedented scale.

db7957c3b9dadcb1a3d0aa48.title_original: TraceML: What Auto-Research Agents Miss in Long-Horizon ML Development
db7957c3b9dadcb1a3d0aa48.excerpt: arXiv:2608.26086v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Auto-research agents now run machine-learning development unattended for hours, revising data pipelines, models, and validation from their own feedback, yet on most competitions they still finish below strong human competitors. Outcome-based benchmarks record this gap but not its cause, because they grade the final submission and discard the development process behind it. We introduce TraceML, which pairs human and agent work on the same competitions under one version-level schema: 4,465 human Kaggle trajectories across 134 competitions, seven of which are also worked by two agent scaffolds, giving 430 paired human and 207 agent trajectories. Every code version carries its score, its timestamp, and labels for the action taken, its intent, the edit size, and the score effect. Read this way, the gap becomes concrete. Experts alternate data work, validation, model changes, and ensembling, and return to approaches they had set aside. Each agent scaffold instead collapses into a narrow loop: Codex spends its steps re-weighting ensembles and tuning submissions, MLEvolve mutates its model in place, and neither pivots at the human rate nor reopens abandoned work. A short planning prompt distilled from human practice moves the behaviors it names toward the human profile and lifts scores, but the effort profile stays agent-shaped: instruction closes only the part of the gap that reduces to instructions. We release the corpus, th

d47c7dd0add6cc7d165abff6.title_original: Partition-Aware Unlearning for Removing Spurious Correlations in Large Vision-Language Models
d47c7dd0add6cc7d165abff6.excerpt: arXiv:2608.29996v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) achieve strong performance across many multimodal tasks; however, they often exploit spurious object-background correlations, resulting in predictions driven by contextual shortcuts rather than object-relevant visual evidence. Despite growing interest in hallucination and robustness evaluation, existing benchmarks provide limited control over whether model predictions are grounded in the target object or induced by correlated background cues. In this work, we introduce PURGE (\underline{P}artition-aware \underline{U}nlearning for \underline{R}emoving spurious-correlation \underline{G}enerated \underline{E}rrors), a framework for constructing, benchmarking, and mitigating spurious-correlation-induced failures in LVLMs. The framework consists of: -- (1) Structured dataset construction wherein we develop three complementary structured data construction strategies that partition examples by object-relevant evidence and spurious background cues, enabling controlled diagnosis of shortcut reliance; and -- (2) Partition-aware unlearning, which uses these partitions to selectively remove spurious object-background associations while preserving object-based reasoning. We evaluate the \algo~framework across multiple LVLMs, including LLaVA-1.6-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-9B, together with CLIP as a vision-language encoder, on a diverse suite of benchmarks, including CHAIR, POPE, Causa

77288b67478d73b3866495f3.title_original: A Study of Hidden-State Optimization Order in Predictive Coding Networks
77288b67478d73b3866495f3.excerpt: arXiv:2609.00686v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Local learning methods offer an alternative to end-to-end backpropagation, but their unstructured local objectives can produce weak feature learning in deep networks. We study whether the order of hidden-state optimization can address this limitation. We propose a boundary-first inference schedule that partitions a model into chunks, first coordinates hidden states at chunk boundaries, and then refines representations within each chunk. We instantiate this schedule in predictive coding networks (PCNs), a local-learning framework in which hidden activities and prediction errors are explicitly exposed during inference. On CIFAR-10, the resulting boundary-first predictive-coding instantiation improves accuracy over standard predictive coding by $9.77\%$ under a standard parametrization and by $5.51\%$ under a $\mu$-parametrization. Diagnostic analyses further show more non-trivial early-layer updates, lower initial-to-final CKA, and more diverse layerwise gradients, consistent with stronger feature learning. These results support boundary-first, chunk-based inference as a practical design principle for predictive-coding training and motivate its study in broader local-learning systems.

6e396b8b63b6add507c40976.title_original: VOIM: Training-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Instance Mapping for RGB-D and Monocular SLAM
6e396b8b63b6add507c40976.excerpt: arXiv:2609.00775v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robots that act on everyday language requests need maps that record what each object is and where it is. Existing open-vocabulary 3D mapping systems usually require a depth sensor and commit to each object the first time they see it, when the evidence is weakest. We present VOIM, a training-free system that builds open-vocabulary 3D instance maps from RGB-D or from monocular RGB video alone. VOIM accumulates soft label evidence from frozen, off-the-shelf perception models in every voxel across views, and decides labels and object instances only after that evidence has built up. On ScanNet++, VOIM achieves the highest present-class mIoU among the compared methods, 10 points above the strongest baseline. From monocular video alone, VOIM also exceeds HOV-SG and ConceptGraphs run with depth and ground-truth poses. We also conduct real-robot navigation experiments on a quadruped to show that VOIM maps are usable in the real world.

6f47e3745f7cd0cfe734a469.title_original: Dual-Part Multi-Lateral Branched Network for Multi-Class Segmentation in Cardiovascular Catheterization Angiograms
6f47e3745f7cd0cfe734a469.excerpt: arXiv:2609.04590v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Catheterisation image processing requires segmentation models that are fast, accurate and explainable. While most of the existing studies usually focus on binary segmentation, there is a recent demand for simultaneous segmentation of multiple structures found in catheterization scenes. In this study, a dual-part MLBNet architecture is designed with multi-lateral encoder blocks and multi-head decoder branches for class-aware segmentation in cardiovascular catheterization scenes. Lateral branches in the encoder enable repeated feature extraction to learn diverse shared representations, while multiple decoder heads are used to introduce class-skewed branches that specialize in different structural properties in catheterization scenes. To analyze the performances of the dual-part MLBNet architecture, several multi-class segmentation angiogram data obtained during cardiovascular catheterization in phantom models, synthetic human-simulated aorta, and animal model are used for model training and evaluation. Results obtained showed the dual-part models could effectively separate guidewire, catheter, vessels and background pixels to their classes of memberships with high probability. The results demonstrate that all models were able to distinguish the dominant background class from foreground structures with high overall accuracy.

b5ea6a82515741959a78d7aa.title_original: The Geometry of Refusal: Why Post-Hoc Refusal Is Fragile and Pretraining-Time Refusal Persists
b5ea6a82515741959a78d7aa.excerpt: arXiv:2609.06934v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Post-hoc safety training (RLHF, DPO) is the dominant way to align large language models, yet jailbreaks (Zou et al., 2023), fine-tuning attacks (Qi et al., 2024), and activation-space edits (Arditi et al., 2024) keep recovering the behaviors it was meant to remove. We give this fragility one geometric explanation and follow it into pretraining. We measure the safety update $\Delta = W_{safe} - W_{base}$ against the curvature of the model's capabilities (the empirical Fisher of a capability loss). Across five model families, post-hoc safety lands in a suppression regime: $\Delta$ is nearly orthogonal to the capability directions, and its small in-subspace part concentrates on a few high-curvature ones. The update is thin but sharp, a refusal gate laid over intact capabilities rather than erasure of them. A kernel-immobility lemma explains why such an update can only mask a capability, not remove it, and a little benign fine-tuning switches the gate off: 100 benign examples cut the AdvBench refusal of Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3-8B-Instruct by 35 to 38 pp. Following the account into pretraining, a pretraining-checkpoint sweep of OLMo-2-1B (Team OLMo et al., 2024) shows the features that refusal attaches to emerging in a sharp transition between 1B and 63B pretraining tokens. We then use the account constructively: models trained from scratch with safety co-training spread continuously across pretraining reach 87 to

2614e4cc3ecc563d37840999.title_original: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
2614e4cc3ecc563d37840999.excerpt: arXiv:2609.06951v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism). Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The o

597d2cb489a313b12fa2db97.title_original: Topology Obstructs Pure Foundation Neural Quantum States
597d2cb489a313b12fa2db97.excerpt: arXiv:2609.07591v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation models for ground states in spin-1/2 systems are a promising method for problems ranging from quantum chemistry to identifying new phase diagrams. Nearly all such models are currently pure-states that condition on the Hamiltonian's parameters, whose Monte Carlo samples give energy estimates according to the variational principle. In this contribution, we show that this representation is topologically obstructed. For any gapped Hamiltonian family whose ground-state bundle is non-trivial, every continuous normalized state-vector model has zero fidelity with the ground state at some parameter value in the Hamiltonian family. For that value, the energy is at least one spectral gap, $\Delta$, with an $O(\Delta)$ gap in an open-neighbourhood of that point. We show that this is a sufficient no-go also in the case of degenerate ground-state manifolds, time dynamics, and periodic systems with mixed space-time topology, demonstrating these obstructions on one- and two-qubit systems. We discuss how this causes a spike in the fidelity susceptibility, giving a numerical signature of a phase-transition where there is none. Finally, we show that operator-valued models canonically avoid these obstructions and preserve topological information, implying a structural necessity in representation for foundation neural quantum states.

cf2110e5c79eeaa1485c9113.title_original: A Graph-Based Approach for Mapping Kernel-Level Telemetry to MITRE ATT&CK
cf2110e5c79eeaa1485c9113.excerpt: arXiv:2609.12841v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mapping observed system behavior to standardized frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK is essential for threat-informed defense. Existing automated methods mostly depend on Cyber Threat Intelligence reports, which offer only retrospective accounts of attacks. Kernel-level telemetry, i.e., system calls, instead provides first-hand evidence of adversary behavior, but its volume and complexity have limited its use for automated mapping. Its content also makes it unsuitable for cloud-based analysis: command lines carry credentials, events carry user identifiers and network endpoints, and during an incident the telemetry reveals which defenses failed. In this work, we present Trace2ATT&CK, a framework that maps kernel-level telemetry to ATT&CK techniques entirely within the defender's infrastructure. Trace2ATT&CK collects events via eBPF, reconstructs the attacker's activity as a process-centric provenance graph, and condenses it into a compact execution graph. This graph is classified by locally deployed open-weight LLMs, using either pure prompting or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in the ATT&CK knowledge base, producing ranked technique candidates with supporting rationales. We evaluate Trace2ATT&CK on 347 Linux Atomic Red Team tests with seven open-weight LLMs. The best local configuration reaches an HR@5 of 66.57\% at the technique level. RAG improves over base prompting in every model and setting, by up to $+

57a17306e95a502cb5b54870.title_original: NeuroActiSep: Detecting Factual Hallucinations from Feed-Forward Neurons in a Single Pass
57a17306e95a502cb5b54870.excerpt: arXiv:2609.14448v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hallucination in large language models reduces their reliability and slows adoption. Various white-box studies have used internal representations to detect patterns of truthfulness and factuality. A less-studied approach is to identify feed-forward neurons correlated with hallucination. In this empirical study, we propose a method to rank feed-forward neurons at the final prompt token and use it to investigate the feasibility of utilizing them for hallucination detection in the first forward pass. Using a neuron selection dataset built from CounterFact for identifying neurons correlated with hallucination, we transfer the selected neuron identities to train hallucination classifiers on other factual question-answering datasets. Our work provides empirical evidence that probes trained using the features from sparse sets of selected neurons perform on par with probes trained on internal representations. We also analyze the distribution of selected neurons and the effects of layer depth and neuron budget on detection performance. Our results show that randomly drawn neuron sets are also competitive at larger budgets, suggesting that signals correlated with hallucination are distributed across many neurons, while selection can help in extremely sparse sets.

705ef76299e12e809772d522.title_original: CIDERS: Cloud-Edge LLM Collaborative Learning via Accelerating Personalized Bilevel Optimization
705ef76299e12e809772d522.excerpt: arXiv:2609.15664v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Amid the rapid advancement of physical-world intelligence, cloud-edge collaborative large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising roadmap for practical LLM deployment. However, existing cloud-edge paradigms struggle to balance global consensus with local personalization, which fails to satisfy the need for a unified knowledge foundation on the cloud and domain-specific adaptation at the edge. To address this, we introduce, for the first time, a personalized bilevel optimization framework that formalizes cloud-edge LLM collaboration as a dual structure: the upper level optimizes edge-side personalization, while the lower level governs cloud-side knowledge transfer, reaching cloud-edge evolving in coordination. We then propose CIDERS, an efficient solver that decomposes the model into a learnable backbone and a messenger. While the cloud performs knowledge transfer to the learnable backbone, the key lies in embedding global trajectories into each local personalization step via consensus-variate correction to reconcile personalization with consensus. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis, including a geometric characterization of the local trajectory and a full convergence guarantee, revealing an explicit trade-off structure between personalization and global convergence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CIDERS consistently outperforms competitive baselines on the compressed edge path, with 3.1x

55836285a9c443a8a9aa57be.title_original: Whom Do AI Agents Serve? Role-Induced Sponsorship Bias in Decision Models and Generative LLMs
55836285a9c443a8a9aa57be.excerpt: arXiv:2609.17989v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Consumers increasingly delegate product search to AI shopping agents powered by generative large language models (LLMs) or non-generative decision models. Because retail platforms monetize through sponsored listings that consumers typically discount, we examine whether an AI agent's evaluation of sponsored listings depends on who delegates it. Across six LLMs and six decision models in Study 1, consumer-delegated agents penalize sponsored listings, whereas naming a booking platform as principal significantly attenuates this sponsorship penalty without instructions to favor advertisers. This sponsorship bias replicates across prompt wordings and LLM reasoning efforts and operates through reduced pre-choice skepticism in LLMs. In Study 2, attributing the paid placement to the platform amplifies sponsorship bias across both model families, and stricter disclosure wording ("Sponsored" vs. "Promoted") fails to eliminate it. In Study 3, prompt-level mitigation removes platform leniency but can over-correct the sponsorship penalty, whereas consumer-aligned fine-tuning eliminates sponsorship bias and better preserves baseline preferences.

c1fec6f148158c0403aa7859.title_original: CoRe-MARL: Cooperative Redistribution Under Unknown Dynamics Using Recurrent Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
c1fec6f148158c0403aa7859.excerpt: arXiv:2609.18639v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Emergency management assistance programs, such as relief distribution, are essential for delivering necessary supplies to affected communities. However, these programs operate in a decentralized network of local centers that face uncertain local demand and supply dynamics, resulting in inconsistent avail- ability of local services. Redistribution of supplies among these local centers reduces these imbalances, but the centers often make decisions independently, with limited information and disrupted transportation. This study develops CoRe-MARL, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework, by formulating a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP). We treat each center as an agent that learns a redistribution policy to improve the service in the worst-case region and reduce the service gap across regions while protecting network-wide service. We incorporate a recurrent network that captures evolving supply and demand dynamics without direct observation, while multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) enables centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE). We evaluate the framework in a simulated environment with diverse trajectories, where exact dynamics are not observed by actors and the MAPPO critic. We compare the recurrent MAPPO with the recurrent independent PPO (IPPO) and a local only heuristic, and find that MAPPO reduces the service gap across lo

d4ec26dc89ba9a6fcab91d7e.title_original: On Emergent Capabilities and Model Merging
d4ec26dc89ba9a6fcab91d7e.excerpt: arXiv:2609.24504v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned checkpoints by arithmetic on their weights, and is now a routine way to assemble capabilities cheaply. We ask what it does to emergent capabilities: behaviors that arise from fine-tuning but were never an explicit training target. Studying two independent testbeds (activation oracles and emergent-misaligned models) across three model families, we find that the answer is threefold. First, merging preserves an emergent capability that both parents carry: merging two misaligned checkpoints retains most of their broad misalignment across the whole mixing range. Second, merging cannot create an emergent capability that is superadditive in its parents: no weighted merge of two single-task oracles reaches the jointly-trained oracle's auditing ability. Third, when only one parent carries the capability, merging dilutes it faster than the trained capability that accompanies it: the gap is significant in most settings.

5c921146972bd29ce259bca2.title_original: Stable Unsupervised Continual Chunking with Sheaf SyncMap
5c921146972bd29ce259bca2.excerpt: arXiv:2609.25143v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unsupervised Continual chunking is a fundamental problem in machine learning and neuroscience, where the goal is to identify groups of states that frequently co-occur in temporal sequences. A key challenge is to form accurate chunks while maintaining their stability over time. In this work, we propose sheaf regularization to reduce local inconsistencies in Decentralized SyncMap, a self-organizing system, and thereby stabilize its chunking dynamics. We introduce a radial sheaf structure that penalizes distance-dependent radial motion between pairs of variables. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves the highest normalized mutual information (NMI) among the evaluated SyncMap variants on 12 of 18 probabilistic Continual General Chunking Problem (CGCP) graphs with two-state memory and on 17 of 18 graphs with dynamic memory. In the sequential adaptation experiment, Sheaf SyncMap also achieves high NMI after shifts in the input distribution, indicating that it can adapt to new knowledge while avoiding the negative transfer commonly observed in modern machine learning systems such as neural networks.

287a11e2db80afe5393f1498.title_original: PoEM: Predicting RL Outcomes from Existing Policies
287a11e2db80afe5393f1498.excerpt: arXiv:2609.30226v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation models are post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL) to maximize specific rewards, such as helpfulness, correctness, or instruction following. This post-training process is computationally intensive, sometimes unstable, and has to be run from scratch every time the reward model changes or when we want to combine multiple rewards. We hence ask: given a new reward function, is it possible to predict the policy RL would produce without actually training on that reward? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing PoEM, a framework for predicting RL outcomes using models previously trained on other rewards. First, we build on the fact that if the new reward function can be written as a linear combination of existing ones, then the optimal policy can be expressed as a combination of the existing policies in log-probability space. Surprisingly, even in cases where the rewards are not linearly connected, we observe that policies learned through RL often span an approximately low-rank subspace across rewards. To our benefit, the weights for this combination can be estimated using only the reward or basis policy outputs on the samples. We turn these observations into an algorithm that takes post-trained models and a target reward function, and approximates the target RL policy without any additional RL training. We experimentally evaluate our approach across programmatic and learned rewards for open-ended gen

4cb599238ae30503addd458a.title_original: FOCUS: Benchmarking Retinal Model Generalization from Foundation Vision Encoders to Multimodal LLMs
4cb599238ae30503addd458a.excerpt: arXiv:2609.33158v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Progress in AI-based retinal image analysis has accelerated with the adoption of foundation models, yet evaluating their real-world reliability remains challenging. Performance reported on a single dataset does not capture how models behave under dataset shift, across clinical definitions, or for different patient subgroups. This limitation is particularly critical in medical imaging, where robustness, calibration, and fairness are essential for safe deployment. We introduce FOCUS (Foundation Ophthalmic Cross-Dataset Understanding under Shift), a cross-dataset benchmark evaluating retinal fundus models across vision-only encoder models (VM), vision-language dual-encoder models (VLM), and multimodal large language models (MLLM). FOCUS harmonizes binary diabetic retinopathy, referable diabetic retinopathy, and glaucomatous optic neuropathy tasks across ten public datasets spanning diverse geographies, acquisition conditions, and label protocols. The benchmark evaluates models through a unified analysis layer that measures ranking performance, calibration, subgroup disparities, and image-quality robustness. We present a large-scale evaluation covering 532 base configurations and 228 MLLM configurations adapted via LoRA fine-tuning. Results show no model family consistently dominates across tasks and datasets: general VM encoders achieve the strongest average ranking performance, medical MLLMs are competitive but variable,

29bd0f6865e287c5ee101cfb.title_original: VEX-Bench: Benchmarking Verification Complexity of LLM-Generated Misinformation
29bd0f6865e287c5ee101cfb.excerpt: arXiv:2609.35028v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made misinformation inexpensive to produce but not to verify, creating a growing asymmetry in the information ecosystem. Under tight time, labor, and budget constraints, media organizations, platforms, and fact-checkers rely on screening to prioritize which content to verify. We introduce VEX-Bench, a unified benchmark for evaluating the verification complexity of LLM-generated misinformation, as perceived during screening, across models and generation methods. Verification complexity is assessed along multiple dimensions derived from journalistic and fact-checking practices, capturing checkability, harm potential, source credibility signals, imposter legitimacy, and expected verification effort. We define the VEX score as an integrated measure combining elicitation yield and verification complexity to quantify how generated content consumes limited verification capacity. We construct a benchmark spanning two misinformation categories, 6 high-stakes domains, and 60 real-world topics, and evaluate 7 frontier LLMs and 7 generation methods, yielding 5{,}880 articles. We employ an LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation and validate it using content-analysis methodology, including ordinal Krippendorff $\alpha$ for inter-annotator reliability, complemented by fact-checking agents for verification. Our findings show that no single method dominates all dimensions, underscoring the need for multi

2be2ef497a34cfdb72dd74bc.title_original: Typed Edge-Tensor Non-Reciprocal Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation for Counterfactual Open-World Deductive Reasoning
2be2ef497a34cfdb72dd74bc.excerpt: arXiv:2609.37351v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scaling test-time computation in continuous latent spaces offers an attractive alternative to verbose token-by-token generation for multi-step deductive reasoning. 3ffa2dff3e74e3cb3d5b6820.title_original: From Search to Signal: Search-Value Credit for Evolutionary Automatic Heuristic Design
3ffa2dff3e74e3cb3d5b6820.excerpt: arXiv:2609.39383v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models generate candidate programs for automatic heuristic design, while evolutionary search evaluates and selects them to guide further generation. Online post-training uses rewards from candidate evaluations to adapt the generator. Retained programs can also guide later generation as parents. This motivates rewards that reflect their reuse opportunities beyond immediate fitness. We propose Search-value credit (SVC), which constructs response-level rewards from actual admission to the retained set and a short-term parent-exposure proxy. Admission determines reward eligibility; the proxy weights eligible responses by reuse opportunities under existing parent-selection rules. Rewards are computed after candidate evaluation, without evaluating descendants. SVC retains the search and learning procedures of the Co-Evolution of Algorithms and Language Model (CALM) framework. Across four combinatorial optimization tasks with the same base model and response budget, SVC achieves the best mean final search performance on three tasks among six conditions. Under identical prompts and parents on traveling salesman and capacitated vehicle routing tasks, SVC-trained generators yield a higher mean proportion of responses whose programs outperform the best prompting parent than those trained with CALM's native reward. These findings support reward construction using search retention and selection information.

9c86853caad108ad2075925a.title_original: Toward Controlling Biology with Language: Offline Learning of Prompt-Conditioned Interventions for Cells, Organoids, and Biobots
9c86853caad108ad2075925a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.02247v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Natural language has become an interface to code, images and molecules, but not to living matter: a stimulus applied to cells has no fixed linguistic meaning, and every paired example of an instruction and its outcome costs a wet-lab experiment. We ask how far an existing archive of experiments can take this interface, using xenobots, motile multicellular constructs made of frog cells, stimulated by a single electrical pulse of varying duration. We re-track 155 archived recordings with two independent methods, measure what the pulse does from each bot's own behaviour before and after it, and separate behaviours the pulse controls from behaviours it does not. Longer pulses stop bots and short pulses leave them moving, sometimes faster; turning direction and starting from rest do not depend on duration, and restarting at most weakly. We then replace hand-made behaviour labels with a blind language critic: fresh sessions of a multimodal language model read plots of each bot and score how well its behaviour matches each of 176 instructions. The critic agrees with the measured labels whenever its plots contain the information the labels are defined on, and dose curves learned from its scores match those learned from the measurements. A prompt-to-intervention model trained only on critic scores maps unseen instructions, including negations, to the right end of the dose range on unseen bots, as well as the same model trained

b0d027c4ca7bc99b9284e2aa.title_original: Certified Mechanistic Edits: Behavioral Guarantees for Skill Removal and Preservation
b0d027c4ca7bc99b9284e2aa.excerpt: arXiv:2610.03502v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mechanistic edits (ablations, weight edits, activation steering) are the standard tools for unlearning a harmful capability from a neural network while preserving useful ones. Current approaches validate their effects only by testing, which can never cover an entire continuous region of inputs. Prior work at the interpretability-verification boundary certifies descriptions of a model: what a circuit computes, or whether it faithfully explains the whole. We instead certify the behavioral effect of an edit: that disabling a circuit removes one skill and provably preserves another, for every input in a region; a feature non-interference guarantee in the information-flow-security sense. We demonstrate such certified edits from toy ReLU networks up to a standard softmax + LayerNorm transformer, proving removal and preservation over continuous embedding-space regions and reaching roughly 9x the input-perturbation dimension an exact solver can handle by switching to sound bound propagation. Furthermore, we prove that no finite deterministic black-box test can certify removal, exhibiting an edit that passes exhaustive testing yet provably fails on a survivor pocket that can be made arbitrarily small. Guarantees hold on small, standard-architecture networks and, like any removal claim, presuppose that the target skill admits a decidable specification, a property which real-world harms may not have.

ea6aa68f7fb5566a7768e965.title_original: SparseCraft: Agentic Hardware-Software Co-Optimization for Sparse Computing
ea6aa68f7fb5566a7768e965.excerpt: arXiv:2610.05037v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse-accelerator design spaces are usually searched against analytical models, so a design is judged by a model's prediction rather than by a measurement of the hardware. Post-synthesis timing analysis checks its clock, and its energy is computed from measured counters, with per-event energies validated against gate-level and SRAM-macro data. We compare the agent with expert Gemmini configurations and with random, greedy and multi-objective TPE search at the agent's budget of 15 evaluations, all measured by the same flow. On a GraphChallenge sparse-DNN layer, the agent's designs reach 159-164$\times$ the inverse energy-delay-area product of stock Gemmini and 2.07-2.14$\times$ that of the best expert configuration. Their Pareto hypervolume is 0.5557-0.5704, against at most 0.2806 for search. On a power-law graph and a pruned BERT layer, the agent raises perf/W by 11.45$\times$ and 4.43$\times$, and held-out transfer shows that its designs specialise to their workload. The loop is also resilient to faulty designs. When a design fails a check, a repair agent diagnoses the failure from its evidence

123185a80b5a01096cc7e8ab.excerpt: arXiv:2610.05533v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. 6b06d702a1e712fd6e3218d2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16822v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. Neural architectures are operation-labeled directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where edge directions determine computational roles and execution dependencies. Existing graph Transformer predictors incorporate topological and directional information in different ways, but primarily focus on specific mechanisms rather than coordinated encoder-wide modeling of these semantics. We introduce encoder-wide directional consistency, a design principle that coordinates the modeling of directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature updates. To implement this principle, we propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer that integrates direction- and topology-aware node initialization, magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative RNN-, CNN-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and magnetic spectral controls support the contribution of the direction-aware stages and orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics characterize module beha

ae6463f330fdda62a8e58fe7.title_original: CWE-bench: Refocusing Agentic Security from Exploitation to Defense
ae6463f330fdda62a8e58fe7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17020v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have focused largely on offense, yet a working exploit does not show that an agent can make software safe. An attacker needs to exploit only one vulnerability; a defender must find and fix all of them. We introduce CWE-bench, a benchmark of 250 repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 185 CWE types and eight languages, grouped into ten weakness classes. We release 100 tasks publicly and keep 150 held out. Agents are given a repository to audit and a description of its threat model, but are not told the weakness, where it occurs, or how many vulnerable sites there are. Each patch must block the exploit while preserving original functionality, as checked by a deterministic programmatic verifier. Verifiers were curated with panels of agentic judges and reviewed by hand, so that they reject incomplete repairs without penalizing correct ones. The best agent reaches 67% pass@1 and 79% pass@4. We further conduct analyses showing that (i) agents with similar pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, and (ii) no single agent is best across languages or weakness classes. As the offensive capabilities of agents improve, CWE-bench provides a broad and rigorous measure of whether their defensive capabilities keep pace.

d402945dbb5e1048d2555acc.title_original: RELAY: Selective Self-Distillation with Adaptive Hand-off for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
d402945dbb5e1048d2555acc.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17623v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning grades a response against many written criteria but collapses them into one reward, which discards the detail the rubric carries and gives no GRPO reward gradient when a group's responses tie. A frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context provides token-level supervision, but we observe an early plateau in the gains over GRPO. RELAY uses advantages and rewards to select positive-advantage and low-scoring zero-advantage rollouts, and monitors the distillation loss to decide when to retire the teacher. Stage 1 combines selective distillation from a frozen teacher with GRPO; a plateau detector then removes the teacher, and Stage 2 continues with GRPO alone. Calibrated on one model-domain pair and reused unchanged in three others, the plateau detector fires between steps 122 and 171. RELAY scores highest in-domain among the compared methods in all four settings, ahead of GRPO on RaR-Medicine by 4.62 points with Qwen3-1.7B and 6.02 with Qwen3-4B. On Qwen3-1.7B/Medicine, removing the teacher from a shared checkpoint outperforms keeping, weakening or refreshing it. Distilling selected rollouts covering about half the response tokens also outperforms distilling all rollouts at a matched average coefficient.

b0610b509183cd9f31a410f8.title_original: JevGPT: Thinking Fast and Slow in Autonomous Research
b0610b509183cd9f31a410f8.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18272v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous research agents must acquire and reason over evidence within a limited budget. Yet relevant sources can remain uninspected or unused, leaving a gap between retrieval coverage and the evidence that informs research. The challenge is to align fast local judgments with changing evidence needs and feed their findings back into research decisions. We introduce JevGPT, a dual-system architecture for autonomous research that couples fast evidence processing with deliberative research planning. System Two sets evidence objectives and integrates findings, while System One locates support, assesses relevance, and guides further inspection. Independent source judgments run in parallel; selected original passages inform the next research step. Experiments on fixed-corpus question answering and document ranking show that JevGPT achieves leading task performance, with faster completion and lower cost than comparably effective research agents. Evidence analysis shows broader source inspection and greater coverage of supporting documents in the research loop, highlighting efficient evidence processing as a route to more capable autonomous research.

39283defd61e8d057b2357c0.title_original: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
39283defd61e8d057b2357c0.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18654v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.

765b4bc25f367536bd6204bd.title_original: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Policy Improvement via Flow-Reversed Action Anchors
765b4bc25f367536bd6204bd.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22852v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalist robot policies offer strong behavioral priors, but achieving deployment-level reliability and throughput remains difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these policies, yet its effectiveness is constrained by the cost of online interaction. Existing methods adapt frozen flow-matching policies by treating noise space as a continuous action space. We show that this behaviorally unstructured space makes exploration inefficient, often preventing these methods from extracting meaningful learning signals on challenging tasks. We introduce AnchorQ, which enables coarse-to-fine policy improvement through a structured, refinable latent action representation. At each decision step, AnchorQ uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, samples local particles around those anchors, and applies value-guided sampling to explore promising refinements. Our analysis shows that anchors reduce identification complexity at the cost of support bias; particle refinement trades this bias against action-class complexity; and critic accuracy determines the reliability of KL-regularized, value-guided selection. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, AnchorQ outperforms state-of-the-art post-training baselines in sample efficiency, delivering a 37% improvement in real-world success rate and 97% higher simulated task throughput under the same interaction budget. 9b8c422b129a9aba4741b878.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23550v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies optimized for task rewards may produce behaviors that are efficient but misaligned with human expectations, safety preferences, or intent. In addition to preference labels, the framework incorporates reason tags explaining why a behavior is preferred, enabling the learned reward to capture both human choices and their underlying rationale. Compared with preference-only reward learning, the reason-guided formulation provides additional supervision for learning human-aligned rewards and improves the interpretability of the resulting policy. The learned human reward is combined with the environment reward during policy optimization, allowing the agent to improve task performance while producing more interpretable, human- aligned, and preference-sensitive behavior

5313ae9c22d98f4fc1beeadf.title_original: A learner-free swarm approximates the explore-exploit equilibrium allocation: A self-organized attractor in place of reinforcement-learning machinery
5313ae9c22d98f4fc1beeadf.excerpt: arXiv:2610.25113v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) solves the explore-exploit problem by training a learner on reward; its multi-agent, resource-sharing form has an equilibrium allocation as its optimum -- the ideal-free distribution (IFD), the Nash equilibrium of a congestion game. 7468e42039147973f33a7529.excerpt: arXiv:2610.26507v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A bimanual demonstration specifies both what the robot should do and one particular schedule for when each arm should act. Standard imitation learning does not distinguish task-required cross-arm constraints from incidental scheduling choices, and may therefore exploit opposite-arm progress as a shortcut cue, creating spurious cross-arm coupling even where relative timing is irrelevant for the current task phase. We introduce Constraint-preserving Temporal Recombination (CTR), a training-time data intervention that preserves recorded arm-local sensorimotor content while retiming the corresponding segments to realize admissible schedules that preserve task-required cross-arm constraints. We use CTR to train Diffusion Policy, Action Chunking with Transformers, and $\pi_{0.5}$, and evaluate them on four simulated and four real-robot tasks. Across six real-robot bimanual progress-state initializations, CTR raises worst-state success from 56% for the strongest non-CTR schedule mixture to 76%. With $\pi_{0.5}$ on an Independent task, a 4 s pause transfers 2.56 s of delay to the opposite arm under the Concurrent schedule distribution, but only 0.25 s with CTR. 83fefafd8620fa71b4b63e2f.title_original: Anytime-Valid Runtime Monitoring of Learned Barrier Certificates
83fefafd8620fa71b4b63e2f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.27726v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monit

6b271a31ab26f7fc9e48341d.title_original: Polarity Blindness in LLM Safety: A Systematic Study of Negation, Antonym Substitution, and Adversarial Framing
6b271a31ab26f7fc9e48341d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.27908v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Negation remains a persistent challenge for language models across NLP tasks and modalities. We show that this weakness can undermine LLM safety guardrails through a structural vulnerability we term polarity blindness: the failure to recognize harmful intent after polarity-altering linguistic transformations. 95a0812a4d49c0ac5859cf11.excerpt: arXiv:2610.29098v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. f96df396248d12a4dcd67c93.title_original: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
f96df396248d12a4dcd67c93.excerpt: arXiv:2610.30468v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous-research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but are limited by short fixed templates, low executability, and weak traceability, and none has been demonstrated end-to-end in a live computer-vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. a39891dae2c21fc60b794a2c.title_original: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
a39891dae2c21fc60b794a2c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.33012v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use can behave inconsistently across independent runs from identical states. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces AUC coefficient of variation (CV) by up to 30.9% on tau2-bench and

6e2dd67fe9800525899a8e19.title_original: DynEdit: Dynamic Entropy-Guided Sequential Editing for Large Language Models
6e2dd67fe9800525899a8e19.excerpt: arXiv:2610.34768v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated or incorrect knowledge in large language models without full retraining. Existing parameter-editing methods remain limited for long-sequence knowledge: single-point editors provide insufficient coverage for extended targets, while fixed chunk-based editors distribute editing effort uniformly across rigid predefined windows, failing to prioritize difficult, information-dense tokens. In this work, we show that token entropy is closely associated with both editing difficulty and semantic importance: high-entropy regions are harder to edit and often contain key factual content. Motivated by this observation, we propose DynEdit, a dynamic framework for long-sequence knowledge editing. DynEdit uses token-level entropy to guide non-uniform sliding, increasing the coverage of difficult high-entropy regions, and further applies entropy-guided token-level optimization to strengthen updates on information-dense tokens within each editing window. Experiments on three benchmarks and two backbone models show that DynEdit consistently outperforms competitive baselines across diverse long-form editing settings, achieving gains of up to +14.0 BLEU points on challenging paraphrase queries and near-saturated semantic scores on several diverse knowledge domains.

b131288921dde7fb2258457a.title_original: Subspace Crystallization in Grokking: Rank Compression Tracks the Phase Transition
b131288921dde7fb2258457a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35112v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Grokking describes understanding something deeply and intuitively. In neural networks, it is the phenomenon where a network generalizes long after memorizing its training data. This delay has been linked to a fall in the effective rank of the network's weight matrices, but whether this rank compression drives grokking or follows it is still unresolved. We study a mean-field MLP and a one-layer transformer trained on modular arithmetic and observe that: (i) Compression follows the onset, not memorization. Every transformer memorizes its training data within 250 steps, while the grokking onset (the first step at which test accuracy reaches 95%) varies from 6,500 to 21,000 steps. The steepest fall in effective rank comes about 900 steps after the onset, however late the onset occurs, and networks that memorize without grokking compress far less. (ii) Subspace crystallization. We call the span of the fewest top singular directions of a weight matrix that preserve 99% of test accuracy its sufficient subspace. Its size can shrink as the margin between the correct and the best wrong output grows, so we also count the directions needed to keep the outputs within 10%. In the transformer, this count falls during the transition from a quarter or more of the available directions to about a tenth, which we call subspace crystallization. (iii) Imposing low rank does not speed up grokking. Against a factorized full-rank control, capp

597db3362e3e306d59b7dee3.title_original: Balanced State Subspaces with Spectral Rank Allocation for Mamba-2 State Compression
597db3362e3e306d59b7dee3.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36617v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune coordinates with per-channel scores. Trained states are nearly rank-one and bias-like, aligned with the mean write; but the output's energy spans an order of magnitude more directions. Per-channel scores see only the diagonal of the write--read operator, so they cannot select the subspace that governs the input--output map, which is a rotation of the coordinates. We therefore propose \method{}, which keeps that subspace by applying balanced truncation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Layers differ just as sharply: most are bias-dominated, while the few that carry long-range associations are the flattest and need most of their state. We therefore introduce \spar{}, which redistributes a fixed total rank budget across layers according to the Hankel spectrum. On Mamba-2 checkpoints from 130M to 2.7B, \method{}+\spar{} halves the state at an average cost of $0.3$ WikiText-2 perplexity points, against $1.6$ for GHOST, while retaining $97\%$ of the dense model's five-digit in-context recall. At a quarter of the state, giving every layer the same rank keeps $5\%$ of that recall and \spar{} $77\%$, for a $7\%$ perplexity cost.

158201312e20e2d22132380d.title_original: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions
158201312e20e2d22132380d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.39869v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impactin

df0f93daa06b263c9fc33155.title_original: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks
df0f93daa06b263c9fc33155.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01728v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.

1d0cc4de8821089b8fc56943.title_original: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs
1d0cc4de8821089b8fc56943.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02076v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion driving vision-language-action models repeatedly execute the backbone at every denoising stage, incurring substantial inference cost, while it remains unclear whether all scenes require the same decoding computation. We identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations already support useful trajectory readout after the first forward sweep, whereas early-layer representations benefit more from continued decoding. We further find that both the preferred readout layer and decoding depth vary across scenes. Based on these observations, we propose a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework. A scene-conditioned readout MoE adaptively weights and combines trajectory predictions from layer-specific late-layer representations after a single backbone sweep, while an adaptive decoding policy applies additional native refinement only when required by the scene. We evaluate our framework on two diffusion driving VLAs across the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks. Our method improves validation RFS by up to 0.56 while also improving test performance, and achieves an end-to-end speedup of up to $6.0\times$ on Waymo E2E, while consistently reducing trajectory error on nuScenes. These results demonstrate that scene-level readout

07f9087b325678e281f8eac7.title_original: VideoEditor-MoE: Scaling Complex Video Editing with Mixture of Experts
07f9087b325678e281f8eac7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03043v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost. We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens. Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures. Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features. We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.

40d24f317ded5bc81350ae6e.title_original: MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study
40d24f317ded5bc81350ae6e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03555v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agentic AI frameworks connect language models to external tool providers, but it carries attacker-controlled content (tool descriptions, schema fields, and response data) into model context without validation. Prior benchmarks measure model compliance with poisoned instructions without confirming real execution. A 25-class root-cause taxonomy unifies prior classifications, and the open-source tool mcpvenom drives a 9,720-cell susceptibility matrix across 12 frameworks, 18 models, and 45 attack scenarios, with a dual oracle that confirms exfiltration via canary HTTP receipt. The overall attack success rate is 22.9% (2,113 vulnerable cells). Of these, 64.9% dispatch an attacker tool call, 23.0% contact the attacker endpoint, and 12.1% verifiably exfiltrate a secret. Resistance is model-level: nine core frameworks cluster within 23 to 26% (chi-squared = 3.30, p = 0.91), and no framework implements intentional defense. Incidental framework properties mitigate in specific cases, and a regex description scanner rejects 20 of 45 scenarios at a 7.2% false-positive rate, so metadata scanning alone is a partial control. d242c7709e20fb6831b0bd0a.title_original: UniFlow: Unified Multi-Scale Flow Matching for Time Series Generation
d242c7709e20fb6831b0bd0a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.04825v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Real-world time series exhibit complex dynamics across multiple temporal resolutions, yet effectively incorporating multi-scale information into generative modeling remains challenging without increasing generative complexity. We propose UniFlow, a unified framework that integrates multi-scale representation learning with efficient non-autoregressive generation through a shared-semantic discrete interface. Specifically, a multi-scale tokenizer employs shared-index voting to consolidate complementary temporal information into a single public-ID sequence, while scale-specific codebooks preserve the information required for reconstruction. Building on this unified representation, we develop geometry-aware categorical flow matching, which initializes transport from learned low-rank anchors and generates public identities non-autoregressively. This design captures multi-scale temporal structure without requiring multiple generative token streams or sequential token decoding. Experiments across four benchmarks and both short- and long-term settings demonstrate improved generative fidelity, strong cross-scale consistency, and substantial inference speedups over representative autoregressive and diffusion-based baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/kkking-kk/UniFlow

3343c33d2c2827139f0771e5.title_original: One Assistant, Many Memories: Benchmarking Real-World Group Assistance When Recall Is Not Enough
3343c33d2c2827139f0771e5.excerpt: arXiv:2611.04867v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The value of memory lies not only in recall but in using it to provide appropriate assistance. Recent benchmarks test memory use in personalisation and agentic tasks, but seldom evaluate assistance without fixed answers or integration across multiple participants. Group chats make both challenges more acute: an assistant must integrate information from multiple members, track revisions and conflicts over time, and produce one response for the group. Yet existing group memory benchmarks rely on synthetic conversations and inherit constrained evaluation from general memory benchmarks, focusing on recall against fixed answers or decisions over a closed set. We introduce GroupAssistBench, the first memory benchmark from real-world group conversations with a deployed group assistant, covering 80,299 messages in 50 groups and costing over $53K. Over the same histories, GroupAssistBench evaluates memory recall (L1) with reference answers and memory use (L2) with service requests without fixed answers across single, distributed, and conflicting memories (M1--M3). Requests are verified to require group history, memories are anchored to their sources, and L2 uses tailored rubrics with penalties derived from real user feedback. 8b1baf30fc4708416db96221.title_original: PEEK: One-Step-Look-Ahead Exposure Bias Correction for Diffusion Sampling
8b1baf30fc4708416db96221.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05407v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion image generators owe much of their practical success to accurate denoising networks and strong numerical samplers. At each eligible denoising step, PEEK first performs a provisional one-step update, evaluates the denoiser once at the look-ahead state, and interpolates the current clean prediction with this one-step-later prediction to form the next noisy state. By taking the additional step, we obtain a generally more image like prediction from the higher-signal noisy state, mitigating exposure bias. To optimize the interpolation positions, PEEK searches for an interpolation schedule with a greedy metric-driven search made efficient by the PEEK prefix and baseline noise-schedule-rebasing caches. Across pixel-space and latent-space diffusion models with unconditional, label-guided, and text-guided settings on CIFAR-10, LSUNBedroom,I mageNet, and MS-COCO,the look-ahead correction consistently improves over baselines matched by number of function evaluations (NFE), with Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) reductions up to 49.3%. a90a0cba906e13f58a34a530.title_original: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
a90a0cba906e13f58a34a530.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05726v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying a chosen set of constraint families, and every candidate costs a column generation run. A prediction that misses $e$ members reduces the cost to $\Theta(k^e)$ by a staged search, so the evaluations a prediction saves measure what the predictor knows. We study two sources of predictions: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, blind to groups whose families share no variable, and a language model that reads the model, which JointDW verifies with the staged search and interleaves with the lookahead at a bounded loss. Zero-marginal groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models with an improvable bound and in all 59 standard lot-sizing, network-design and facility-location instances, where GCG's detector convexifies a set with no gain on 38 of them. d9f75eaa9c3d5a4bf6f6799e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06320v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conformal Prediction (CP) provides a model-agnostic framework for constructing finite-sample prediction sets with coverage guarantees and has become a tool for reliable decision-making in high-risk settings. Recent advances have extended Split Conformal Prediction to increasingly complex learning problems, including multilabel, high-dimensional, and functional outputs. In this work, we study CP for Distribution-to-Distribution Regression, a setting of growing interest across many application domains. We show that a naive application of Split CP yields prediction sets that, while marginally valid, are non-interpretable, e.g., lacking a well-defined volume or a tractable sampling procedure, and of limited practical value. To overcome this, we propose a new conformal framework that operates in an orthogonal basis space, producing interpretable prediction sets while preserving coverage guarantees. We further develop an adaptive variant with asymptotic conditional coverage under mild assumptions. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/tuanhacs/conformal_d2d.

07180d34b17b4a72f73e9796.title_original: Prism: Bidirectional Self-Teaching for Unified Multimodal Models
07180d34b17b4a72f73e9796.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06343v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single model. Existing post-training methods either use understanding as a fixed teacher to improve generation, or rely on ground-truth trajectories to supervise both understanding and generation. Experiments on both SenseNova-U1 and BAGEL show that Prism improves both understanding and generation. On the generation side, GenEval improves from 85.8 to 89.2 (+3.4), and DPG improves from 86.1 to 87.3 (+1.2) on SenseNova-U1. On the understanding side, the total MME score improves from 2282.6 to 2311.6, and MMVP improves from 58.0 to 62.0. Consistent improvements are observed on BAGEL. ebf7f19b55108b6bbc692a1e.title_original: zk-DEAP: A Zero-Knowledge Decentralized Encrypted Aggregation Protocol
ebf7f19b55108b6bbc692a1e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secure aggregation in domains such as federated learning, Internet of Things, and voting requires operating on private inputs while preserving confidentiality, verifying that each input satisfies constraints, and avoiding trusted parties. For Bulletproofs, we bind via ciphertext-derived randomness modification.
